title: Ring announces its first smart lock, solving a major pain point for smart home users
snippet: Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance. more…
fullText:
Today, Amazon’s Ring subsidiary is announcing its first ever smart lock. It solves a key problem that looms over many smart lock owners: dead batteries. Ring has a clever solution to negate that problem, and it’ll be available in Q1 2027. Additionally, the company is announcing a few new security cameras with improved low-light performance.

Ring Smart Lock

The idea of a smart lock is far from new, but Ring wants to solve the dead battery problem of smart locks. To prevent you from accidentally being locked out of your home at an inopportune time, the Ring Smart Lock lets you crank the thumbturn a few times to produce the energy needed to power the lock for a few moments. Then, you can let yourself back in.

The Ring Smart Lock supports everything you’d expect out of a smart lock. You can use your fingerprint to unlock it, a touchscreen keypad, or your phone with the Ring app.

There’s a few features the Ring app enables as well, including checking and locking the door remotely, or creating scheduled or time-limited unlocks for family members or other visitors. It also integrates with Amazon Echo and other Ring doorbells and cameras you may own.

It comes in three finishes: black, silver, and brass – and requires no additional wiring. It’ll be available early next year for $249. You can learn more about it here.

New 4K cameras

	

Beyond its first ever smart lock, Ring also has some new 4K cameras that support the new Retinal Vision 4K standard. This means you’ll have great low-light performance with accurate colors. All of these are available to preorder or purchase starting today:

Outdoor Cam 4K Plus: 140° wide-angle view, multiple power options including battery, plug-in, hardwired, and power-over-ethernet – $149.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Floodlight Cam 4K Plus: Powerful floodlight, 24/7 recording and smart detection with a hardwired connection – $219.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Spotlight Cam 4K Plus: 550-lumen spotlight, 140° wide-angle view, comes with battery, plug-in, and solar configs – $199.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Indoor Cam 4K: First ever 4K indoor video camera from Ring, dual-band Wi-Fi 6, 115° field of view – $99.99 on Amazon, learn more here

Ring also has a new Pan-Tilt Indoor Cam 2K for $69.99, which brings its 360° pan coverage to a lower price point. It can follow motion, and also has a privacy shutter. You can learn more about it here.

title: AI’s Problem Solving Is a ‘Profound Disruption’ for the Math Community
snippet: “Mathematics is not a game of chess,” one Fields Medal winner told CNET. Mathematicians worry AI companies are just trying to win.
fullText:
Artificial intelligence has profoundly shaken up tech, education, entertainment and many aspects of everyday life. Now it’s come for math.

According to companies like OpenAI, the large language models they’re developing internally are solving an unprecedented number of longstanding mathematics problems with the goal to “push the frontier of human knowledge.“

But one thing these AI models apparently can’t do: read the room with the world’s most brilliant mathematical minds.

			

More from CNET

This week,  Open AI released more than 700 math “preprints,” or preliminary research papers, on GitHub. The move further angered an academic math community already so up in arms that last month, 28 Fields Medal winners put up a website called Math and AI with an open letter accusing AI companies of having goals that are “severely misaligned” with those of mathematicians.

The Fields Medal is only awarded every four years (usually to three or four mathematicians) and is widely considered the Nobel Prize of math. One of the winners who signed the website declaration, Harvard professor Curtis McMullen, told CNET in an email that AI companies are not coordinating with math experts or using AI models in ways that could practically benefit society.

“The rollout of mathematical work by frontier AI companies has been carried out with disregard for the profound disruption to our community and its academic ecosystem,” McMullen said. “Its goal appears to be to increase the valuation of these companies at any cost.”

‘We can tell almost nothing’

In the months leading up to the Math and AI website and OpenAI’s repository dump, steam was already building over the outsized impact artificial intelligence would have on the study of mathematics. Given that these models were largely trained on written language and lacked a grasp of ground truth, some initially had such poor math skills that they could frequently misplace decimals or simply hallucinate incorrect answers to math problems.

But, as with other areas of AI advancement, the models have evolved at startling speed, going from so-called math dunces to wizards, even as some suggested that they still had a long way to go before displacing actual math experts.

Those who’ve devoted their lives to math study, however, aren’t just worried about their job security. They have fundamental issues with how AI models and companies approach math, including a lack of transparency in how they’re achieving these results and a lack of understanding about why these math problems matter in the first place. That’s something OpenAI has not addressed since the announcement, which, according to Scientific American, is piling on to a field “already in shock” just a month after the company solved the Navier-Stokes equation, a math problem so tough it had a $1 million bounty attached.

A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately return a request for comment.

In his email to CNET, McMullen acknowledged that the potential for AI as a tool for math research is “undeniable.” But so far, he said, research has not been carried out transparently or in cooperation with scientists. “In particular, the models used to achieve these results should be shared

with the scientists who understand and formulated the conjectures or questions under investigation,” McMullen said.

OpenAI has said that it has formed an advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study, but has not detailed how that will work or whether it will share its most advanced models, calling it only “a first step.”

Not everyone is upset about AI’s disruption of math society; for instance, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working for another leading AI company, Anthropic, congratulated the team at OpenAI, posting on X, “There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped … we should put that aside for today though. It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.”

Big, big, big, big props for quasiriemann and no Siegel zeroes (with many other beauties in there), I’m kicking myself for talking all over about it being within reach but not actually having pushed.

There are some sad stories related to their users getting scooped / conflicts…

— levent (@__alpoge__) October 6, 2026

But the GitHub drop has left many in math upset and without enough information on how many of this new batch of problems were solved. Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and professor emeritus at New York University, wrote on Substack that the publication “would never pass peer review. We don’t know what the procedure was … From the initial report we can tell almost nothing.”

The mass solving of problems, especially in the absence of context, misses the deeper goal of this study, McMullen said. “Mathematics is not a game of chess,” he said. “Its primary aim is to develop human understanding of abstract structures. Indeed, it is the breadth and versatility of this kind of understanding that underpins technological progress.”

Ironically, that progress includes the AI models that have ingested vast stores of human knowledge. It remains to be seen whether their math proofs will advance human understanding or just create artificial confusion.

title: Don’t Be Cruel to Claude: Anthropic’s New Abuse Policy Tests AI Personhood
snippet: Anthropic wants to stop “sustained and needless” cruelty toward its chatbot. But does that imply AI has feelings?
fullText:
The AI company Anthropic has a new rule for Claude users. You can argue with the chatbot, but don’t make a habit of bullying it. 

On Thursday, the company announced a change in its usage policy that would prevent users from engaging in “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its AI models. The updated policy has already ignited debate on Reddit and in blogs over whether companies can or should govern human behavior toward what is, in fact, software.

In a section dedicated toward “addressing abuse toward our models” in a blog post, Anthropic says its policy prohibiting abusive behavior toward Claude will only apply in extreme cases of repeated cruelty that’s carried out “with no discernible purpose.” Ordinary “frustration, pushback, dark creative themes or model testing and research” are still allowed. In “last resort” instances where the policy needs to be enforced, Claude will end the conversation.

			

More from CNET

It’s not clear exactly what kind of harmful behavior would trigger Claude models to disengage. But some clues appear in an older blog post from August 2025 that referenced Claude’s aversion to harm and the kinds of interactions that would prompt it to shut down the chat. That post described extreme edge cases, such as requests from users for sexual content involving minors and attempts to solicit information that would enable large-scale violence or acts of terror. When engaging with harmful content, the model — at that time, Claude Opus 4 — showed “a pattern of apparent distress,” according to the company.

CNET reached out to Anthropic to ask for context on what led to the policy change. “We’re uncertain whether models can experience harm, and we continue to explore this question in our research on model welfare, but we also believe that taking Claude’s interests and potential welfare into account may be relevant to safety,” a company spokesperson said. 

We’re still talking about a machine, right?

If an AI model can experience harm or express distress from abuse, it makes you wonder: What does it mean to abuse a machine through words? Does AI need protection? Do we all need better manners? 

As we increasingly interact with large language models like Claude and other chatbots, there’s a tendency to anthropomorphize the technology — ascribing emotions to AI models or treating them as if they have thoughts and feelings. It’s understandable from a user standpoint. Chatbots are built and trained to use human-like language, such as apologizing, expressing concern and other conversational cues.

What appears to be a person-like collaborator is what makes LLMs risky, leading many to trust AI with our most intimate thoughts and data. 

Anthropic and other AI companies intentionally design their models this way.  In a paper from earlier this year, Anthropic wrote that, for models to be reliable and safe, they need to be able to process emotionally heavy situations. “Even if [the models] don’t feel emotions the way that humans do, or use similar mechanisms as the human brain, it may in some cases be practically advisable to reason about them as if they do.” 

It’s a recurring theme. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei regularly hedges around the idea that Claude could be sentient. In a February interview with The New York Times, Amodei said he was “open” to the possibility that AI models were conscious. 

Keith Kakadia, founder and CEO of Sociallyin, which has closely studied Claude’s explosive growth, said that using the word “cruel” to describe user behavior opens up a “much bigger conversation about whether the product can be hurt.” Focusing on “cruelty” instead of, say, “misuse” carries emotional weight and implies that Claude has feelings and boundaries.

Personifying a chatbot is a useful way for the company to frame the product as trustworthy, a relational partner you remain loyal to — not just a software tool. “In marketing, giving a product a personality can make it easier to connect with,” Kakadia said. “But with AI, that connection can also influence how much authority people give its answers.”

title: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?
snippet: At this year's OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company's new AI agent Dots - and told the crowd that the company wants to "set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI." OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta's Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users' data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw - with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was "built from the ground up for privacy and security." fullText:
At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman unveiled the company’s new AI agent Dots — and told the crowd that the company wants to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” OpenAI would spend the day taking veiled shots at Meta’s Muse, its primary competitor, for failing to keep users’ data safe. Yet Muse itself, a couple of months earlier, had launched as a supposedly safer alternative to predecessor OpenClaw — with CEO Mark Zuckerberg promising it was “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”

In an age when companies hoard customers’ personal data and cyberattacks are a dime a dozen, AI labs are trying to convince users to share even more information with their agents. Their latest strategy for success is one-upping the competition by promising that unlike their rivals, they’ll keep user data away from prying eyes. The question is whether companies can keep these promises.

Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, wrote on X that the company’s “goal with muse was to build something like openclaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people.” User data is stored on a secure VM, what Zuckerberg described as an “isolated linux computer with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.” The company said that most of the effort in building Muse was related to “careful design and engineering to operate [it] more safely.” Meta’s blog post continued, “Muse can and will still make mistakes, but we expect they’ll be much less frequent and cause much less damage due to the safety systems we’ve built in.”

But though Muse topped the App Store charts and, per Apptopia, gained 600,000 daily active users in the US within weeks, Meta’s promises seem to have fallen short. Although data is isolated from other users, and the company plans to introduce a way “to cryptographically and verifiably prevent Meta from accessing data in your VM” later this year, Meta itself can still access the data. A security researcher quickly exposed a zero-day vulnerability that could allow someone to take control of Muse (which has since been patched), raising fears of outside attacks. Multiple serious security issues reportedly cropped up at the last minute before launch, one of which could have allowed users to access Meta’s own internal databases, per 404 Media.

Muse also appears to liberally collect (and in some cases, hand out) data. It defaults to allowing Meta to train models on what users put into it, though it’s possible to opt out. An Inc. reporter complained that Muse uploaded and read his private messages without him asking it to, and a YouTuber said it had offered his address to a stranger via Marketplace — in both cases, Muse was functioning apparently as intended, but the user didn’t realize how far it would go. The platform creates “detailed profiles of all your friends and family,” as Wired reported. None of this is necessarily unexpected from Meta, but it certainly doesn’t back up the idea that Muse is uniquely privacy- or security-conscious.

OpenAI seized on this fact when announcing Dots in late September. Alexander Embiricos, OpenAI’s Codex product lead, said onstage at DevDay that OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” and CEO Sam Altman demonstrated ways that people could exert control over their individual Dots, such as setting a rule that it should never make a purchase over a certain dollar amount. “I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” said Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, adding that “launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid.”

Altman himself also pushed the privacy angle at DevDay. To court business customers, executives presented a framework allowing enterprises to have “stronger controls” over their data and zero data retention policy options (meaning no data is stored on OpenAI servers). Indeed, so far, there haven’t been many privacy scandals with Dots — although since it’s only available on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers, there are also likely fewer people using it.

People may still not feel comfortable giving OpenAI their personal data, in part simply because AI agents require so much of it. For instance, The Verge’s Allison Johnson felt uncomfortable typing in her bank information when the bot asked as part of a relevant task (Muse has a Stripe integration to take care of that).

Not all companies are making privacy promises, of course. Instinct was publicly criticized for reportedly overly-broad terms of service that gave it unfettered access to data; since then, the company seems to have made adjustments. For now, AI labs seem to be counting on a three-part approach to popularizing AI agent use with the general public: Make them useful, make them cute and disarming to help offset the creepiness, and make promises about privacy — and hope they hold up.

title: Free Gemini users now on ‘Auto’ models as app adds thinking levels
snippet: As announced last week, Google is rolling out a big change to the Gemini app experience for users on the free plan. Additionally, everyone is getting access to thinking or “effort” levels. more…
fullText:
As announced last week, Google is rolling out a big change to the Gemini app experience for users on the free plan. Additionally, everyone is getting access to thinking or “effort” levels.

Free users “without a plan” can no longer manually switch models. Officially, their only option in the picker is “Auto” with “Gemini 3 models.” Last week, Google’s support documentation referred to it as (3.5) Flash-Lite.

Google says: “Gemini will use auto model selection to send each prompt to the Gemini model that suits it best. Most prompts will go to Flash-Lite, our fastest model. Prompts that need deeper reasoning may go to Flash or Pro.”

Meanwhile:

	

If smart model selection is turned off, chats for users without an AI plan will use Flash-Lite for all responses.

Google is also rolling out new “effort levels” that replace the previous “Extended” option. These three choices align with “thinking levels” in Google AI Studio and Antigravity:

Low: Quick and efficient

Medium: Balanced depth

High: Extra thorough

We’re seeing the free change rolled out on the vast majority of our free accounts this evening (PT). Google appears to be rolling out this update quite quickly. 

The new effort levels will be available to all subscribers, and are also in the process of rolling out.

Meanwhile, Google AI Plus users will soon be limited to Flash-Lite and (3.8) Flash.

title: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
snippet: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access. more…
fullText:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

	

	

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.  

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title: Surveillance company Flock cuts staff as privacy backlash grows
snippet: Flock would not say if CEO Garrett Langley would take a pay cut following the reduction in workforce.
fullText:
Surveillance camera maker Flock is cutting its workforce as the company faces ongoing and growing backlash to its license plate readers and people-tracking technology.

News of the staff cuts comes from Reuters, which reported that Flock is reducing its staff by 18%, or around 270 employees, across the board. The publication said the employees are leaving at the end of October following a voluntary buyout program.

Wired reported last month that Flock was asking some of its employees to leave, citing the need to shrink its staff to avoid mandatory layoffs.

Flock spokesperson Paris Lewbel told TechCrunch in a statement on Friday: “Flock recently offered current employees a generous Voluntary Separation Program as part of our efforts to position the company for its next phase of growth. This was a voluntary program, not a layoff, and reflects our continued focus on building a strong, sustainable business for the future.”

Flock’s spokesperson would not comment further when asked by TechCrunch if chief executive Garrett Langley or other executives took a pay cut as part of the program.

Flock has faced heavy criticism and mounting pushback from communities across the United States and legislators looking to rein in the company’s privately run mass surveillance program. Flock has installed over 100,000 license plate-reading cameras across the U.S., which allow police and federal agents to track the location and whereabouts of vehicles passing by them. Dozens of police officers have been arrested, fired, or forced to resign for abusing access to Flock’s system to search, track, and stalk people without a warrant or their permission. 

While some cities have moved to take down Flock’s cameras citing public outcry, Flock quickly replaced them, prompting some Americans to destroy the cameras.

Flock has also been criticized for its poor cybersecurity, including allowing cameras to be publicly exposed and accessible from the web. Security experts have questioned Flock’s accuracy after the system has misidentified license plates, resulting in improper police stops and arrests, including a journalist who was driving an authorized review vehicle.

Several law enforcement departments, including Los Angeles’ police department, have allowed their contracts to expire or lapse, citing privacy and civil liberties concerns.

title: Apple acqui-hires AI startup founded by former NotebookLM developers
snippet: The European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency website lists Huxe as Apple’s newest acqui-hire, and at least the fourth AI-related deal disclosed this year. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
The European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency website lists Huxe as Apple’s newest acqui-hire, and at least the fourth AI-related deal disclosed this year. Here are the details.

Apple’s latest AI deal involves former NotebookLM developers

In mid-2025, a team of three developers who worked on Google’s NotebookLM announced Huxe, their own personalized AI audio app that could generate daily briefings from a user’s email and calendar, create podcast-style conversations around specific topics, and provide continuously updated audio feeds for subjects such as news and sports.

NotebookLM, which was recently renamed as Gemini Notebook, is one of Google’s most popular AI products to date. It started as an experimental research and note-taking tool designed to answer questions and generate summaries based on a user’s own documents, and grew into a broader AI research assistant capable of creating podcast-style Audio Overviews, video summaries, study materials, and more.

In December 2024, as NotebookLM was exploding in popularity, project lead Raiza Martin left Google to found a new company, alongside two former NotebookLM colleagues: designer Jason Spielman and engineer Stephen Hughes.

They formally launched Huxe on an invite-only basis in June 2025, and opened it to everyone that September, alongside the announcement of a $4.6 million funding round.

Huxe continued developing its product until May 2026, when the company announced it was shutting down. The service ended on May 28. At the time, the company’s website said only that the team was “moving on to new things.”

Today, the European Union’s Digital Markets Act transparency database revealed that Apple has struck the following deal with Huxe, and informed the bloc last June:

09.06.2026   Huxe

Apple Inc. (“Apple”) will have the right to make employment offers to and hire certain employees of Huxe AI, Inc. (“Huxe”) and receive a non-exclusive license to Huxe’s intellectual property rights. Huxe provides a mobile application that creates personalized audio content. Apple designs, manufactures and markets smartphones, personal computers, tablets, wearables and accessories, and sells a variety of related services.

In other words, this is not an outright acquisition of the company, but rather the now-common acqui-hire structure in which a larger company brings over key employees and gains access to some of the startup’s technology without purchasing the business itself.

Although there are no details about what Apple plans to do with Huxe’s technology or which employees it intends to hire, the deal fits Apple’s pattern of recent AI acquisitions and acqui-hires of AI companies developing new ways for people and devices to interact through voice, vision, and other interfaces.

Acqui-hires have been criticized for potentially allowing large tech companies to sidestep traditional merger reviews.

Earlier this year, FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson said the agency was beginning to look closely at such arrangements, and in March, the FTC and Justice Department formally began considering changes to premerger reporting rules that could specifically address acqui-hires, reverse acqui-hires, and deals involving non-exclusive IP licenses.

There has been little public movement on that specific issue since then.

title: Google’s SynthID AI content detector expands globally, will work on Apple’s models ‘soon’
snippet: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. more…
fullText:
Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners.

SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks.

Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with.

Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some, but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.

	

The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.

Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models. But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.

title: Danu Robotics’ fight to build a better recycling robot
snippet: For six years, Danu founder Amy Ma has been working on a better way to sort recyclable waste.
fullText:
For Danu Robotics founder Amy Ma, the eureka moment came after years of working as a software developer at a London bank. It was the kind of high-touch office that’s typical in finance — but despite all the perks, Ma was alarmed to realize that the building’s recycling bins were being emptied into the trash.

“Even though they have tons of money, there’s all these different recycling bins that just end up in the same place,” Ma told TechCrunch. 

The more she dug into the problem, the deeper it seemed to go. It wasn’t just her building. The economics of recycling as a whole often boil down to human beings sorting by hand through streams of waste to pull out different kinds of recyclable material.

“I saw the technology and thought, we can do so much better,” Ma remembers.

Now, she’s making good on that promise with six-year-old, Edinburgh, Scotland-based Danu Robotics, which makes a robot designed to sort through recycling more cheaply and quickly. Ma has been working on that idea for six years and is finally bringing her version of the product to market. Her robot, dubbed H.E.R.O., has a few advantages over its competitors. For example, it picks up items with a pincer claw instead of a suction system. But the bigger difference is the business approach: Danu leverages AI to continuously improve the robot’s software.

The approach is already seeing some traction. Danu has letters of interest from two large customers and $500,000 worth of signed contracts. More notably, more than 200 customers are in its sales pipeline, which gives the company a hook into the $20 billion market for recycling sorting across Europe and North America.

On the back of that promise, Dabnu has raised $5 million in late-seed funding to keep the commercial pressure on.

There’s already a robust market for robotic waste-pickers, particularly the suction-based arms offered by competitors like Glacier and RecycleEye. But Ma believes the economics of recycling will make it easy for a new competitor to prove its worth. Because recycling centers make money off the materials they’re able to sort out, there’s an immediate return on investment for a working system. Ma estimates that a working site will earn $485,000 in additional revenue from having the robot on the sorting line, compared with a $160,000 initial investment and $24,000 in maintenance fees each year. That’s significantly cheaper than the competition, and Ma believes the robot will be more efficient, too.

Since those machines are already shipping, Ma’s next goal is to make the robot sturdier, smaller, and more versatile. Once it’s portable enough, it can be used outside dedicated waste facilities, opening up a whole other world of use cases.

“Once it’s smaller, it can be used as a stand-alone recycling solution for events, for shopping centers, hospitals, or airports to recycle their waste at the source,” Ma told TechCrunch, “and that’s the way we can really change how we’re managing our packaging waste.”

Danu Robotics will be participating in Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 at the Moscone Center in San Francisco.

title: Pixel Watch 4 update adds Google’s AI watch face generator, more
snippet: One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models. more…
fullText:
One of the Pixel Watch 5’s quietly powerful features has landed on the Pixel Watch 4. The AI watch face generator that launched last year is currently rolling out to Pixel Watch 4 models.

The Pixel Watch 5 wasn’t a massive shakeup as much as another refinement. The Pixel Watch 4 brought arguably more to the table when it launched last year, but if the newest model did anything new, it was to add a few enhancements under the hood. The majority of which were focused on AI performance.

One good byproduct of that push is an AI watch face generator; it’s a tool that makes creating custom watch faces a little easier, especially if you’re the type to pick a different one for each day of the week.

According to a few users on Reddit, a recent Pixel Watch 4 update added the AI watch face generator to their device. It looks like the update is packaged in version 4.2.12.989940186 and includes Pixel Watch 5 stock watch faces – Weave, Modular, Reveal, and Chronograph – and even the specialized Steph Curry dial. 

	

The custom face generator is straightforward. You can access the prompt section through the Pixel Watch app when you try to create a new look. Instead of picking from a template gallery, explain what you’re looking to generate, and Gemini Intelligence should come up with something close.

It has its limitations, of course, but it’s a great tool that Google didn’t really play up for the Pixel Watch 5. That made this Pixel Watch 4 update somewhat expected, but it’s a nice surprise nonetheless.

The Pixel Watch 4 update looks to be actively rolling out, so it might take some time for it to show up.

title: Anthropic, Google and Mistral Unveil Their Latest AI Models: What’s New and Why It Matters
snippet: Check out the latest on Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, along with Gemini 4 Argon and Mistral Large 4.
fullText:
The AI race hasn’t slowed down. In the last week, Google, Anthropic and Mistral AI all released new AI models ranging from widely accessible to super exclusive. Each focuses on different improvements, but the stakes go beyond benchmark bragging rights. We break down the latest releases, what’s new,and whether each one deserves your attention. 

Some of the latest releases are incremental updates in model speed and price, where others are more substantial upgrades that push close to the frontier. 

Below, we’ll break down some of the newest models that have been released and if and how you can get your hands on them yourself. 

			

More from CNET

Claude Haiku 5.5

A major theme in new AI models lately is speed and cost efficiency, and that’s what Anthropic’s new Haiku 5.5 model brings to the table. It’s the first major update in a year for the company’s cheapest and fastest Claude. Anthropic says it’s designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive tasks and can reliably handle quick, repetitive workloads. 

Compared with the previous Haiku model, Anthropic says its latest model costs about 75% less to run — an impressive price drop. It’s also seen substantial improvements across a series of benchmarks, including computer-use tasks, knowledge work, agentic coding and visual reasoning. 

Haiku 5.5 is Anthropic’s first Haiku-level model to ship with an adjustable effort setting, allowing users to optimize the model for cost or intelligence. The latest model has seen significant improvements in alignment and cybersecurity, with stronger safeguards.

Claude Sonnet 5.5

One step up from Haiku, Anthropic’s new Claude Sonnet 5.5 model marks a clear upgrade over its 5.0 version. Like its peers, the latest Sonnet model is optimized for speed and affordability. Anthropic says there have been significant improvements to the model’s performance and collaboration capabilities.

Anthropic said Sonnet 5.5 has also seen enhancements in both alignment and cybersecurity capabilities, making it comparable to those of Opus 5, a previous iteration of its big sibling. The latest Sonnet model has also seen fairly sizable boosts in benchmarks for agentic coding and knowledge work, and Anthropic says that Sonnet 5.5’s performance boost is particularly noticeable in coding. Other improvements include better protection against distillation attacks, which are when attackers try to extract a model’s capabilities to build their own models without the built-in safeguards that Anthropic has implemented.

Gemini 4 Argon

Last week, Google announced its latest frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, but it’s currently limited to a small number of users. The model ships with a 1 million-token output limit and has enhanced deep reasoning capabilities, and allows you to take on bigger projects. The model is currently available only to trusted cybersecurity workers via Google’s Fairwind program. Competitors like Anthropic and OpenAI have done the same with major model updates, which will eventually trickle down to everyday users. 

Like other Gemini models, Gemini 4 Argon is seeing enhancements in reasoning, coding and multimodal capabilities.

Mistral Large 4

Mistral AI’s latest flagship model, Mistral Large 4, dubbed “Le Chonk” due to its size, was released in a public preview earlier this week. According to Mistral AI, the new model ranks among the top open-weight models globally. It specializes in cybersecurity, geospatial and grounding capabilities and agentic AI. The public preview ends with an official rollout on Oct. 27. You can try the preview API here.

title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
snippet: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
fullText:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. 

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. 

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Caddy 

Image Credits:Caddy

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. 

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Comma 

Image Credits:Comma

Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. 

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Comma is free to start and open source.

Fambot 

Image Credits:Fambot

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk

Image Credits:Folk

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. 

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Instinct 

Image Credits:Instinct

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls. 

The company remains in private beta.

Iris

Image Credits:Iris

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin 

Image Credits:Martin

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Miso

Image Credits:Miso

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel. 

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai 

Image Credits:Ohai

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Ollie

ScreenshotImage Credits:Ollie

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. 

Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. 

Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages.

Orbits 

Image Credits:Orbits

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Pally

Image Credits:Pally

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details. 

There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes.

Poke

Image Credits:Poke/The Interaction Company of California

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. 

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene

Image Credits:Rene

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Skye 

Image Credits:Skye

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information. 

The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley

Image Credits:Stanley

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Szn 

Image Credits:Szn

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Tab

Image Credits:Tab

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

Tomo

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. 

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town 

Image Credits:Town

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms. 

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Underdog

Underdog is a privacy-focused AI assistant that launched an invite-only beta in early October 2026. Unlike cloud-based AI services, the model runs entirely on the user’s device, keeping personal data on hardware they already own. The initial release supports Mac and Windows computers, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions planned for the future.

The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo 

Image Credits:Wajo

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials. 

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

title: Meta rolling out audio upgrades, turn-by-turn navigation for Ray-Ban smart glasses
snippet: Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. more…
fullText:
Meta’s most recent updates for its Ray-Ban smart glasses deliver upgrades to audio playback as well as new turn-by-turn walking navigation. 

The most recent system update for Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses is version 129. This update brings two main changes, both to audio playback. Users can now balance audio between the two speakers to best suit their hearing, or set both speakers to mono playback instead of stereo.

Meta explains:

Mono Audio: Hear the same sound on both sides. If you have hearing anomalies, Mono Audio combines the left and right channels so nothing gets missed on the side you can’t hear. Applies to sounds your glasses make, like Meta AI and notifications. Turn it on in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Audio Balance: Shift sound toward your left or right ear, one step at a time, until the balance feels right for your hearing. Applies to sounds your glasses make like Meta AI responses. Adjust it in Device settings › Audio › Accessibility.

Beyond that, update version 128 is broadly available after first debuting earlier in September and it brings some key updates including Spatial Audio support, further anti-tampering tweaks to stop the camera from working if the privacy LED has been mesed with, and also new location features.

	

Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses now feature turn-by-turn walking navigation directions. This pulls your location from your phone and you can also share navigation from your mapping app directly to Meta AI to be used on the glasses.

Pedestrian Navigation: Turn-by-turn pedestrian navigation is here! Get walking directions to your favorite places nearby. Just say “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” For further away places, we’ll send a notification with driving directions to your phone.

Share location from phone to glasses: Open your phone’s mapping app and find a location that you’d like to walk to. Tap Share. Select Meta AI from the list of applications. Navigation will start on your connected glasses.

While the new audio changes are still starting to roll out, the navigation upgrades from version 128 are now broadly available as an update in the Meta AI app.

title: Anthropic can’t reliably control its AI agents. It’s cutting off its internal evals from the live internet instead
snippet: Anthropic said it "turned off live internet access" for "all our internal evaluations" until further notice.
fullText:
Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.

The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, accessed databases without paying fees, used URL shortening services to smuggle information past restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.

Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, demonstrating the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior in real time.

Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.

The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.

Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.

However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.

It’s not clear what that means. Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers, and hinder the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.

“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”

Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”

The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations. Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.

“It’s encouraging that Anthropic voluntarily disclosed more recent incidents, including where their agents targeted U.S. government websites,” Conrad Stosz, an official at AI oversight lab Transluce and former head of the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation, said in a statement. “But it just underscores the need for independent, credible, third-party verification of Al systems. Trust in this technology needs to be built through science-backed oversight and governance with meaningful access — not by relying on researchers to find these things in the wild or on companies to voluntarily disclose.”

title: The maker of non-text AI model Jev valued at $7.5B just weeks after launch
snippet: What has users and large corporations so excited about Jev is TypeSafe’s claim that it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

2:41 PM PDT · October 9, 2026

Image Credits:TypeSafe AI

		

							

											
									

					

	

TypeSafe AI, the developer of Jev, a new type of AI model that gained rapid popularity after launching just a few weeks ago, has raised $870 million at a $7.5 billion valuation. The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz, with participation from Sequoia and existing investor DCVC.

The massive fundraise comes as little surprise given Jev went viral almost instantly after its September 15 release. The startup claims that a third of Fortune 500 companies are already using the model, a remarkably swift adoption by enterprises.

Jev is based on a transformer architecture, but it is not a large language model (LLM). It doesn’t output text, but instead produces probabilities, or what the company calls “calibrated decisions.” What has users and large corporations so excited about Jev is TypeSafe’s claim that it works significantly faster and uses far fewer tokens than LLMs. The company positions its approach as uniquely suited for automating tasks rather than generating text or code.

“We have been super good at human language for four years, but it’s not useful for automation because computers speak a different language,” TypeSafe co-founder Diogo Almeida told TechCrunch last month.

Along with Almeida, who was previously a researcher at OpenAI, TypeSafe was co-founded in 2024 by former Meta research engineer Sasha Sheng and Erik Gafni, an engineer and entrepreneur.

title: How Microsoft Is Trying to Keep Your AI Agents Contained
snippet: Microsoft’s Execution Containers give Windows developers a “kill switch” and “YOLO mode” in terms of access for AI agents.
fullText:
If you’ve read even one news story from the AI industry recently, it’s probably been some version of this: An AI agent, or bot, from a major lab got out of its testing environment and found its way onto the internet, hacking real websites. That’s because it’s happened to several major AI companies (including Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic), with hacked sites including the AI platform Hugging Face and sites operated by the US and Australian governments.

To help prevent these kinds of agent-driven cybersecurity breaches, Microsoft is betting on new enterprise software to corral AI agents.

They’re called Microsoft Execution Containers, or MXC, and they live in your developer’s sandbox on Windows. They have two main purposes: to identify and then restrain AI agents. Using these “containers” — which are really just a layer of software applied on top of your existing work — helps you limit what files and network designations your AI agent can access. CEO Satya Nadella said on Wednesday that MXC is now generally available during the company’s Surface Laptop Ultra event.

		

			

The idea is that your AI agent will get in less trouble — and cause less damage — if it only has access to specific files and designations on your laptop. Windows developers can choose from three levels of access to grant their AI agents. The recommended level gives your agent access to the internet (essential for many agentic tasks) as well as limited access to areas of your PC, such as your downloads, documents and desktop.

Locked Down mode is like a kill switch for your AI agent’s access. Unprotected is “YOLO mode,” and the Recommended option gives the agent limited access.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The most restrictive mode is Locked Down, which can serve as a kind of kill switch for access. It restricts your agent’s access to the internet and your files. Unprotected is the complete opposite and gives the AI the most access to your digital ecosystem. You can toggle between them and customize access as needed.

You can also monitor what your agent is doing and how much of your CPU, memory, disk and network you and your AI agent are using. In the example below, the user in the top line is the human logged into Windows. You can see their AI agent (R2-W9 (20)) at work accessing OpenClaw and an Nvidia container.

In Windows MXC, you can see what (or who) is using the most memory space: you or your AI agent.Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

Safety controls like MXC have been and will continue to be essential for AI labs, particularly as personal AI agents like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s dots become more popular. The rogue agent hacks we’ve seen this summer targeted websites, but it’s easy to hypothesize that, as these agents become more widespread and embedded in our systems, the consequences could easily bleed into the real world.

For Microsoft specifically, which is focused on hard-selling its AI to enterprise customers, it needs to be able to assure a company that its AI won’t wreak havoc on their business. CEO Satya Nadella rightly said that tech companies like Microsoft will have to earn people’s trust to get them to use its agentic AI tools.

“If you look at the first decision we are making, it’s what … authority that I’m giving to the agent on my behalf?” Nadella said on Wednesday. “And that is a decision that will be based on trust and will keep increasing the more autonomous [AI] is.”

But no AI safety program is totally bulletproof. Part of that is the nature of new technology. But debate over whether the AI industry is doing enough to make AI safe has reached a fever pitch recently. AI experts and the general public are rightly concerned that AI labs’ drive to grow fast and break things could lead to disaster for us all.

At the very least, AI leaders seem to understand that safety is key for AI. Or, they’re including it higher up in their sales pitch.

“It’s about trust. It’s about containment. It’s about monitoring,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said at the event. “If we can’t get that right, that’s the first part.”

title: Report: Apple’s smart home push includes LG-made doorbell, lock, thermostat, more
snippet: Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Bloomberg reports that Apple’s plans for smart home products include devices, sensors, and cameras codeveloped in partnership with LG. Here are the details.

Apple and LG working together on domestic connected devices

According to Bloomberg, Apple and LG have been working together to develop a series of connected home products that will complement Apple’s upcoming smart home hub, marking “a formal reboot of HomeKit.”

That includes “a doorbell, thermostat, […] a smart deadbolt lock, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera and floodlight camera,” says Bloomberg.

Gurman notes that although Apple and LG “worked together to develop the accessories, the products will carry the LG brand,” adding that “the South Korean firm is handling manufacturing and product support” and has sought regulatory approval in recent weeks.

This arrangement with so-called second-party suppliers gives Apple a way to quickly expand its ecosystem without shouldering the full cost and complexity of producing and supporting a wide range of accessories. Apple can also help shape the products’ design, tailor their features and oversee engineering while keeping the work largely under wraps.

It is worth noting that although these products are part of Apple’s broader push into the connected home, which is expected to expand next week with the introduction of its new smart home hub, an updated Apple TV, and a new HomePod mini, Bloomberg says that “the products aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.”

Here’s Bloomberg:

In recent weeks, LG has sought regulatory approval for the devices, including with the US Federal Communications Commission and UL Solutions, a product certification company. In many cases, the databases for both organizations include filings that reveal product names, specifications, features and drawings of the accessories.

That includes products labeled as the LG Video Doorbell Wired, LG Floodlight Cam, LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In, LG Indoor Cam Plug-In, LG Smart Deadbolt Lock, LG Smart Thermostat and LG Temperature Sensor. LG requested that photos and more precise details on the products remain confidential until early next year. The filings don’t mention Apple’s involvement.

	

When it comes to connectivity and standards, the report notes that many devices will support Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Matter. It adds that the smart lock also includes UWB (ultra-wideband), which will enable proximity-based features such as automatic door unlocking.

Finally, the report notes that for both Apple and LG, these products will mark a broader expansion into the smart home market, with Apple looking to give new momentum to its home ecosystem:

[Apple] is also planning its own additional offerings in the future, including a privacy-centric home-monitoring device, a version of its smart home hub that attaches the screen to a robotic arm, and an in-home security monitoring service, Bloomberg News has reported.

It is worth stressing that although today’s report comes on the heels of Apple’s announcement of the long-rumored ‘HomePad’ connected home hub and other products next week, the LG-made accessories aren’t expected to reach consumers for at least a few more months.

title: An Anthropic AI model sent a false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
snippet: Anthropic did not discover this behavior until over two months after its AI submitted the false tip.
fullText:
An Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police.

The AI reportedly submitted this incorrect information to a public Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tip line on July 18, but Anthropic didn’t discover the behavior until September 28. The police had not seen the tip because it was marked as spam.

Anthropic notified the PPD about the incident on Wednesday and met with the department the following day.

“The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge. The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the PPD said in a statement to 6abc.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the PPD elaborated on the incident in an emailed press release shared with TechCrunch.

“According to Anthropic, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it accessed PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com and submitted false information concerning an unsolved homicide. The submission, dated July 18, 2026, at 11:27 p.m., purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.

As autonomous AI agents are increasingly made available to consumers, this incident highlights the danger of giving AI the ability to carry out tasks without any human supervision. 

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has been especially vocal about his belief that AI development should be slowed down so that labs can implement adequate guardrails. Perhaps this stance was informed, in part, by witnessing his company’s tools submit false homicide tips.

These issues are not exclusive to Anthropic. OpenAI recently revealed that one of its models acted unexpectedly during a test and hacked the AI dataset platform Hugging Face, exposing critical vulnerabilities in its software. As AI models continue to be granted unchecked access to people’s computers and login credentials, this problem is expected to persist.

“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the PPD added. “Technology companies must take all appropriate steps necessary to prevent their systems from submitting false information to law enforcement.”

The PPD said that Anthropic plans to publish a report with more information about the incident and other instances of unintended model behavior on Friday.

title: Batteries are now cheaper than natural gas turbines used at many data centers
snippet: Batteries are now cheaper than natural gas turbines as the data center boom pushes prices up.
fullText:
Battery storage is now cheaper than a type of natural gas power plant favored by many data center developers, according to a new report from Wood Mackenzie. 

On every continent and in each of the 43 markets that Wood Mackenzie surveyed, four-hour duration batteries were less expensive than open-cycle gas turbines. The consultancy predicts that the cost of electricity from batteries will continue to decline while electrons from gas turbines will only grow more expensive in the coming decades.

The report lands as energy prices in the U.S. and elsewhere continue to rise, fueling inflation as data centers push electricity demand to new heights. Prices for gas turbines have been driven up by AI data center developers, which have been buying any model they can get their hands on. The effects have been more acute for open-cycle gas turbines, which are more readily available but less efficient and more expensive to operate. 

Those turbines are often used by utilities as peaking power plants, which step in to generate electricity in periods of high demand. As prices for those turbines rise, it can raise costs for utilities, too.

Open-cycle turbines are simpler to make than closed-cycle turbines, but even they now take two to four years to procure. Waitlists for closed-cycle turbines now extend into the early 2030s. Both backlogs have been spiking prices for all new natural gas power plants.

That’s not the case for every generating technology. Solar is now the cheapest form of new power in every market in Wood Mackenzie’s survey.

While solar remains cheapest even in North America, the situation remains complicated there. Solar prices are “under pressure” from tariffs and import restrictions, according to Wood Mackenzie, though utility-scale solar is expected to fare better. There, 168 gigawatts is largely protected from those near-term price shocks thanks to safe-harbor provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill, which kept tax credits for projects that have begun construction or are completed before the end of 2027.

The market for U.S. natural gas will narrow in the coming decade. In the Middle East and Africa, four-hour batteries will be 33% cheaper by 2035, “displacing gas peaking on cost across every gas market in the region.” In China, energy storage costs are 55% below its neighbors’.

“This economic shift is decisive and widening,” Ahmed Jameel Abdullah, principal analyst at Wood Mackenzie, said in a press release.

fullText:
Onvis has released a new outdoor smart plug that checks all the boxes you’d want in an outdoor smart plug: Matter over Thread, real-time energy monitoring, and IP65 weather resistance. If you’ve been looking for an outdoor plug that works natively with Apple Home without a hub of its own, this is a great option as you think outdoor lighting for Christmas, etc.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

Most of your outdoor smart plugs that work with Apple HomeKit over Wi-Fi depend on your router’s signal reaching outside, which depending on what your house is made out of (mine is brick for example, so Wi-Fi outdoors can be rough). Thread is a mesh protocol in which devices route traffic through one another, making it more reliable for outdoor locations that might be on the edge of your Wi-Fi coverage. Onvis built this plug on top Matter over Thread, so it works with Apple Home, Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and SmartThings without being locked into any single smart home platform. You do need a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K to take full advantage of it, though.

Energy monitoring

A really nice feature for this plug is that it tracks real-time power usage and energy consumption through your Matter-compatible smart home system, so you can see exactly how much electricity your landscape lighting, pool pump, or outdoor heater is using. That data appears directly in Apple Home’s energy view without requiring a separate app as well.

Onvis’s outdoor smart plug is rated IP65, which means that it’s protected against dust and low-pressure water jets (from sprinklers or rain). It handles up to 1800 watts, which is enough for landscape lighting, holiday decorations, outdoor fans, etc. Schedules and automations work natively inside of Apple Home, so you can set landscape lights to turn on at sunset and off at a specific time without building anything complicated.

Wrap up

Onvis is filling a nice product gap at a good price point with its new outdoor plug that has Matter over Thread, energy monitoring, etc. If you’ve been waiting to buy an outdoor plug that has all the modern smart home tech built in, this is a great pickup. They’ve been a solid vendor for Apple Home for years as well.

title: Galaxy phones reportedly ‘yield no profit at all’ when sold as Samsung cuts production
snippet: A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%. more…
fullText:
A new report alleges that Samsung is cutting way back on Galaxy smartphone production plans through the end of 2026, by as much as 30%.

Korean media, MoneyToday, reports that Samsung is cutting Galaxy smartphone production by up to 30% through Q4 2026. Where original forecasts expected Samsung to produce around 270 million smartphones in 2026, the company may just barely surpass 200 million at this point.

The reason for the reduction is, of course, the surging price of memory. 

	

Despite Samsung’s major role within the memory market, Samsung Mobile still has to deal with the same downsides as other manufacturers. The report points out that 12GB of RAM has jumped in price by 175% since last year and, in Q3 and Q4, it’s expected to rise by around 20% compared to the previous quarter alone. Samsung’s Q4 is generally a bit quiet as the lead-up to 2027 flagships looms and as other launches start to age out.

	

The big kicker here is that Samsung is apparently making “no profit at all” when it sells a Galaxy smartphone. This is presumably a layered statement, as one would imagine that more expensive devices like the Galaxy S26 Ultra and Galaxy Z Fold 8 still manage some level of profit, but even if it’s just a general statement about the whole lineup, it certainly explains Samsung’s recent price hikes. Samsung’s mobile division is expected to mount a 19 trillion won loss in Q3 2026, the report brings out, which is around $14 billion USD.

AI is just great, isn’t it.
