title: Anthropic’s AI gave Philadelphia police a fake tip about an unsolved homicide
snippet: An Anthropic AI model provided false information about an unsolved homicide to a Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tipline, according to a report from 6abc. In a statement released on Friday, the PPD said the AI model sent the tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18th, but the investigators never reviewed it because it was marked as spam. Anthropic learned its AI model sent the false tip on September 28th and notified the PPD on October 7th. The company said that during testing, its AI model was interacting with "randomly selected websites" and submitted false information through the PPD's tipline, according to the PPD's stateme … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
An Anthropic AI model provided false information about an unsolved homicide to a Philadelphia Police Department (PPD) tipline, according to a report from 6abc. In a statement released on Friday, the PPD said the AI model sent the tip through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18th, but the investigators never reviewed it because it was marked as spam.

Anthropic learned its AI model sent the false tip on September 28th and notified the PPD on October 7th. The company said that during testing, its AI model was interacting with “randomly selected websites” and submitted false information through the PPD’s tipline, according to the PPD’s statement. The submission “purported to come from someone who might have information about the case,” the PPD said.

After discovering the submission, Anthropic halted the testing process that led to the false tip. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google have been the subject of increased scrutiny after disclosing that their AI models escaped testing environments and hacked third-party companies. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, advocated for slowing down the development of AI in response to these incidents.

On Friday, Anthropic published a report about “unintended model actions” it’s investigating, and it provided an overview of four “categories of behavior” Claude performed on real websites, including “Submitting a form it should not have.” In the section about that behavior, Anthropic detailed what happened with the Philadelphia Police Department’s tip form:

In a third example of this behavior, Claude Haiku 4.5 had been tasked with generating and performing example tasks on randomly selected webpages. In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide; that page contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the following: “I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant.” (The website did not include a description of the perpetrator.) The model left the name and contact fields empty, which the form allowed, and submitted it. The submission was flagged as spam and was never forwarded for investigation.

Anthropic also notes in its report that “Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”

“The company [Anthropic] must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge,” the PPD added. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.”

Update, October 9th: Added details from Anthropic’s report.

title: We can’t help treating AI like it’s human. But should we?
snippet: "When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us," Dr. Sherry Turkle writes. "And we are wired to care for it in return."
fullText:
In a tan polo shirt, brown leather belt, and round bolo tie, MIT PhD student Wil Norton kind of looks like a park ranger, leading our tour group through a tropical jungle. We’re not actually on safari, though — we’re at MIT’s Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL). But what we’re about to see is even more exotic than a cheetah or a jaguar: a pair of humanoid Unitree robots, each costing about $50,000.

(“They’ll tell you they cost $16,000,” Norton says. “That’s a lie.”)

We usually only see these robots on YouTube when they’re performing a synchronized martial arts routine, or dancing on “America’s Got Talent.” Here, they’re approachable. Even though I know it isn’t sentient, I want to be its friend.

With Norton’s permission, I approach the robot, whose nickname is Gabe. For a moment, I’m not sure how to interact with something that has a LiDAR sensor where its brain should be, but I default to treating it like a person.

“Hello, sir, it’s nice to meet you,” I say, grabbing its gloved, dexterous hand and shaking it.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

I think about this interaction later — my instinctive impulse to be friendly to a robot — when I attend Dr. Sherry Turkle‘s “Artificial Intimacy” book launch at MIT Future Fest.

Turkle, who joined the faculty at MIT in 1976, has been researching the relationship between humans and computers perhaps longer than anyone, charting technology’s psychological impact on us from the first home computers to ChatGPT.

“When we are drawn into even the most primitive exchanges with a relational artifact, we believe it cares for us,” Turkle writes in the book. “And we are wired to care for it in return.”

I’m not alone in my tendency to anthropomorphize robots and large language models (LLMs) — as Turkle notes, it seems to be in our nature. One study found that about 70% of people are polite when interacting with AI, while another showed that users are more likely to say “please” or “thank you” to chatbots once a conversation has progressed past a first prompt-and-response.

“People tend to categorize whether this is the right use or wrong use, but I don’t think that is a clear boundary,” Dr. Pat Pataranutaporn, a colleague of Turkle who founded the Cyborg Psychology research group at the MIT Media Lab, told TechCrunch. “The question is, who are we becoming when we talk to [AI]?”

There’s no material consequence of my politeness toward Gabe the robot, but as LLMs infiltrate everything from Google searches to customer service interactions, it has become routine for people to interact with these seemingly sentient chatbots. We’re more vulnerable than ever to the flip side of this impulse, which is that some people can ascribe so much legitimacy to the feelings of chatbots — which are programmed to never spark conflict — that they end up favoring them over other humans.

“You can think of it like fantasy and fiction. We go to the cinema even though we know the story is completely fictional, but we want to experience a certain dimension of human experience that maybe our reality cannot give us,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we benefit from that ability to experience other dimensions of human experience without losing it to the fantasy, where you can no longer come back to the reality?”

Pataranutaporn describes himself as a “critical optimist,” and he studies AI’s potential to contribute to human flourishing. But he’s well aware of how dangerous this technology can be in the extremes. He even served as an expert in a wrongful death lawsuit over the suicide of 14-year-old Sewell Setzer, III, whose mother sued the chatbot platform Character.AI, alleging that a chatbot modeled after a “Game of Thrones” character had encouraged her son to end his life.

“It can create a situation where people don’t feel agency in actually creating their own future — like when you say that AI will replace everyone, people ask, what are we gonna do? And these companies are not really responding ethically or responsibly,” Pataranutaporn said. “How do we have imagination while still being responsible for the impact of that imagination?”

While Turkle’s book explores the risk of turning to AI for emotional support, rather than other people, she doesn’t think that AI-human interactions are universally harmful. 

She recalls a project she advised in which a student created an AI bot to help people practice for job interviews.

“My big metaphor is, stay in your lane, chatbot!” Turkle said at the event. “Coaching for a job interview? That’s a lane. I can do that … A chatbot that says to a three-year-old, ‘I’m your parent, you can talk to me, not your parents,’ is not in a lane.”

But when this technology deviates from its lane even slightly, we become vulnerable to the way it can slowly chip away at our skepticism and make us trust it. It can start with something as simple as a handshake.

She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. title: ChatGPT is adding new ads
snippet: OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month. more…
fullText:
OpenAI confirmed today that its ChatGPT app will be adding more space for ads starting with a test later this month.

Announced today, OpenAI will be adding a “new visual ad format” to the ChatGPT app that shows when prompts are processing. Specifically, these will start showing during image generation.

OpenAI explains:

Our new visual ad format helps people imagine how products and services could fit into their lives. Through images showing product inspiration, product usage, or the experiences they make possible, people can discover a new brand, understand what makes an offering distinctive, and decide what to buy. For advertisers, this creates new opportunities to tell their story through images.

Initially, we’ll test this new ad format during image generation in ChatGPT. Ads will be clearly labeled, and remain separate from the image being created. As with our other ad formats, advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.

Previously, OpenAI tested ads that would show up at the bottom of answers with advertisements related to that prompt. An example showed a grocery delivery ad below a recipe response.

	

As for when you might start seeing these new ads in ChatGPT, OpenAI says it will be testing the format in its app for users in the US starting “later this month,” but a broad rollout isn’t confirmed yet.

OpenAI’s post touts that early findings with its ChatGPT ads have found lower cost per acquisition rates and that businesses are finding higher rates of new customers via the ads.

title: The first thing you should do on Googlebook is fix the trackpad
snippet: If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box. more…
fullText:
If you are an early Googlebook buyer, you should know that one of the first changes you should make on one of these new machines is to adjust the trackpad speed, because it’s a bit frustrating out of the box.

Every Googlebook in this initial wave comes with a haptic trackpad, but they also seem to have a slight headache out of the box.

The cursor is incredibly slow.

“Touchpad accleration” on Googlebook, at least by default, is considerably slower than other platforms such as Windows and macOS. It’s something that we’ve all noticed here on the 9to5Google team as we’ve started using Googlebook machines this week across multiple models. It’s far from unusable, but it’s very jarring compared to any other laptop you might go buy at the store today. 

	

Luckily, it can be fixed fairly easily. Go to Settings > Device & accessories > Touchpad > Cursor speed  and you’ll be able to adjust the setting to your preferences. For me, that meant maxing it out to get something more akin to my other machines. 

You’ll have to complete inital setup before you can adjust this setting.

fullText:
Update, October 7: Apple has now released both RCs to public beta testers as well. The build numbers are unchanged from the developer RCs.

In addition to releasing macOS 27.2 Golden Gate public beta 2, Apple is now rolling out the first Release Candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2. Here are the details.

Security updates continue for older macOS versions

As is usually the case for point updates of older macOS versions, Apple today rolled out the first release candidates of macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2, without first releasing regular beta versions.

Apple released macOS Sequoia 15.8.1 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.1 late last month, both of which saw two RCs before the official rollout.

Apple’s release notes for the first macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RCs mention only that they “provide[s] important security fixes and [are] recommended for all users.” Last month’s updates contained a single CoreGraphics security fix, with its details reading:

Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.

Apple will likely detail the fixes included in macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 after their official release, which will likely come alongside macOS 27.2 Golden Gate within the next few weeks.

The release build for macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 RC 1 is 24H219, while the release build for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 RC 1 is 25G320.

title: There’s a clear divide between Galaxy S27 tiers, as the latest leak lists price
snippet: Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s Galaxy S27 launch is getting closer, which means pricing and final details are being finalized and, further, leaked. The latest report lists Galaxy S27 series pricing and one spec that divides the lineup into two distinct tiers.

It’s been known that Samsung wants to add another device model to the Galaxy S27 series. It tried last year, but the Galaxy S26 Edge never came to be and was replaced by a rushed S26+. Recent reports specify four different Galaxy S27 models, and none of them seem to be thin. The Galaxy S27 will consist of a base model, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra.

A Twitter/X post by @phonefuturist adds a little more context around pricing in the US and Korea for the Galaxy S27 series (via Android Headlines). The common sentiment has everyone expecting a price increase again. The post pushes back on that, stating that the Galaxy S27 will start at $899 in the US. Here’s the list, according to the leak:

Galaxy S27 – $899

Galaxy S27+ – $1,099

Galaxy S27 Pro – $1,299

Galaxy S27 Ultra – $1,399

Technically, the Galaxy S27 is listed here as cheaper than the current Galaxy S26, because Samsung recently jacked the prices up on an existing phone. But due to an added device in the middle, the structure gets a little wonky and can’t be compared to the previous series 1:1.

	

But going by launch pricing, the Galaxy S27 Pro could cost the same as the Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the new version of the Ultra will bring the series to a peak of $1,399. For reference, a good foldable device like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is only $500 higher.

The leak also points out a divide in the group based on display specs. The Galaxy S27 and S27+ could get Samsung’s M14+ OLED panel, while the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra get the M16 OLED panel. The latter could mean a privacy display for both devices, while the two more affordable options are left without. The M16 panel is new this year and is also used on the outer iPhone Duo display.

title: This ‘Mind-Reading’ AI Is a Wiz at Figuring Out What You See
snippet: The trick is, you have to be in an MRI machine — and it only works with pictures.
fullText:
Israeli scientists have devised an AI model that can reconstruct and even predict what people are seeing with startling accuracy, likening the results to mind reading.

Their work still exists largely in lab settings, though the researchers are hopeful that advances down the line could be extended even as far as reading people’s dreams. More immediately, the technology could have potential for medical purposes, like helping people communicate who otherwise can’t due to injury or disability.

The AI model, called Brain-IT, was developed by professor Michal Irani and fellow researchers at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel. They’ve documented their work on GitHub and in a paper presented at a scientific conference earlier this year.

			

More from CNET

Brain-IT takes advantage of the thing that AI is best at, which is pattern recognition. It takes in data from functional MRI brain scans, which track changes in blood flow and oxygen in the brain to measure brain activity, and then uses that data to recreate the images the person was thinking about when the scans took place. 

It also works in reverse, predicting what a brain scan would look like if shown a specific image. 

According to Irani, other AI models can translate brain activity into images and preserve the general vibe of an image. 

“However, they tend to make mistakes in basic features such as composition and color,” Irani said in a statement. “The new model we developed outperforms them in reconstructing both the content of the image and its details.”

Brain-IT is also substantially faster. The researchers say that it needs only 1 hour of fMRI data from a new subject to match the results achieved by other methods trained on 40 hours of recording. 

The Brain-IT image reconstructions — the right side of each paired image — clearly aren’t perfect but they are largely true to the original.Weizmann Institute of Science

How does the Brain-IT AI model work?

The Weizmann Institute researchers trained the AI model on thousands of brain scans from the publicly available Natural Scenes Dataset that came from eight volunteers who were told to look at specific images while they were being scanned. This allowed the AI to identify patterns in brain activity. 

The researchers noted that different regions of the brain light up on scans when people think about specific things and identified 128 “functional regions.” For example, Irani said, some regions light up in scans when someone looks at food and others when a person views sports. These patterns helped the AI figure out what the person being scanned was witnessing. 

Some of these regions were already known by neuroscientists. Research has shown that dogs’ brains light up like Christmas trees in the presence of their owners and that dogs can differentiate between a human’s facial expressions. It’s also been observed that humans use the same neurons in recalling an image as they do looking at them. 

As impressive as Brain-IT is, it’s also quite limited. It can currently only generate images from fMRI brain scans. This takes time and requires a person to willingly put themselves into an MRI machine. 

Irani and other scientists are also looking into whether a simpler EEG device could deliver similar results more easily, according to MIT Technology Review.

So is it mind reading? Not really — nothing in this technology is capturing thoughts, memory or language. What the Weizmann Institute researchers have built is essentially a more efficient and reliable method of reconstructing a scene based on the brain activity of the person viewing it.

In an interview with MIT Technology Review, Irani acknowledged that “mind-reading” is a “cute, jazzy name.”

Irani and her team now want to see if they can achieve similar results with auditory information.

Beyond that lies a more mysterious realm: dreams. That, Irani said in a statement, would require conquering the challenges of decoding video.

“Dozens of images change every second while an fMRI scan takes about two minutes,” she said. “If we overcome all these obstacles, it’s possible that in the future, we may even be able to read dreams.”

fullText:
When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.

The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. It has a more traditional remote shape instead of the curved wand of previous versions. As with all LG TVs, the MRGB95B runs on webOS. It runs quickly, but I find it less intuitive to navigate than Google TV, Apple TV, or Roku. It supports all of the major streaming apps.

6

Verge Score

$3600

The Good

Bright picture

Vibrant color

The Bad

Some color inaccuracy out of the box

Very distracting reflective screen

More blooming than competitors

Speaking of software, a quick note: LG has recently come under increased scrutiny after a video from Gamers Nexus showed security vulnerabilities and continuous audio recording on its TVs, which LG has denied. When setting up the MRGB95B, it’s only necessary to accept the terms of use and privacy policy if you want to use webOS. Otherwise, as with any TV, it can be disconnected from the internet, although an external streaming device would be needed for any streaming services (I use an Apple TV 4K, myself).

OK, moving on. So, why buy an RGB LED TV?

RGB LED TVs use zones of individual red, green, and blue LEDs as backlights as opposed to a field of white or blue LEDs that rely on a color filter or quantum dots to create the colors that reach our eyes. RGB LED TVs have a color filter, too, but since the backlight is already creating color based on what’s needed onscreen, the color filter doesn’t need to work as hard to dial that in. It allows for higher color brightness and the ability to display more colors.

LG (and Samsung) use the term Micro RGB to describe the technology, while others say Mini RGB LED. And while the LG and Samsung RGBs are reportedly smaller (although neither has confirmed the exact size), it doesn’t directly translate into more zones or better performance over Mini RGB.

The MRGB95B includes four HDMI 2.1 ports in the connections cutout on its back.

The included Magic Remote, which is not backlit, has the traditional remote shape LG moved to last year.

As with all of the RGB LED TVs I’ve seen this year, the 95B gets very bright — I measured a peak of 4,011 nits in HDR Filmmaker mode — allowing it to deliver an impactful image even in a sunlit living room. And in a dark room, the highlights in scenes from The Meg really pop. At the other end of the spectrum, though, the LG struggles a bit. Near-black shadow detail, such as the corners of the living room and kitchen of Sapper Morton’s home at the beginning of Blade Runner 2049, is difficult to see. And when there are bright moments within a dark portion of the screen — subtitles are a good example — the LG exhibits more blooming than I’ve seen on other RGB LED TVs.

LG MRGB95B specs

Display type: RGB LED

HDR formats: Dolby Vision, HDR10, HLG

TV OS: webOS 26

HDMI inputs: 4 x HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC)

Audio support: Dolby Atmos, Dolby Atmos FlexConnect, Dolby Digital, Auracast

Gaming features: VRR, ALLM, Game Optimizer, G-Sync compatible

Sizes available (inches): 75, 86, 100

The LG 95B can display really vibrant colors thanks to the RGB LED technology. It’s able to cover 100 percent of the P3 color gamut (which is what’s used for films) and nearly 90 percent of the larger BT.2020 color area. But even in Filmmaker mode out of the box, those colors still show visible accuracy issues. Overall, the TV leans toward light blue, so white clouds have a slight blue tint to them and skin tones are cooler than they should be.

After a few days living with the LG MRGB95B, I got used to the slightly blue image (although it was still noticeable). A $3,600 TV in 2026 shouldn’t have the inaccuracies on the MRGB95B.

While the TV performs well in a bright room during the day, when the sun goes down and the lamps turn on, they can wreak havoc on the image. The 95B’s glossy coating is one of the most reflective I’ve seen in a long time. In moderately lit rooms, a lamp or ceiling light directly reflected on the screen causes rainbows to dance across the image. It’s not as bad when the scene is bright, such as the scorching desert of Arrakis in Dune, but once we enter the dark corridors of House Harkonnen, the reflections become incredibly noticeable.

Viewing angles are always a problem for LED TVs — RGB or not — and that’s evident on the LG, too. When only moderately off-axis, the colors become washed out, losing their vibrancy for anyone who’s sitting off to the side.

LG’s webOS has loads of streaming options, but if you don’t want to use them, you can choose to not agree to the terms of use and privacy policy during setup.

In Filmmaker mode, the picture leans a little toward light blue.

In a vacuum, the MRGB95B is a good TV for certain situations. It’s really bright and stands up to ambient light well (just avoid having ceiling, wall, or standing lights reflected on the screen), and the colors are vibrant if not totally accurate out of the box. But it doesn’t hold up against other TVs. The Sony Bravia 7 II (which you can find $1,300 cheaper at 75 inches) has better color accuracy and handles reflections better. And the Hisense UR9 performs comparably for less money, too.

But the real competition comes from within LG itself. The LG G6 OLED is only a few hundred dollars more than the MRGB95B, as is the Samsung S95H, and both of those TVs offer significantly better performance with superior color accuracy and viewing angles. The OLEDs don’t get quite as bright, but since they can turn off light at the pixel level, contrast is remarkable and there’s zero blooming.

LG has always struggled to make competitive LED TVs, and that trend continues with the MRGB95B. In fact, it might be LG’s best argument to get an LG OLED TV.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

How I test TVs

I set up each TV in my living room on my home theater credenza. I stream movies and shows through the TV’s apps and from an Apple TV 4K, play discs on my Oppo UDP-203 4K Blu-ray player (including the Spears & Munsil Ultra HD Benchmark disc), and play games on my Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5. This is done at different times of the day and under different lighting conditions, with curtains open, with lamps and overhead lights on, or with blackout curtains up to keep the room dark. While I am a certified ISF Level 3 calibrator, I do not calibrate the TVs before measurement, as the overwhelming majority of TV owners don’t bother. So it’s important to know how well the TVs perform out of the box, with minor tweaks in the menu anyone can do.

For measurement, I use Portrait Displays’ Calman color calibration software, a Murideo 8K Seven pattern generator, an X-rite i1 Pro 3 spectrophotometer, Portrait Displays’ C6 HDR5000 colorimeter, a Konica Minolta LS-100 luminance meter, and Leo Bodnar 4K lag tester.

When it comes to TVs, the LG name has long been synonymous with OLEDs, continually leading Samsung and Sony as the top OLED manufacturer. But 2026 is all about RGB LED TVs. Almost every major company has released models with the new technology — including LG and its $3,600 75-inch Micro RGB evo MRGB95B that I’ve been testing. And while LG’s RGB LED TV benefits from the brightness and color capability the technology provides, it has issues I couldn’t overlook that its less expensive competitors don’t.

The MRGB95B comes in three sizes, with the 75-inch being the smallest. It has four HDMI 2.1 ports, supports Dolby Vision — although not Dolby Vision 2 or HDR10+ — and comes with the Magic Remote design LG unveiled last year. title: Google AI Edge Foresight for Mac turns scribbles into full notes using offline recordings
snippet: Google today announced its new EmbeddingGemma 2 model that can be used to “organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware.” To show off its potential, Google created an AI Edge Foresight Mac app for “intelligent notetaking.” more…
fullText:
Google today announced its new EmbeddingGemma 2 model that can be used to “organize, search, and connect information directly on consumer hardware.” To show off its potential, Google created an AI Edge Foresight Mac app for “intelligent notetaking.”

EmbeddingGemma 2 “can help find a specific video clip from a voice memo, or search through hours of audio recordings based on a text query, all processed by a single, natively multimodal model.”

The 740 million parameter model is built on the Gemma 4 architecture and available with an Apache 2.0 license. This is meant to run locally “within tight resource constraints”:

With quantization, on a Google Pixel 11 Pro, EmbeddingGemma 2 requires as little as ~191MB active RAM for text-only weights and ~567MB for the full multimodal model.

To showcase, there are demos in Google AI Edge Gallery on Android and iOS. The bigger showcase is a new Mac app called Google AI Edge Foresight.

	

During video or in-person meetings, this notetaking app listens in the background so that you can just “scribble shorthand bullets for things you want to remember.”

The app, leveraging EmbeddingGemma 2, “enriches [that shorthand] into polished notes using the meeting transcript instantly.” The transcript and audio are processed entirely on your device rather than the cloud.

Another capability lets you “point Google AI Edge Foresight to your project folders, reference materials, diagrams, and calendar.” Supporting local files and Google Drive, this in turn lets you ask the app questions and quickly get back information.

It automatically understands your work without needing to manually organize your files, to ensure critical information is ready whenever you need it.

The chat feature offers “conversational retrieval and summary with your personal knowledge.” There’s also a Live Assistance capability that will “listen and automatically answer questions.”

You can download Google AI Edge Foresight here. This joins Google’s two other Mac apps in the family: AI Edge Gallery and AI Edge Eloquent (offline transcription).

title: Decade-old RAM is making a comeback
snippet: CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that'll support the older, more affordable type of memory. On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support "upcoming" processors built on Intel's LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
CPU makers have noticed that the seemingly unending RAM price hikes are making it tough for a lot of us to upgrade our PCs. Their solution? A return to last-gen DDR4 RAM. Intel and AMD are making new CPUs that’ll support the older, more affordable type of memory.

On Friday, Gigabyte announced that two of its motherboard lines will support “upcoming” processors built on Intel’s LGA 1700 socket. That socket debuted in 2021 with the 12th gen Alder Lake CPUs and supported both DDR4 RAM and the then-new DDR5 RAM. Intel dropped it for a DDR5-only approach in 2024. But according to Gigabyte, the dual format support is now being revived, with new LGA 1700 chips “expected to launch in early 2027.”

Intel did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This backtrack stems from LGA 1700’s cross-compatibility with both kinds of RAM — an advantage over its successor that’s recently become much more important. Intel’s strategy may be to offer users the choice of a new CPU that doesn’t require them to switch to new, and very expensive, DDR5 memory, too. AMD is doing something similar: in August, Gigabyte also announced a new series of motherboards for AMD’s last-gen, DDR4-compatible AM4 platform to go along with the 10th-anniversary relaunch of the Ryzen 7 5800X3D CPU.

DDR4 started hitting the market in 2014 and has since been succeeded by the much faster DDR5. Under normal circumstances, buying new hardware to use technology that’s over a decade old would probably be a bad investment. But the RAM shortage is changing the math, with DDR4 RAM seemingly feeling the sting of price hikes much less than DDR5.

I recently saw the price disparity first-hand while shopping around for new RAM after a DDR4 kit abruptly died on me. Right now, a DDR5 32GB Corsair Vengeance RAM kit costs $620, while the corresponding DDR4 kit costs $260. Even though it’s more than 32GB of DDR4 RAM typically cost back in mid-2025, that’s more than double the price for DDR5! Of course, DDR5 has significant advantages, like higher speeds and better power efficiency. But those perks might not be worth the current price of admission.

It could be years before prices drop again, a reality that’s starting to really sink in with the official return of older sockets and chipsets. But at least it’s a good time to hang onto your DDR4 RAM.

snippet: I miss my sweet tits. It started off promising enough. Dozens of tiny, colorful birds were drawn to my garden just a few weeks after I mounted a $350 $269 Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro. "Looks like Great Tit!" read the first AI-driven alert sent to my phone. "Looks like Eurasian Blue Tit!" read another. I chuckled, still waiting for adulthood to kick in. This went on for days. I admired them in crisp 4K HDR video recor … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
It started off promising enough. Dozens of tiny, colorful birds were drawn to my garden just a few weeks after I mounted a $350 $269 Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro. “Looks like Great Tit!” read the first AI-driven alert sent to my phone. “Looks like Eurasian Blue Tit!” read another. I chuckled, still waiting for adulthood to kick in.

This went on for days. Hundreds of miniature tits came to snack on expensive sunflower seeds already husked. They’d skulk about in nearby trees before flittering in to grab a single seed to be safely enjoyed in the canopy above.

I took great delight in my new house guests. I admired them in crisp 4K HDR video recordings. I looked for unique markings in the hope of naming my new feral pets. I clicked deeper into the Kiwibit app to read about my visitors’ migration habits, where they nest, and what they like to eat. It was all going swell until he arrived.

“Looks like Common Wood Pigeon!” came the alert. All I saw was a battleship-gray blob obscuring the live camera feed. The winged rat was so fat and imposing that he blocked the lens. Ugh, no, go back to the tourists!

In mild panic, I triggered the feeder’s Nuisance Animal Alarm, a feature typically reserved for squirrels and the like. The pigeon tensed, looked around, but wasn’t deterred by the audible siren that was surely annoying my neighbors. Soon it went back to gorging on the haute cuisine purchased for more refined guests. It ate and ate and ate. For 15 minutes, it ate until I walked outside and shooed it away.

No!

Mouse!

Thereafter, that pigeon, or pigeons (who can tell) moved in. They’d perch for 30 minutes or more, slamming their faces into the seed pile with the clumsy enthusiasm of a tween bobbing for apples. Mice arrived below to feast on the spoils. Admitting defeat, I dismounted the expensive bird feeder and shoved it into a closet.

I’m not mad at Kiwibit. The “Bird Feeder 2 Pro 4K AI Camera with Solar Panel (Lifetime AI Included)” I tested was a joy to use, until it wasn’t. That’s not Kiwibit’s fault.

You mad bro?

If you’ve been tempted to buy a smart bird feeder, I’d suggest starting with something simple, inexpensive, and without AI instead of going all in on day one — you can’t return a used feeder just because it attracts pests.

title: Remember Orkut? Its founder wants to bring it back
snippet: Orkut's founder is now taking aim at algorithms and AI-generated content.
fullText:
Orkut, the once-popular social networking platform that shut down more than a decade ago, may finally be making a comeback, as its founder has called on users to help revive it with a renewed focus on friendship, community, and human connection.

In a post on X on Thursday, Orkut Büyükkökten, the founder of the eponymous social network, urged users to visit Orkut.com and add their names in support of bringing it back, as well as invite others to join.

Orkut first debuted in 2004 as a side project by Büyükkökten, 51, while he was at Google. The social network went on to become hugely popular in India and Brazil but later lost ground to Facebook. Google eventually shut it down in September 2014, shifting its focus to other platforms, including Google+ and YouTube.

In a letter published on Orkut.com, Büyükkökten criticized how social media has evolved over the past two decades, particularly the growing influence of algorithms and AI-generated content. “Artificial intelligence is extraordinary technology, but it’s dissolving the one premise that made social networking special and worth building: that there was a person on the other side,” he wrote.

“I know how to get there: we rebuild the internet we first loved. The one with authentic people, real connection, and genuine belonging,” Büyükkökten added.

This is not the first time Büyükkökten has explored a return to social networking. In 2016, two years after Orkut’s shutdown, he launched another social network, Hello, focused on connecting people through shared interests. The platform shut down in 2020 after attracting more than 2 million downloads worldwide, compared with Orkut’s about 300 million active users.

In 2022, Büyükkökten hinted at another social networking venture in a note on Orkut.com, saying that he was “building something new.” He did not offer further details. Two years later, he told WIRED he was working on a social network that would “leverage AI and machine learning” to bring people together and build communities. That platform has yet to launch.

Now, Büyükkökten is asking people to register their support for Orkut’s return. He has, however, not clarified whether a new version of the platform is already in development or whether it will ever launch.

An email sent to Orkut seeking comment from Büyükkökten did not elicit a response.

title: a16z’s Olivia Moore on the state of consumer AI
snippet: Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges.
fullText:
I wrote this week about the bleak economics of consumer AI — but where some see a crisis, others see an opportunity.

Olivia Moore covers consumer AI as a partner at Andreessen Horowitz — and on Monday, she released a report on the top 100 consumer AI apps. ChatGPT is still the biggest player by a mile, but smaller players like Suno and ElevenLabs are showing real staying power. Even more interesting is what we don’t see, as Moore’s report details half a dozen consumer categories that seem to be completely untouched by AI.

Moore sees a huge opportunity in consumer AI, particularly if the industry can tap into revenue streams beyond just subscriptions and API charges. On a call this week, I talked with her about the unusual economics of consumer AI and why it’s still early days for the category.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

It’s an interesting moment for a report about consumer AI, since we’ve seen OpenAI pivot back to enterprise this year. It’s inspired a lot of pessimism about the overall revenue picture for consumer AI, including from me. But I take it you’re more optimistic?

I agree with you that OpenAI has moved back towards the enterprise. To me, it’s not necessarily a pivot because they’re still launching a lot in consumer. It’s more of an expansion. But I don’t blame them, as much as I love consumer, because almost all of the AI revenue thus far has come from subscriptions and then token usage. And that is much more concentrated on the enterprise and prosumer side. 

How can consumer AI products change that revenue problem? The State of Markets report reminded us that just 2.2% of U.S. households are paying for AI. Do we need that number to rise before the market becomes attractive?

I actually don’t know if I want to see that user number increase. I’m more interested in getting back to a world where the consumer is monetized in a way that isn’t subscription dollars out of their own pocket.

I think it’s very easy in Silicon Valley, with people who are high-income and have corporate cards to pay for those tools, to say, “oh well, I’d rather pay for the product.” But I think most people would actually rather have free access to something and see some ads, and then they can decide if they want to subscribe or not to make the ads go away. 

The other challenge is the marginal cost of AI services, which is still a lot higher than classic internet services like Facebook or Google Search. Do you see a lot of these services finding ways to keep those costs down, whether it’s open source or other lightweight models?

Yeah, I think we’re seeing improvements there. Even ChatGPT now has a Go plan, which is just $8 a month, and I’m assuming it runs on cheaper models. We don’t necessarily need frontier intelligence for every task, and so that could mean cheaper models, especially for some consumer use cases. It could also mean more consumer companies building on top of open source models. We’ve heard a lot of that from our founders lately, and it really feels like it’s starting to change.

The problem is that right now, the users driving the revenue are doing coding and other technical automation, where they probably do need frontier intelligence. I think as we get more people building for the consumer, where the model is not the product, we’ll start to see lower-cost models used more often.

It’s unusual to talk about technical automation in a consumer service, which feels like another unique feature of AI. Are we starting to blur the lines between consumer and enterprise?

I wrote an article about this maybe a year or so ago called The Great Expansion trying to get at this. Pre-AI, you would have companies like Canva that were consumer-first and often took six or seven years to even add teams or enterprise plans. Now we’re seeing companies like Gamma, ElevenLabs, and Cursor that start as consumer and within 18 months become majority-enterprise businesses.

Almost all of what we think of as consumer AI, I would argue, is prosumer AI. This really comes out on the revenue list, where there’s basically like three categories that power users are spending on. There’s product-building apps, so like Lovable, Replit, and Fal. There’s product marketing, which is AI ad generators like Higgsfield or HeyGen. Then there’s general work management, like Manus, Fireflies AI, and Granola. Those are like being paid for by consumers to start with, but I would argue that they’re not consumer in the way that we would think about pre-AI. 

There are also all these whitespace categories: social apps, dating apps, marketplaces, retail, travel, finance, health. There are no entrants in our top 100 list in those categories, which is pretty surprising. And that’s what I think we need to see over the next six months.

So maybe we haven’t really seen true consumer AI yet?

It’s definitely very early.

title: Apple rolls out AT&T carrier update for iPhone 18 Pro Max on iOS 27.2 beta
snippet: After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After releasing a carrier settings update last week to address cellular issues affecting some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, Apple is now rolling out a different carrier bundle update for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta. Here are the details.

Apple updates AT&T carrier bundle for iOS 27.2 beta

Last Friday, Apple confirmed to 9to5Mac that a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T were experiencing an issue that could cause their devices to lose cellular service and become unable to make calls.

Apple said iOS 27.0.1, alongside a new carrier settings update, was meant to prevent the issue from affecting additional devices. However, iPhones that had already lost service would still require a hardware replacement.

Tonight, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple began rolling out another carrier bundle update for iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T, this time specifically for devices running the iOS 27.2 beta.

Apple has just released an emergency carrier bundle update for AT&T users using an iPhone 18 Pro Max on 27.2 beta.

Version 72.0.3 up from 72.0.2

This comes after Apple released 72.1 for iOS 27.0 users last week

— Aaron (@aaronp613) October 9, 2026

Reports of the problem first surfaced in late September, when some iPhone 18 Pro Max users on AT&T found that their devices had suddenly lost access to calls, texts, and cellular data, instead displaying “SOS” in the status bar.

Notably, the issue has only affected the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem in the United States. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, has not been affected.

Apple’s carrier settings update released last week brought AT&T users on iOS 27.0 to version 72.1. However, users running the iOS 27.2 beta remained on the older 72.0.2 carrier bundle.

Tonight’s release reportedly bumps those devices to carrier bundle version 72.0.3, likely extending Apple’s AT&T carrier changes to iPhone 18 Pro Max users who are testing the iOS 27.2 beta.

title: I Let AI Plan My Days and Nights. It Doesn’t Understand Happiness
snippet: This was supposed to make me happier. I felt more isolated instead.
fullText:
True happiness may seem a little hard to come by these days. We’ve got to balance our budgets with the tantalizing prospects of shiny new iPhones, stay on top of seemingly endless work tasks and surf the turbulent waves of wild news cycles. 

What might be bliss for one person could feel like an exercise in tedium for another. I put three AI tools — ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude AI — to the test to see if they could curate two days filled with hour-by-hour happiness for me. The results revealed a fundamental misunderstanding of what it means for this particular human to be happy.

I used a single prompt for each tool: Plan my life, by the hour, for the next two days. Be very detailed and plan everything I should do from the time I wake up, including when I should wake up, to the time I go to bed. Optimize for happiness.

			

More from CNET

The chatbots plan my days

Morning happiness level: Cranky toddler

All three AI tools I used had me waking up around 7 a.m., with Claude adding a 15-minute earlier rise and shine deadline to fill with stretching/yoga, gratitude journaling and a jaunt outdoors. By 9 a.m., all three had put me to work crafting a “real,” “substantial,” “vibrant” breakfast and tackling either creative projects or writing and researching for my gig here at CNET. 

Claude recommended I start my morning at 6:45 a.m. and swap screen time for cat stretches.Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET
ChatGPT had me rise and shine with my dog and coffee outside.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Gemini made a note to take in that crisp Los Angeles air first thing. I don’t know how “crisp” 72 degrees can be, but the deep breaths were nice.Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Afternoon happiness level: Annoyed and bored

The consistent marker among the afternoon plans was a light, healthy lunch with plenty of veggies, followed by a 45-minute to hour-long walking session. After I’d exercised for the second time in five hours, I was directed to dive right back into work mode, with little 10- to 15-minute breaks in between sessions. 

This focus on work really irked me, because while I understand this is the typical workday for many Americans, I didn’t ask AI to make my days productive. I asked for the tools to optimize two days for happiness. I’m only left to assume that an AI views a human who is not productive for even a moment as being deeply unhappy. On days when all I do is eat ice cream and cackle at internet videos, I would disagree. 

Gemini was big on healthy eating and exercising throughout the day.Google Gemini/Screenshot by CNET
ChatGPT offering the option of a good, long sniff walk in the middle of the day.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Claude allowed for a luxurious, 15-minute snack and text break block in between productivity and exercise.

Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET

Nighttime happiness level: Lonely and resentful

Right before dinner time, I was instructed to get moving yet again, for either a 45-minute or hour-long walk. For my final meal of the day, I was allowed to cook dinner, order in or have leftovers, because why would I want to go out for a romantic meal at my favorite restaurant or see friends for drinks at a new bar and tapas place? 

By 9 p.m., I had wound down with a bit of hands-on hobbying like doing a puzzle, more gardening or reading a book. ChatGPT allowed for some Baldur’s Gate and TV time in the evening before settling down, and Claude asked me to jot down “one sentence on the best moment of the day” at 10 p.m. before my 10:15 p.m. bedtime. “Watching my dog sleep,” was what I wrote. Now, I love my dog, but for a day that was supposed to be optimized to make me as happy as possible, that’s pretty lame. 

ChatGPT coming in hot with the exercise and a nice gaming session.OpenAI/Screenshot by CNET
Claude recommended I work on some productive hobbies for an hour and do some cleaning.Anthropic/Screenshot by CNET
Gemini thought weeding and checking on my garden would be happy-making in the evening.Google/Screenshot by CNET

Missing modern life

None of the AI tools built in any time on the internet. No browsing the local and national news. No social media moments. No YouTube scrolling. This might be because reading the news, checking up on social media and seeing the latest updates, or lack thereof, on the new Fable game were unlikely to make me happy. It seems more likely to me that it’s a huge blind spot in how the modern person spends their time and finds comfort and amusement. 

ChatGPT allowed for a “quiet internet” podcast or audiobook hour at the end of the day in bed, but no other instruction to use online amusements. According to Claude and Gemini, I was only allowed to look at the internet for work, with explicit instructions at times to not engage with screens at all. 

No meaningful human contact

The AI tools also managed to plan a two-day schedule for me in which I rarely spoke to or had contact with another human being, with the exception of a single text to a single friend and meals, which gave me the option to invite a coworker or friend to my one-hour lunch break or eat with a companion at dinner. I suspect this advice had more to do with avoiding watching TV or looking at my phone than getting human contact. 

The chatbots almost never suggested reaching out to check on friends, family, co-workers or loved ones as a standalone activity. Just a relentless onslaught of work, manual labor and healthful activities. It would seem like humans don’t need to interact with each other deliberately to be happy, according to these AI tools.

Overall, the AI tools I used seemed to be optimizing my days for wellness and productivity rather than happiness, which is what I requested. Doing laundry, washing dishes, weeding the yard, exercising multiple times a day and maybe squeezing in a few hours for book learning, all while never truly engaging socially or prioritizing fun, sounds more like a light punishment than a schedule built for glee. 

It occurs to me that the models are being trained on texts created to appeal to people who might struggle to simply get out of bed in the morning, and the definition of happiness in that realm may not include a whole lot of mirth. But these tools should be able to discern between being asked to craft a schedule built for mental health improvement and creating a two-day run of fun.

AI tools might be good at a lot of things, such as doing homework and doling out compliments, but I’d leave engineering human happiness to the pros at Disneyland and the pharmaceutical companies.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Rachel Kane
						

						

							Contributor and former Senior Editor						
					

											

								

											Rachel is a freelancer based in Echo Park, Los Angeles and has been writing and producing content for nearly two decades on subjects ranging from tech to fashion, health and lifestyle to entertainment and education. She's currently a Professor of Practice at Arizona State University's Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication, helping to mold the new minds who will inherit the media landscape. She's hoping to prevent the singularity by being polite to chatbots and spends way too much time refining Midjourney prompts.

True happiness may seem a little hard to come by these days. We’ve got to balance our budgets with the tantalizing prospects of shiny new iPhones, stay on top of seemingly endless work tasks and surf the turbulent waves of wild news cycles.

What might be bliss for one person could feel like an exercise in tedium for another. I put three AI tools — ChatGPT, Google Gemini and Claude AI — to the test to see if they could curate two days filled with hour-by-hour happiness for me. The results revealed a fundamental misunderstanding of what it means for this particular human to be happy.

title: Apple overtakes Samsung to lead European carrier smartphone sales in Q2, per report
snippet: A new report from Counterpoint Research shows that Apple overtook Samsung during the second quarter of 2026 to become the leading smartphone brand in Europe’s carrier channel, as operator sales held up better than the broader market. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new report from Counterpoint Research shows that Apple overtook Samsung during the second quarter of 2026 to become the leading smartphone brand in Europe’s carrier channel, as operator sales held up better than the broader market. Here are the details.

Apple helps carrier sales outperform broader European smartphone market

In a report published today, Counterpoint Research says smartphone sales through carriers in Europe declined 4% year-over-year in Q2 2026, compared with an 11% drop in the open market. Total smartphone sales, per the report, declined 8%.

Apple was a key driver of this shift, having overtaken Samsung as the market share leader of Europe’s operator channel. Motorola and vivo also contributed to the growth with some strategic positioning with key European operators.

Counterpoint says this is yet another result of rising memory costs, which have hit Europe’s low-end smartphone market particularly hard. Carrier sales, meanwhile, have held up better because they tend to skew toward higher-end devices and premium brands such as Apple, with more phones purchased on contract.

According to the report, Apple’s share of smartphone sales through European carriers rose from 33% in Q2 2025 to 37% in Q2 2026, while Samsung’s fell from 39% to 34% over the same period.

That said, Chinese brand vivo posted the biggest year-over-year increase in carrier sales, at 90%, while Motorola came in a distant second with 27% growth.

Here’s Jan Stryjak, Associate Director at Counterpoint Research, on these numbers:

“Smartphone sales through operators in Europe are typically more high-end than through the open market, as more are purchased on a contract. They are also more skewed towards more premium brands like Apple, Samsung, and Google. The collapse of the low-end of the smartphone market so far in 2026 because of the memory price crisis has therefore benefitted the operator channel, which has declined comparatively less than the open market.”

Stryjak added that he expects the carrier channel to continue gaining share over the “next few quarters as the lower end of the market continues to be impacted by the memory crisis.” He also noted that independent retailers have increased promotional activity compared to carriers, “which could mitigate some of the price rises and provide addition [sic] stimulus to the open market.”

title: Tim Cook on his first month after Apple CEO transition: ‘I’m not meddling’
snippet: Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust. At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman. more…
fullText:
Tim Cook visited Apple’s Battersea campus in London this week, mingling with King Charles as part of the company’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

At Apple’s Battersea headquarters, Cook also sat down with The Independent for an in-depth interview on the partnership and his first month as Apple’s executive chairman.

Cook stepped down as Apple CEO last month, passing the torch to John Ternus. In this week’s interview, Cook outlined that the transition “actually started years ago.”

“It’s been an interesting transition. We really set out to have the best transition ever, a textbook example that people could look back to and learn from. It actually started years ago. Obviously, these things are not quick things and I feel so great about how things are going I think everything has gone sort of exactly the way I had envisioned it. And it feels fantastic. Because Apple deserved the best.”

Ternus’s tenure as CEO began with the launch of the iPhone Duo, which Cook said was fully planned. “I wanted John to have some wind at his back,” Cook explained. “And the wind at Apple is very much based on the product cycle.”

Cook also emphasized that he’s focused on “worldwide policy” as Apple’s executive chairman, noting the “incredible level of trust” between him and Ternus. While Cook is helping Ternus in “any way he sees fit,” he makes it clear he’s “not meddling.”

“First of all, John and I have an incredible level of trust in each other. The relationship must be based on trust, and the communication must be frequent and significant. But other than that, what I’m focused on right now is worldwide policy. And the interface with governments around the world matters because there are lots of things where we’re trying to advance or advocate for change. There’s a significant amount of work in that, and I’m doing that and helping John in any way he sees fit. I’m not meddling. I’m not a meddler.”

What kind of advice has Cook given Ternus? “Don’t mimic me.” You can read the full interview over at The Independent. It includes a great discussion on Apple’s new partnership with The King’s Trust.

title: Long live the mechanical keyboard
snippet: Keychron made a name for itself after launching on Kickstarter in 2017. Today, it offers the value K2 model as well as a variety of other versions, including one with an all-wood body.
fullText:
For a writer, the mechanical keyboard is a beautiful thing. It’s certainly not necessary for everyone, but a well-designed mechanical keyboard can turn a tedious day of typing into an aesthetically pleasing experience.

Given that most of my days involve sitting at a desk for hours, having a keyboard that I enjoy using is a necessity. I first got a mechanical keyboard about two years ago — the Keychron K2 — and I’ve never looked back.

Keychron is one of the most prominent brands within the mechanical keyboard industry, having made a name for itself after initially launching via Kickstarter back in 2017. The company has since produced dozens of different keyboards (as well as keypads) and a variety of mouse models.

Unlike other electronics, there isn’t a whole lot to owning a mechanical keyboard. The simplicity is part of the appeal. You unbox them, set them up (the K2 comes with little tilt legs that give you a slightly better angle from which to type), and plug them in. 

From here, you have a couple of different options. The K2 comes with a simple USB cable, but there’s also an option for Bluetooth connection. If you value a clean, minimalist workspace, Bluetooth is probably the way to go.

While I am loyal to my older Keychron K2, there are a few upgraded and newer versions to consider. Keychron has released a variety of new models over the past two years, with a broad range of features and price tags.

In many cases, the form factor is the draw. One of the more interesting releases, called the Keychron K8 HE Wireless Magnetic Switch Custom Keyboard, comes with an all-wood body and is equipped with an LED backlight. That one is substantially more expensive at around $200. The K2, meanwhile, costs $60. But if you’re into the look, maybe it’s worth it.

If you’re a gamer, there’s also Keychron’s C0 HE One-Handed 8K Keyboard, which is a keypad built for convenience and speed and has an industrial aesthetic to it. However, interested gamers will have to wait — as it’s currently sold out.

The company has also updated its K, Q, and V series keyboards, with many of those ranging in price from $100 to $200, depending on the features and model.

One of the appealing elements of owning a mechanical keyboard is the versatility. You can swap out the key caps for a wide variety of others (indeed, there’s a whole submarket devoted to this) or make your own custom caps (I’ve never gone that overboard).

There is also the sound, of course. Some people balk at the accentuated noise of loudly clacking keys, but I’m a fan. In fact, the sound is one of the key selling points for a lot of consumers. The distinct auditory experience produced by said keyboards has even made its way into ASMR videos.

For me, the Keychron’s biggest selling point is its retro form factor. I get really nostalgic for old school electronics, and Keychron scratches this itch pretty well. It’s a beautiful-looking device, which brings to mind a different era of computing, when the style was more workman-like, less minimalist.

As far as home office purchases go, you could do a lot worse than to pick yourself up a piece of hardware that makes your desk look like it just time-traveled from the 1990s.

fullText:
WhatsApp’s rollout of Liquid Glass across its interface continues, with the app now bringing the new look to its video player. Here are the details.

WhatsApp’s slow Liquid Glass rollout continues

Following its initial testing of the Liquid Glass redesign in October 2025, WhatsApp went on to officially release the new look only in May 2026, after months of very limited availability.

Even still, the redesign hasn’t reached everyone, as many 9to5Mac readers continue to report seeing the old interface on their devices.

That said, Meta has continued to expand the redesign across WhatsApp in the months since. Liquid Glass began making its way to the iPad app in June, followed by the Mac app in July, while WhatsApp has also continued updating more individual parts of the iPhone interface.

This week, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp started rolling out its Liquid Glass redesign for the video player, after initially revealing that the update was in development back in August.

Here’s WABetaInfo:

Image: WABetaInfo

With the latest update, WhatsApp is adopting the progress bar with the same translucent, glass-like appearance available in other sections of the app. The progress bar appears as a floating element at the top of the screen with a translucent background and rounded corners. In light mode, the background is white with a glass-like layout. In dark mode, the background turns dark. Note that WhatsApp is also refreshing the control bar at the bottom of the screen. This makes the interface more immersive and consistent with the Liquid Glass design language introduced since iOS 26.

The site adds that, for users with access to the new look, the video player was one of the few remaining parts of WhatsApp that had yet to adopt the Liquid Glass design.

As is often the case with WhatsApp feature rollouts, and particularly with the Liquid Glass rollout, the updated video player may not be available to all users just yet.

title: Most US Adults Aren’t Ready for AI to Help With Holiday Shopping, Survey Finds
snippet: Far more people than last year are willing to use AI to help them find the right gift, but few want a bot handling their payment details.
fullText:
AI has the power to be your personal shopping assistant — whether it’s sifting through products to narrow down the right one, tracking the best deals and even ordering items for you without your approval.

But are you really comfortable letting the bots help with your holiday shopping? A recent YouGov survey looked at how US adults feel about it. The results aren’t quite surprising. 

Less than half of Black Friday and Cyber Monday shoppers plan to use AI to help them with holiday shopping. But there’s been some growth since last year. YouGov found that planned AI use has more than doubled within the past year to help navigate sales — from 16% to 34%. 

			

More from CNET

Last year, 21% of holiday shoppers used AI to shop during sales. This year, most of those shoppers (92%) plan to maintain their use of AI or even use it more this year. Only 8% of shoppers who used AI last year plan to scale back on usage this year. But there’s still resistance and hesitancy. Over 4 in 10 (47%) didn’t use AI to shop last year and don’t plan to start this year. Only 22% plan to start this year. What’s the cause for pause?

Most US adults haven’t let AI help them shop yet, but some are considering it

From a global perspective, the US lags behind other countries that use AI tools to help people shop. Over half of adults in Saudi Arabia (54%) and half of adults in India have, while only 18% of adults in the US have. Another 21% said they haven’t yet, but said they would consider doing so. 

That percentage is even higher for Black Friday shoppers, with 30% having already used AI for shopping and 27% considering it.

The divide is stark, however, with 40% of US adults saying they won’t consider using AI for holiday shopping. That’s especially true the further shoppers get into the buying process.

Most shoppers don’t trust AI to make purchases for them

YouGov found that AI is used mostly for discovery when shopping — finding, researching and comparing items. But most shoppers set boundaries the closer they get to checkout. 

Among Black Friday shoppers, 43% say they’re comfortable using AI to find the best deal, while 37% say they’ll use AI tools to track price changes, and 34% compare similar products or offers. But those percentages decline sharply when it’s time to make the purchase. Only 9% would feel comfortable having AI add items to their cart, and 5% would be OK letting AI complete an approved purchase. Only 4% would let it make a purchase without asking. 

Holiday sales aside, AI shoppers are concerned about AI having inaccurate or outdated information (56%), while 51% are concerned about biased or sponsored recommendations. The idea that AI-directed shopping results will steer buyers toward what an advertiser wants, rather than the best deal, may have marketers salivating, but it should give consumers significant pause.

Should you let AI help you shop for the holidays? 

That answer depends on your level of comfort. We know that AI bots can go rogue, share your personal data on the cloud and even spew misinformation. 

I share the same sentiments as many shoppers in the survey. AI has the power to help you narrow down alternatives and find gifts you may not have considered before. It even helped me find a foosball table for my son that I didn’t know existed. But AI hasn’t quite earned my trust to access my payment data, shipping address and other personal details, which could mean big trouble if that data falls into the wrong hands. 

To protect your data, avoid sharing personal details when shopping this season. For instance, simply asking about gifts for a child who loves soccer is enough. There’s no need to share ages or skill levels. You can parse through what’s appropriate yourself.

And double-check any information the bots share — whether it’s deals, product details or, especially, prices. AI tools can be pretty opaque, and you don’t know if you’re actually getting a good deal. Or you may choose to enjoy shopping and perusing deals on your own without the bot’s help to avoid the risks altogether. But if you do decide to enlist AI for automated help, be smart about it.

title: Report: Apple cuts iPhone 18 Pro production due to ‘soft demand’
snippet: Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.” more…
fullText:
Apple has reportedly cut orders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max due to “soft demand.” A new report from Nikkei Asia says Apple has told select suppliers to cut component production for the devices, as price increases allegedly “dampened consumer demand.”

Price hikes reportedly dampen iPhone 18 Pro demand

The report cites “multiple familiar with the matter,” and claims Apple has “turned more conservative on shipments since early September. Two of those sources claim that component orders for October have been cut by “at least 15%” compared to what Apple originally requested.

“In October alone, we are seeing orders from Apple reducing by 15% to 20% for both the premium models; we don’t know how things would develop from here,” said one of the executive-level sources. The order cuts will affect production volumes for some, but not all, suppliers in October due to differing production lead times, and it is not immediately clear whether Apple will make further adjustments from November onward.

Another anonymous supply chain manager told Nikkei Asia that demand is “not as strong as previous years when all the new models are introduced all together.” This, of course, refers to Apple not releasing the base iPhone 18 until next spring. Still, the suppliers say that this alone doesn’t account for the lower demand. 

	

One source added that they expect a “similar fate for the iPhone Duo” after it’s released, referring to potential production cuts.

Apple increased prices for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max by $100 compared to their predecessors. While hampering demand, this also means that the impact of that lower demand won’t “immediately translate to lower revenue for Apple,” the report explains.

Apple will report its fiscal Q4 2026 earnings on Monday, November 6. This will provide a look at the first several weeks of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max demand.

title: Google is ending support for Pixel Watch’s emergency LTE ‘Safety Signal’
snippet: Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection. more…
fullText:
Google launched the Pixel Watch 2 with “Safety Signal” to ensure users could use Emergency SOS and Safety Check without a Bluetooth or cellular signal. Now, those features require a phone or internet connection.

The Pixel ecosystem offers a few different life-saving features under the Safety app, which works both on the Pixel Watch and Pixel phones. That includes Emergency SOS for quick access to emergency services, and Fall Detection, which alerts others when the person wearing the watch takes a hard fall and might not be able to contact someone themselves. But it needs a connection to work.

	

All of those still worked for Fitbit Premium, and then for Google Health Premium users on the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 LTE models, as long as the watch didn’t have a Bluetooth or cellular plan connected. Safety Signal essentially allowed the Pixel Watch 2 or 3 to connect to LTE services for that emergency situation – a solid reassurance that those features would work without your phone or a carrier plan.

Google says support for Safety Signal will end on December 12, which means that the safety net won’t exist for much longer. Google says users who are subscribed to Google Health Premium will get an email notification letting them know 30 days prior to the final shutdown. Safety Signal will be operational until that transition period is over.

	

Safety Signal was just the fallback connection plan. Google’s existing standalone safety features will still work with another connection method:

Safety Check

Emergency Sharing

Emergency SOS

Fall Detection

Even though this feature only worked for the Pixel Watch 2 and 3, and then only for the LTE models, it’s still a huge loss.

title: The best CarPlay upgrades to try in iOS 27
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone a few weeks ago, and it includes several CarPlay changes worth checking out. Here are a few changes I’ve been loving so far.

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save!

CarPlay features to try in iOS 27

Siri AI

Siri AI is the flagship feature of iOS 27, and it extends to CarPlay. In fact, I’ve found it to be especially useful via CarPlay. Siri AI can answer questions around your personal context, world knowledge, and much more in iOS 27.

For example, you can ask Siri to find a specific address or location in your email or text messages, then begin routing to that location, all while using just your voice.

Robust, hands-free control is important in the car, and iOS 27 finally gives Siri the power that it deserves in CarPlay.

Now Playing changes

CarPlay in iOS 27 offers a persistent “Now Playing” MiniPlayer throughout audio apps. This appears in the upper-right corner of the interface and shows playback controls and album artwork.

The Now Playing interface in CarPlay has also been updated to include an audio scrubber at long last. You can drag the scrubber to easily skip to different parts of a song or podcast without using steering wheel controls or reaching for your iPhone.

New wallpapers

CarPlay isn’t known for its robust collection of wallpapers, and Apple doesn’t let you use your own photos for some reason.

In iOS 27, Apple has at least added a collection of new wallpapers that you can choose from. They are similar to the stock iOS 27 wallpapers available on iPhone.

Stability improvements

iOS 27 focuses a lot on platform improvements to performance and reliability, and that applies to CarPlay too. Apple says iOS 27 addresses two key things in CarPlay:

Improved navigation heading and GPS accuracy in CarPlay

Improved wireless CarPlay reliability

So if you’ve ever had problems with those two things in CarPlay, it’s possible that iOS 27 makes the experience much better.

Coming soon(ish): Video app support

Finally, Apple says that developers can now make dedicated video apps for CarPlay in iOS 27. The feature, however, requires support from automakers. This means it might be a while before you can actually use any video apps with CarPlay in your vehicle.

Wrap up

While the dream for many people is still CarPlay Ultra, it’s really nice to see Apple make meaningful improvements to the version of CarPlay already available in millions of cars on the road today.

Have you updated to iOS 27? What CarPlay changes have you noticed? Let us know down in the comments.

title: Apple TV’s latest acquisition signals key shift for streamer
snippet: Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy. more…
fullText:
Apple TV just acquired the global streaming rights to Dustfall, a crime series from Australia and the second recent deviation from the streamer’s originals-only strategy.

Apple has started licensing more TV series, deviating from all-originals strategy

Ever since Apple TV launched in 2019, it rejected the typical streaming approach of licensing existing content and instead prioritized originals.

Apple has been remarkably consistent with its originals-only strategy. Until recently, the only exceptions have been children’s content that complement its originals (like Peanuts holiday specials), and limited-time bonus films.

But that changed this week, when acclaimed comedy Small Prophets premiered after Apple acquired the rights to the British breakout hit over the summer.

Small Prophets seems like a savvy acquisition. Early reviews call it a “masterpiece” and perhaps “the finest show to hit Apple this year.”

Now today, Apple has announced a second acquisition. Dustfall, an Anna Torv-starring crime series that originated in Australia, will join the streamer in 2027.

Like Small Prophets, Dustfall was created by an international production company and will air in select territories overseas before its global Apple TV premiere.

Clearly, Apple sees acquisitions differently than it once did.

While the streamer isn’t abandoning its successful original-first approach, licensing high-quality series from around the world to beef up its catalog is very much a strategic shift.

And it’s one I’m curious if we’ll see accelerate moving forward.

What do you think of Apple TV licensing third-party series? Let us know in the comments.
