title: Google Home update fixes broken smart light color control
snippet: Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now. more…
fullText:
Color LED bulbs were refusing to do their job because of a Google Home bug. Google says the fix is rolling out now.

According to a few users on Reddit, Google Home isn’t properly adjusting color on smart bulbs. Users say it hasn’t been limited to just one brand, but devices across multiple brands like Philips Hue, Tuya, and Lumiman. The issue was affecting both voice controls and app controls, which are usually more reliable and easier to adjust. But the color sliders did nothing for affected users.

Google responded to the Reddit thread to say a fix is currently rolling out. The post author has since updated the thread to say their voice commands and app are now reliably controlling bulb color.

The post was barely a day old when Google first let users know it was working on a fix. Just a few hours later, an update was rolling out. The quick turnaround is likely appreciated for this bug because it broke a critical component and selling point for not only Google Home but also smart bulb manufacturers.

	

Color control might have been broken while Google works on other additions to the app. Monthly updates are being released to address the functions and bugs appearing as Google Assistant fades into the background, which has officially happened as of last month.

Were/are you experiencing a bug that broke smart bulb color control? It should be fixed now, but if it isn’t, let us know.

title: Formula 1 on Apple TV is getting Dolby Atmos, starting this month
snippet: Beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend on Friday, October 23, Apple TV will offer Formula 1 coverage in Dolby Atmos on supported devices. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Beginning with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend on Friday, October 23, Apple TV will offer Formula 1 coverage in Dolby Atmos on supported devices. Here are the details.

’Bringing exceptional picture and sound together to capture the full intensity of the sport’

Apple and Dolby Laboratories announced a new partnership to bring Dolby Atmos to Apple TV’s live Formula 1 coverage, starting with the U.S. Grand Prix weekend, which begins October 23 in Austin, Texas.

Apple says Dolby Atmos will join “Dolby Vision to deliver an even more immersive viewing experience,” putting “fans at the heart of the action, surrounding them with the energy, drama, and emotion of Formula 1.”

From team radio communications and race commentary to the roar of the engines, on-track battles, and the intensity of the pit lane, Dolby Atmos brings the unmistakable sounds that define the sport to life.

Here’s Oliver Schusser, Vice President of Apple Music and International Content at Apple, on the announcement:

“We’re always looking for new ways to make Formula 1 on Apple TV even better for fans. […] The sound of Formula 1 is such an important part of what makes the sport so exciting, and with Dolby Atmos joining Dolby Vision, fans can experience the energy and intensity of every Grand Prix in a whole new way. It’s another example of how we’re continuing to innovate across the viewing experience to bring fans closer to the action.”

It’s worth noting that Apple TV’s streaming rights for Formula 1 still include only the U.S., but don’t require an extra subscription on top of the Apple TV subscription.

Apple recently made the Bahrain Grand Prix available to stream for free in the U.S., and has also partnered with Netflix to bring Formula 1: Drive to Survive Season 8 to Apple TV in the U.S. As part of the same collaboration, the 2026 Canadian Grand Prix was streamed live on both Apple TV and Netflix in the U.S.

Apple secured the U.S. streaming rights to Formula 1 in 2025 as part of a five-year deal beginning with the 2026 season, and has previously indicated it wants to expand its F1 coverage into additional markets.

Apple’s broader relationship with Formula 1 also includes “F1: The Movie,” which won the Academy Award for Best Sound earlier this year and remains Apple’s biggest theatrical success to date.

Apple TV is available for $14.99 per month or as part of the Apple One bundle. It features hit TV shows and movies like Ted Lasso, Severance, The Studio, The Morning Show, Shrinking, and Silo.

title: Grok Bot just got a lot smarter thanks to Anthropic’s Claude
snippet: SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot kicked off the consumer-friendly AI agent app wave this summer. Facing competition from Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s ChatGPT Dot, Grok Bot just got a new capability upgrade with the help of Anthropic’s Claude. more…
fullText:
SpaceXAI’s Grok Bot kicked off the consumer-friendly AI agent app wave this summer. Facing competition from Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s ChatGPT Dot, Grok Bot just got a new capability upgrade with the help of Anthropic’s Claude.

Grok Bot now uses Claude Opus 5.5 for intelligence

Grok Bot launched in August with dedicated apps for the iPhone and iPad. An iPad version and more affordable plans arrived in September.

For October, Grok Bot is getting a major backend upgrade that will see Anthropic’s Claude be used for intelligence instead of SpaceXAI/Cursor’s less capable models. 

For context, Anthropic became a SpaceX customer this year as it shopped for compute to power Claude usage.

As of today, Grok Bot can now use Claude Opus 5.5, the newest version of one of Anthropic’s most capable models. 

Grok Bot’s upgrade comes as Meta pushes its mostly-free Muse agent, newly available for iPad, and OpenAI builds out ChatGPT Dot, an Astra-powered proactive agent.

Grok Bot is available for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Have you used any of these AI agent systems yet?

title: Elon Musk intensifies attack on Ambani over Starlink India launch delay
snippet: Elon Musk has accused Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani of blocking competition.
fullText:
As SpaceX struggles to launch Starlink in India, Elon Musk has stepped up his attack on billionaire Mukesh Ambani, mockingly calling him the country’s “prime minister” to suggest he wields outsized control over its government and accusing him of blocking the satellite internet service from competing.

On Friday, Musk continued his criticism of the famed Reliance Industries’ chairperson in a post on X, arguing that Starlink could bring internet access to areas that remain unconnected, giving children more opportunities to learn, and helping small businesses reach customers worldwide.

“Naturally, you would prefer to maintain your monopolistic exploitation of the great people of India, but would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?” Musk wrote.

Reliance Jio, Reliance Industries’ telecom arm, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Musk’s latest comments follow his accusations earlier this week that unnamed “oligarchs” were blocking Starlink’s launch in India to protect their business interests. India’s Ministry of Communications rejected the allegations, saying the country’s regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory.” Musk then went further on Thursday, questioning Ambani’s influence in a separate post on X. “Is Ambani the real boss of India?” he asked.

SpaceX has spent years trying to launch Starlink in India. Last year, it even struck distribution agreements with Ambani’s Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, India’s second-largest telecom operator, to offer the service once it received the necessary approvals. However, Starlink has not yet received the go-ahead from New Delhi to begin commercial operations, despite securing key regulatory clearances.

In its Thursday statement, the Indian communication ministry said Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can receive satellite spectrum. The ministry said all three are at “broadly the same regulatory stage,” rejecting Musk’s suggestion that Starlink was being singled out.

Jio and Airtel are also seeking to launch their satellite internet services in India. Jio has a joint venture with Luxembourg-based SES, while Airtel is a major shareholder in Eutelsat OneWeb, which is striving to offer satellite connectivity in the country.

India, the world’s most populous country with over a billion internet users, is a major market for Musk. But expanding there also means dealing with powerful business figures such as Ambani, whose Reliance conglomerate owns India’s largest telecom operator and works with Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government on major projects.

Alongside Starlink’s delayed launch, Musk has also faced challenges expanding Tesla in India. The electric carmaker launched in the country last year after years of anticipation but registered just 699 vehicles in its first 12 months of deliveries, according to data cited by Electrek. Steep import duties pushed the Model Y’s launch price in India to nearly twice its U.S. price. Tesla lowered its prices earlier this year, but its cars remain considerably more expensive in India than in the U.S.

Before Musk’s latest attack, Starlink and Ambani’s Reliance Jio clashed over how to allocate satellite spectrum in India. Musk’s company wanted the spectrum to be assigned through an administrative process, while Jio pushed for an auction. Ultimately, New Delhi went ahead with Starlink and decided to allocate the spectrum administratively.

Starlink’s launch in India remains in limbo. India’s telecom minister Jyotiraditya Scindia on Friday pushed back against Musk’s allegations, saying the country “does not allow a monopoly in any sector.”

title: Google starts rolling out its upgraded Pixel screen savers to the Pixel 9
snippet: When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets. more…
fullText:
When Google added Pixelsnap to the Pixel 10 series, it wasn’t just building in support for all kinds of magnetic accessories — it was also adding in some excellent software functionality, like upgraded screensavers for when your phone is docked and charging. After gaining some new styles and features alongside the launch of the Pixel 11, Google is finally bringing these upgraded styles to older hardware, despite the lack of magnets.

A select group of users are starting to spot these screensavers being added to older Pixels, beginning with the Pixel 9, as reported by Android Authority. Earlier Pixels did have support for a basic screensaver tool, but with this upgrade, every option available on Google’s latest releases have finally been backported to its 2024 hardware. The update appears to include a pop-up demo of these new options, along with everything currently available as of the Pixel 11’s launch. Clock, Charge, Weather, Photos, and Home Controls are all available, and can be swiped through at will. And speaking of Charge, it too seems to be headed to the Pixel 10 series, after having been exclusive to the Pixel 11 for the past two months.

Unfortunately, it does seem like this is one of Google’s classic slow rollouts. There aren’t a massive amount of reports from Pixel 9 users that these styles are live on their devices, implying it might take a few weeks before reaching everyone. The same goes for Charge on the Pixel 10, with plenty of Redditors confirming they have yet to see that specific style arrive.

title: XREAL Aura with Android XR start at $1,279
snippet: XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279. more…
fullText:
XREAL’s first pair of Android XR glasses, XREAL Aura, finally have a price tag – $1,279.

XREAL makes glasses that aren’t a traditional VR headset, nor are they the smart glasses we’ve imagined for the future. They sit somewhere in between, with a display that sits atop a see-through lens so you can mix the display’s content with the real world around you, no cameras needed. 

As we noted in a review of XREAL One Pro, though, the base experience of using the glasses to display content from a USB-C device like a laptop, phone, or handheld game console is a bit limited. Android XR’s promises are set to deliver a big upgrade to the experience, and that’s exactly what XREAL has been building.

XREAL Aura is effectively the same core idea, just with an included puck that has a battery, processing power, and Android XR. And it starts at $1,279, the company has today confirmed. The price of XREAL Aura was the missing puzzle piece for months, and it’s actually well below the company’s promise of “under $1,500.”

	

That’s for the base 12GB/256GB model, with an upgraded version costing a bit more:

XREAL Aura 12GB/256GB: $1,279

XREAL Aura 16GB/512GB: $1,499

There’s no charge for the medium or large size difference.

As far as actually putting in an order, XREAL says the initial delivery wave will arrive “before the holidays,” with a second wave presumably arriving sometime in early 2027. You have to purchase a $199 “Priority Deposit” to place a pre-order, with the cost going towards the price of your Aura glasses.

title: The Feds Might Do Something About Those Distractingly Bright Headlights
snippet: NHTSA blames current vehicle standards for making it hard for carmakers to use the latest headlight tech.
fullText:
The blinding glare of LED headlights from oncoming traffic searing your retinas may become a thing of the past. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration announced this week that it intends to update vehicle lighting standards as part of changes to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108. 

In simple terms, it means the administration could move to make LED headlights less blinding. The last time lighting standards were updated was 25 years ago, which is one reason US lighting regulations have allowed vehicles to have skull-searing headlights not typically seen in Europe or Japan.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison said in a press statement. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.” 

			

More from CNET

LED headlights make sense for an electric car, as they put minimal power drain on the batteries.

James Martin/CNET

The new regulations will update rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams and replaceable light sources. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will appoint up to 18 industry stakeholders, safety advocates and technical experts to evaluate how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility as part of efforts to align US vehicles with international safety standards.

Since 2022, companies have been allowed to use adaptive driving beams, which are dynamic systems that can keep high beams on while dimming portions of the beam to avoid glare to oncoming drivers. However, the implementation of this policy doesn’t match the same standards seen in Europe.

Some companies are already positioned to take advantage of the changes with their upcoming models. Rivian, with its R1T and R1S Gen 2 models, already uses this type of lighting. Audi will debut its 2027 Q9 flagship SUV with the technology.

Better headlights would come as a welcome change for many drivers. Gripes about blinding LED headlights are well documented, with an entire subreddit of 12,000 members dedicated to the topic. Reuters, citing a study from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, says that from 2015 to 2023, headlight glare was cited as a factor in one or two out of every 1,000 nighttime crashes across 11 US states, though it noted that this is far fewer than the number of crashes caused by insufficient visibility.

Anecdotally, complaints about the brightness of headlights are a common topic in one of my group chats, with one member saying they often feel like the headlights are radioactive and can “X-ray and skeletonize oncoming drivers.” 

NHTSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

New Apple TV and HomePod features leaked in code are expected to be announced next week

Next week, Apple will unveil a fresh push into Home products, with new Apple TV 4K, ‘HomePad,’ and HomePod mini models set to launch.

We’ve already gotten plenty of leaks around new features to expect, but yesterday’s beta 3 releases of tvOS 27.2, HomePod 27.2, and iOS 27.2 reveal even more.

Aaron Perris found references in tvOS 27.2 beta 3 to Apple Intelligence coming to Apple TV. Headlined by Siri AI, these AI features are expected to be exclusive to new hardware.

title: Google Wallet rolling out stacked card list redesign on Android
snippet: After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards. more…
fullText:
After updating the bottom half of the homepage earlier this year, Google Wallet for Android is rolling out a stacked list redesign for accessing credit and debit cards.

The previous design made use of a carousel to show your stored payment methods. This design showed just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google allowed you to reorder cards and set a default one.

	

With this stacked redesign, the homepage shows one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen layout that shows most of each card. “Manage payment methods” at the bottom lets you arrange the order and set the default.

You select a card to tap-to-pay. To see card details and transaction history, there’s a new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This adds an extra step compared to the previous approach.

	

This approach is nice for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom. There are no other changes to the Google Wallet homepage.

This redesign started appearing in September and is now seeing broader availability. It’s rolling out via a server-side update and appeared on several devices we checked today.

title: Googlebooks can’t install the Slack web app on day one
snippet: Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is now on sale and shipping to customers and, on day one at least, they can’t install the Slack web app. 

Googlebook as a platform relies on two main forms of apps. The first is native Android apps, as Googlebook OS is, at its core, Android. That’s what you’ll use for many experiences including Gemini, Google Photos, music apps, and more. Others, like Gmail and YouTube, instead rely on progressive web apps. That term might sound familiar if you’re a long-time Chromebook user, as Chromebooks bet pretty heavily on progressive web apps (PWAs).

That history aside, Googlebooks directly tell their users to use Slack through the web app. The Play Store puts up a banner saying that Slack is “better on the website” when you try to download the Android app. 

That’s correct, frankly, as Slack’s Android app has terrible support for anything besides a standard smartphone. 

	

But the Slack web app cannot be installed on a Googlebook at this time.

	

Trying to install the Slack web app as a PWA on Googlebook results in an error message saying that “this app cannot be installed.” You can still create a shortcut that opens as a Chrome tab, but it won’t open in a window. 

Other PWAs we’ve tested including Photopea, Squoosh, SnapDrop, and others seem to be working fine. It’s unclear why Slack in particular is broken, but it’s hard to imagine it’s the only PWA not working on Googlebook on day one. More importantly, Slack is a mainstay in the modern workspace, so lacking any form of desktop-level Slack support on day one is sure to leave a poor impression on early Googlebook adopters.

Update: Google, in a statement, says that Slack is not a “compliant” PWA but that Googlebook will add support for manual installation soon.

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

title: ‘HomePad’ is coming next week, with three features I’ve long wanted
snippet: Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for. more…
fullText:
Apple’s long-rumored ‘HomePad’ product is finally set to be unveiled next Tuesday at the ‘Welcome home’ event. Here are three HomePad features I’ve been waiting a long time for.

#1: Apple Photos on a digital picture frame

Digital picture frames are nothing new. But I’ve never owned one, in large part for two reasons:

All my pictures live in Apple Photos

I don’t want to manually add pictures to the digital frame

There are currently zero digital picture frames with native Apple Photos integration for an effort-free experience. But with the HomePad, rumors indicate there’s a Photos face available that will automatically cycle through pictures from Apple Photos.

This is exactly what I’ve been wanting for years. I hope to put several HomePads throughout the house so they can surprise and delight me with memories at every turn (while providing other key features too).

#2: Apple Music in the home with lyrics onscreen

I own a few HomePods, and enjoy listening to music with them. But what I’ve really wanted for a long time is the chance to see lyrics while listening.

Thanks to AirPlay, I can do this with my iPhone while music plays through the HomePod. I rarely do this, though, because I try to avoid pulling my phone out as much as possible with family around.

With HomePad though, all signs point to the Music app letting you view lyrics onscreen while a song is playing. I’m terrible at picking up lyrics just by ear, so I’m excited for the chance to better learn songs while staying in the moment with family members when we’re listening together.

#3: Siri AI in a HomePod-like device with a display

	

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri. Unlike the old Siri on my HomePods, Siri AI can handle basically any question you throw at it. And with the HomePad, not only will Siri’s intelligence get a boost—it will also be able to show visuals in its responses.

I ask Siri on my HomePods to do basic things like set reminders, or provide info on the weather. But with Siri AI on the HomePad, I imagine I’ll turn to Siri far more often than I ever have. That’s already been true with Siri AI on my iPhone.

Having Apple’s new AI assistant all throughout the house, and equipped with a display for showing visual results, should prove a big improvement from my current HomePod setup.

title: iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, finds mixed repairability results
snippet: Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found. more…
fullText:
Concluding iFixit’s teardown sequence for Apple’s September launches, iFixit today published the teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Here’s what they found.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Ultra 4

After applying heat to the new Apple Watch Ultra 4’s screen, iFixit’s Shahram Mokhtari uses the company’s new metal pick to pry the screen open, exposing the battery and the Taptic Engine.

He notes that replacing the 2.444 Wh battery (versus 2.313 Wh in the Ultra 3) still requires removing the screen, which remains a significant repairability drawback. The four screws on the bottom of the case provide access only to the sensor assembly on the underside of the back cover and the S11 chip on the case itself.

Once the screen is unglued, though, removing the battery and disconnecting the display’s press connector seems straightforward enough, provided that the initial step was done carefully enough to avoid slicing through any of the flex cables underneath.

That said, with no significant improvements in repairability, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 scored 4/10 on iFixit’s repairability scale, the same as its predecessor.

iFixit tears down Apple Watch Series 12

iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple Watch Series 12 revealed a slight repairability improvement, with Apple adding stretch-release adhesive and a pull tab that make the 1.461 Wh battery (versus 1.403 Wh in the 46mm Series 11) easier to remove.

Still, as with the Apple Watch Ultra 4, the Series 12 also requires prying off the glued display to get inside, which remains the biggest obstacle to repairs. Mokhtari noted that the tolerances around the Series 12’s display are even tighter than on the Ultra 4, requiring enough force to make him concerned about potentially damaging the screen.

Mokhtari also noted that Apple replaced the ZIF connector and tape used for the display on previous models with a simpler press connector.

The tradeoff is that replacing the screen now also requires removing and replacing the battery, “which, if you’ve come this far, why wouldn’t you?” he adds.

All in all, the modest repairability improvements were enough for iFixit to give the Series 12 a 4/10 repairability score, a 1-point bump from the last base-model Apple Watch it scored.

For comparison, iFixit gave Google’s Pixel Watch 5 a 9/10 repairability score, noting that its display can be removed with just two Torx screws and a gasket, while its battery can also be removed without dealing with adhesive.

title: Googlebook’s hidden ‘Glowbar Disco’ turns your laptop’s lid into a light show — how to find it
snippet: Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank. more…
fullText:
Buried in the settings of Googlebook is a “Glowbar Disco” app that activates the LEDs on your laptop constantly, instead of leaving it blank.

The Glowbar on Googlebook is a carryover from the iconic light bar on the original Chromebook Pixel. It doesn’t function quite the same, lacking the fun and useful “knock knock” gesture that Google’s original offered, but it still shows battery on plug-in, and serves as a nice accent too.

But, hidden behind the scenes is more control over the glowbar.

The “Glowbar Disco” app is an Easter egg buried deep within the OS, and even Google’s Alexander Kuscher admits it might be “too hard to find.” The app itself lets you set the Glowbar on a Googlebook to show a constant color, a preset animation, a gradient of colors, or even sync with music. It leaves the Glowbar active whenever the machine is turned on and the Disco app is open, and it’s a super fun little addition.

	

Finding the app, though, is not exactly an easy task. 

You’ll have to go to Settings > Apps then allow the search function to show system apps, then search for “Glowbar Disco.” From there you can launch the app, but you’ll need to repeat that process every time you want to access it. And, if you close the app, the effects stop.

If you ask me, this should be baked into the Settings because it is very fun. Hopefully that’ll change in time — Googlebooks certainly need a lot of updates.

title: From Zuck to Musk: Big Tech’s Scandals and Scammers Are Coming to the Big Screen
snippet: Here are the movies to keep an “AI” on through the rest of the year.
fullText:
Hollywood is unleashing a handful of movies this fall, pulling the curtain back to shine a light on some of the big names in tech: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg; Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk; Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes; and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

Plenty of movies have tackled themes of techno-pessimism and dug into the deep well of science fiction. Remember 2001: A Space Odyssey? Blade Runner? M3GAN? But apocalyptic threats and human-versus-machine scenarios feel much more prescient in 2026. 

What’s changed is that there seems to be an appetite for Big Tech to get its comeuppance. The movies being released are real stories about the scandals and scammers affecting our daily lives.  

			

More from CNET

The Social Reckoning (Oct. 9)

The Social Reckoning continues the story Aaron Sorkin began with the 2010 film The Social Network about Facebook. The Oscar and Emmy-winning screenwriter stepped behind the camera to helm the movie, which he once again wrote.

The Social Reckoning highlights the societal damage caused by Zuckerberg’s social media empire. Based on thousands of leaked documents from former Facebook engineer Frances Haugen, the movie draws inspiration from the 2021 Wall Street Journal article The Facebook Files, which documents the whistleblower’s actions and the subsequent fallout.

Succession star Jeremy Strong now plays Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg played the bright-eyed college student 16 years ago). The film also stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White, Billy Magnussen, Bill Burr and Betty Gilpin.

The Social Reckoning hits theaters Friday.

Musk (Oct. 16)

The upcoming documentary Musk is by lauded filmmaker Alex Gibney, whose work includes Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley. 

Running about 4 hours, the movie delves into the life and legend of Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, and (cue Dr. Evil’s theme music) the richest man in the world. Given that the film seems to dismantle the mythos he built and sold along the way, Musk hasn’t had kind words to say, calling the movie a “hit piece” and Gibney a “douchebag” in a social media rant.

For a brief period, ads for the movie were barred from social media platforms Meta, YouTube, TikTok and X. Google and Meta have since cleared the way for promotional materials for Musk, while the other platforms have remained silent.

Musk hits theaters on Oct. 16 and will stream on HBO Max next year.

You Can See Everything (Oct. 16)

In case you’re unfamiliar with the story of Holmes, Gibney’s 2019 movie is a good place to start. You could also try the 2022 Hulu original series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried. Holmes, who was the face of Theranos, a short-lived blood-testing company, was indicted in June 2018 for fraud and conspiracy.

You Can See Everything is a nearly 3-hour-long documentary by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim (the director of the Chris Hanson drama Primetime), which appears more like a psychological horror film than a nonfiction narrative. The new movie follows Fielder into the private life of Holmes and her family, roughly a month before she was to report to prison. You Can See Everything has a hefty amount of buzz behind it and is turning into one of fall’s must-see theatrical releases.

You Can See Everything is released Oct. 16. 

Artificial (Dec. 25)

Italian film director Luca Guadagnino (Call Me By Your Name and Queer) turns his eye on OpenAI’s Altman in his upcoming biopic, Artificial. Just like The Social Reckoning, this isn’t a documentary, and it’s already generating substantial Oscar buzz.

Artificial takes place in 2023 and follows the tumultuous period when Altman was fired by OpenAI and then rehired five days later. Amazon MGM Studios was originally set to distribute the movie, but after signing a multiyear partnership with OpenAI, it stepped away from the project. Neon came in and picked up the film, which also stars Billie Lourd, Monica Barbaro, Chris O’Dowd, Jason Schwartzman, Zozia Mamet and Ike Barinholtz (who plays Musk).

Artificial will premiere in theaters on Christmas Day.

Now streaming: More big tech backlash

If you’re watching from home, you can also cash in on the Big Tech dystopia genre. 

AMC’s The Audacity is a fictional account of the Silicon Valley tech bubble. Season 1 is now streaming on Netflix. While I’m on the subject of Netflix, the streamer has the documentary The AI Doc or How I Became an Apocaloptimist and will soon release AI Gone Wild, a new Instadoc about the rather infamous Hugging Face cyberattack. The streamer will also debut The Altruists, an eight-episode true-crime series about the 2022 collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s cryptocurrency empire, FTX, on Nov. 19. There’s even a legal procedural called Cupertino coming to CBS this week about Silicon Valley lawyers.

title: New Crossy Road game announced as an Apple Arcade exclusive
snippet: Starting November 5, Apple Arcade subscribers will get access to Crossy Road Rush, a new arcade island adventure with solo and four-player multiplayer racing modes. Watch the trailer for the new game below. more…
fullText:
Starting November 5, Apple Arcade subscribers will get access to Crossy Road Rush, a new arcade island adventure with solo and four-player multiplayer racing modes. Watch the trailer for the new game below.

Crossy Road Rush coming November 5

Apple Arcade and Hipster Whale made a joint announcement today, confirming that the new Crossy Road Rush title will be launched exclusively on Apple’s gaming subscription platform starting November 5.

The game follows the classic Crossy Road and Crossy Road Castle aesthetic, with its colorful voxel-style characters and environments, but adds a more adventure-focused structure with combat, exploration, and multiplayer.

Here’s how Crossy Road’s YouTube channel describes the new Apple Arcade-exclusive title:

Swerve, spin, smash and survive an arcade island adventure with the Crossy Road Crew. Chase away an angry Octoboss from peaceful Crossy Cove, free your friends, and restore the island vibes! Ride solo, or connect locally and online with up to 4 players!

The game is scheduled to launch at 4:00 p.m. PST on November 5, but Apple Arcade subscribers can pre-order it now here.

Today’s announcement comes just days after Apple Arcade added five new titles earlier this month: Pusheen’s Place, River City Survivors, Terraria+, Touchgrind BMX 2+, and 4 Pics 1 Word+.

Watch the trailer for Crossy Road Rush below:

Pre-order Crossy Road Rush on Apple Arcade

title: Galaxy Watch 9 drops to $319, but not on Amazon during Prime Day
snippet: The Galaxy Watch 9, Samsung’s newest model, is currently $60 off while most shoppers rush to Amazon to snatch up Prime Day deals. This might be a better option. more…
fullText:
The Galaxy Watch 9, Samsung’s newest model, is currently $60 off while most shoppers rush to Amazon to snatch up Prime Day deals. This might be a better option.

On Amazon, the Galaxy Watch is just as expensive as it always is – $379 for the 40mm edition. For whatever reason, Samsung has chosen not to lower the price for its latest smartwatches on the massive online retailer. Instead, it’s running its own deal.

On Samsung’s official online shop, the Galaxy Watch 9 series is as low as $319 for the 40mm Bluetooth version. The 44mm variant is also $60 off at $349. That’s down from the original $409 price tag.

Samsung’s site is offering a flat $60 off both devices during its current deal. Last month, the price dropped to a similar $299, but it’s gone up just a little. Not enough to mark this deal as negligible, because it’s still a rather good buy for what is essentially a brand-new watch released only a few months ago.

	

Something of note – trading in a Galaxy Watch 8 will remove another $150 from the discount price.

The Galaxy Watch 9 series packs a ton of features we’ve covered in depth, including improved health tracking, One UI 9 for the smartwatch, and better performance. It also offers Gemini raise-to-talk, which is something only available on the Pixel Watch series previously. The watch is also guaranteed five years of updates, which is a first.

We’re not sure how long this deal will last, but it sure beats any Galaxy Watch 9 deals on Amazon. If you don’t need to get the latest version, you also have the option to get the Galaxy Watch 8 from Amazon, which is marked down to $219.

fullText:
Cristian Mungiu’s sixth feature, Fjord, concerns a family on trial. They seem like good people, God-fearing. They’ve just moved from Romania to a small hamlet nestled in the fjords of rural Norway. There is Mamma (Renate Reinsve), Tata (a bald and bespectacled Sebastian Stan), and their passel of children. They are an openly religious and proselytizing family. The parents, unfashionably, believe in punitive consequences to actions. They would never be accused of gentle parenting. All ought to be well, only Norway in 2026 is extravagantly suspicious of the devout — their famous tolerance reserved for the secular.

Fjord starts quietly and builds subtly. We are with the family as they are introduced to their places of learning, employment, and worship. A second, Norwegian, family serves as their foil. Sort of. Questions arise, about what counts as discipline, what as punishment. To those wanting answers, objective analysis, which is to say a kind of measured purity, Mungiu says, come down to the mud with us! In the morally complex world of the movie, nothing is spared — a piano chord, a passing remark, hems of clothes — all are cast in a different light. We are all the more enriched for it.

The Verge spoke with Mungiu, who is himself Romanian, about how his early tenure in journalism informs his writing, what it was like living under Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial reign, Marxist literary theory, and the challenges and pleasures of thinking for oneself.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

I’d like to start with you at Cannes, where you said the question that Fjord raises is: Are there good minorities and bad minorities? I wonder if this question has changed for you since. 

Not so much. I think that as much as we need to understand that there are good values in society, like tolerance for all the other minorities and inclusion of those who are different than us, we should always focus on this idea that sometimes even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well. If not, what makes us believe that we have a more liberal, progressive view on the world?

Of course, there is a limit. We all need to condemn violence, and we all need to be on the same side of helping people out.

But whenever we talk about, for example, religious beliefs, even if we are people who don’t share such beliefs, it’s good to be tolerant with them, if they want to share different views. You need to let them be.

“Even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well.”

There are so many people next to us who share a lot of irrational beliefs, from reading the horoscope to believing in alternative medicine. We let them be. Why would we condemn people for being religious? It’s good to try to convince them that actually it’s good to see that your beliefs are based on something rational, because eventually, we all influence the lives of others, and it’s good to make choices based on rational things. But you need to advance little by little, step by step. I don’t believe in this way of imposing views on others and making rules for others to change what they think. If you do that, you will only radicalize people.

You said you kept chancing upon articles about immigrant families in Nordic countries. Is reading the news part of your practice? Otherwise, where have your ideas come from?

I read a lot of news every day, and I keep a lot of these articles in special folders under different themes. And it took years before I decided to make a film based on the ideas in these articles, because in the beginning they are very spectacular. They are just informing us about something spectacular that has happened. While for me, the film should be something deeper, more profound, in the sense that I’m trying to figure out why those things have happened and what do they tell us about the world around us?

I try to avoid the sensational part of it and to try to dig down, and to understand what is it that it could tell you about your own life, and this is what I did for the original story as well. I needed some eight years from the moment when I read about it to the moment when I decided to make a film out of it.

Tell me more about your excavation process. Can you walk us through what is actually happening in those eight years? And specifically, can you tell us about the moment in the process when you go from research to fiction? What does that leap look like, or maybe it’s seamless?

It’s fair to say that I haven’t used all these 10 years to investigate. But I was aware all the time that this exists. For example, I decided to talk to this family who was involved in the most prominent case, in the most spoken-about case, from three years ago. I talked to them. I talked to their children. I went to Norway. I met their relatives. I went to see the house where everything happened. I took advantage in that moment to investigate more, and I met everybody that I could who was involved in that case. And people who were willing to talk to me. I talked to lawyers. I talked to all the press that covered the case. I talked to the translator they were having when talking to the police. I talked to the Barnevernet [Norwegian child welfare agency]. I talked to the NGOs who were involved a lot in such cases. Later on, I was a witness to the trials they were having on children issues. So I did my best to find all the points of view of people involved, not only in that case but in other cases.

And finally, I crafted the screenplay based a lot on the arguments that I was recording. I didn’t have to invent much. I just needed to organize the material, but I didn’t need to build a lot on what are the arguments of each of these two sides.

The fictional part of the film comes a lot from this second family, which is fully fictional, and that gave me the possibility of following the film from the point of view of the adults. I needed to be with the family, but I wanted to balance this point of view of the family with the point of view of another family with children and sharing the values of the society in which they live, a family with whom they need to communicate with because they are secluded in this fjord at the end of the world, and it was important for me to see how these values collide, and what changes in this process of being forced to communicate with others.

Tell us about your time as a reporter, early in your career. How did you decide to turn to film?

I started working in the press in 1987, and also this was a part of me getting closer to what I wanted to do. I wished that I could become a storyteller, and I wished already at that age — I was 19 — that I could become a filmmaker. Back then, becoming a student at the film school during communist times wasn’t really a fair process, so it wasn’t for me. So I was starting to get closer to becoming a writer. This is what I thought I could do. I started writing. And then I got to this newspaper, and I started practicing my writing and taking pictures. Two activities which were as close as I could to becoming a filmmaker without being able to become one on the spot. A lot of my style of writing screenplays today is still based on that period in which I learned how to write a piece of news.

But happily, you know, the wall fell. Communism collapsed. It was very passionate to be in the press for a while because people were hungry for what they were calling “truth” after such a long period in which we didn’t have a free press.

My style of writing was shaped in that period. I am not bringing, when I describe things, my own point of view. I’m describing an external situation, the way in which these things manifest, but I don’t draw the conclusion. I depict a situation, and I encourage you to use your critical spirit to understand the way it manifests. I am encouraging you also to take on this responsibility as a spectator, in which I’m not guiding you through the story. You have your freedom of interpreting based on facts, and making sure you analyze the facts. If you’re just analyzing what the characters say, you might be very easily manipulated. Manipulated, because, as you know, in cinema, characters lie, and are as manipulative as people are in real lives.

So it’s not that you wanted to be a filmmaker as such, but that you wanted to be a storyteller, and you found film?

I wanted to be a storyteller, and I thought that I’m going to be a writer. Then I was undergoing this period in my life in which I was watching a lot of films, very popular films.

Also being influenced by the Romanian films that I could watch in the period, which were very strange. Maybe it was, in part, the censorship, but probably it was also that the people that were encouraged to make films were not very talented. But they seemed to be made with people looking like us, and apparently using the same language as us, but actually nothing like that ever happened in reality. They were psychologically so unbelievable, and the dialogue was also a message that somebody wrote in the right order grammatically, and it was pure propaganda.

So, we started developing this idea that it shouldn’t be this complicated to make films. You just need to co-opt reality.

I want to tell you something funny about the message that I got today. Following a lot of these cases in the Nordic countries and talking to so many people, I became some sort of an expert.

I got a message this morning from a half-German, half-Norwegian family saying, Help. Help us. Nothing has changed. I’m trying to bring this forward. This is a topic about which we all need to have an opinion. But I’m not this superhero that can solve the situation.

It’s important to make this clear that the film is not just about Romania and Norway and the Barnevernet. The film is about what happens in the States too, for example. I think that this polarization of people needs to have an answer because we can’t continue living in these bubbles. This degree of hatred and aggression, which might end up badly, and very violent.

What do you do when people call you for help?

They text, and I’m answering back.

I started this promotional tour in Norway, and I met a lot of people from both sides talking to me. We ran across this very difficult confession of a spectator, this lady who was crying, telling us that she was experiencing these cases with such emotion that finally she decided, for fear of having her children taken away by the authorities, she decided to rather have an abortion.

We also met people telling us that they are 100 percent behind the point of view of the protection in the film, because if they were in the situation of having their children taken in a conservative society, nobody would care for them. I think this shows that people rather tend to imagine that the wrong and radical way of seeing the society can be compensated by another wrong and radical way, and this shouldn’t be the answer. The answer should be more attempts at integration, trying to be more empathic and more open to dialogue, if we wish to give a good example to the part of the society who think they can’t escape this idea that they already know the truth and there’s no way out.

In the court scene, Sebastian Stan’s character gestures at the ways in which liberal societies privilege physical harm over emotional or verbal harm. There is, of course, no such thing as a view from nowhere. I know you said your opinion doesn’t matter, but I would still like to know how you relate or do not relate to this argument. 

Of course, we need to make this clear. As soon as there is proven violence in a family, we all need to act as soon as we can and save them. Be it children or women. Of course, we need to act.

But the film talks about the fact that in most cases, you are supposed to make a choice, not knowing what happened in the family. You are just having assumptions in most of these cases, and this is why Fjord is crafted as such.

After investigating for two years and talking to all the parties involved, I can’t tell if this real family, which was involved in the real case, was violent or not. I don’t know. I’m not saying that they were not. I don’t know, because even if I talk to them and to their children... But I noticed that when people are making choices in Norway, for example, or us in society in general, we tend to be biased by our own stereotypes about the situation, and it’s very difficult to position yourself in an objective point of view. This doesn’t really exist.

“I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. ”

So you need to be aware that you’re biased, that you are seeing the situation from your perspective, and when you’re mentioning that you’re doing whatever is best for the benefit of the children, actually you tend to believe that your solution is for the best, while the others will believe the same if they act on their opinions.

And of course, you know, we need to make sure that there is enough freedom accepted by everybody into our societies, so that minorities have the right to be who they want to be.

But after making a film that was speaking a lot about how minorities are being discriminated in conservative society, I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. Wouldn’t you expect that they are treated with more empathy for not sharing the same values with the majority? Well, actually, they are not. The fact that you belong to the majority tends to be more important to you than the values that belong to your ideology.

Literary theorist Terry Eagleton has a quote that goes, “Ideology is like bad breath. We only recognize it in other people.”

I understand precise choreography is part of your process. You have talked about how you also try your best to avoid cutting because that is an interpretation. Does that mean the point of art is verisimilitude, capturing reality? And if not that, what are movies for? Why do you make movies? 

I believe in diversity in filmmaking, and I think that making entertainment is also a valid way of making films, but it shouldn’t be the only way. The films that I try to make are films that try to make people think a little bit more, and to make them aware of the world which exists next to theirs. I’m using this as a tool to make you aware that you should be very careful of what happens next to you.

There isn’t anything like an objective point of view, but the best I could do is not to be manipulative with my style. I’m not making a film biased by one of these points of view. I’m taking this risky position of a moderator, bringing two sets of values in front of you so that you can double check your values and to remember when was the last time when you doubted that you are on the good side of things? Everybody else is so convinced that they are as right as you, but you know the first step into entering some sort of a dialogue is listening to others.

Fjord was released in select US theaters October 9th, with a wide release on October 23rd.

title: Google ‘Fitbit Edge’ reportedly costs around $180 as specs & features leak
snippet: A new leak reveals that Google’s upcoming Fitbit Edge tracker will probably have a price somewhere around $180 and offer 7-day battery life. more…
fullText:
A new leak reveals that Google’s upcoming Fitbit Edge tracker will probably have a price somewhere around $180 and offer 7-day battery life.

Having first appeared in a marketing leak and, more recently, a set of leaked images, Google’s Fitbit Edge tracker is a middle ground between the Pixel Watch 5 and the screen-less Fitbit Air. It has a smaller size than the Watch, but has a screen to display notifications and other features beyond what the Air’s minimalist experience delivers.

Today, a second major leak reveals more details about the Fitbit Edge, including its price.

Dealabs reports that the Fitbit Edge will have a price of €179 in Europe and £159 in the UK. By comparison, Fitbit Air costs €99 and £85 in those regions, meaning the Fitbit Edge will likely cost around $180 in the United States.

	

The report goes on to offer more detailed specs for the tracker, including its 1.34-inch display, detailed battery life estimates, and more. Here’s the breakdown.

Fitbit Edge Specs

Display: 1.34-inch AMOLED

Battery Life: 7 days without always-on display, 2 days with always-on display

Charging: 24 hours of battery in 5 minutes

Water Resistance: IP68/5ATM

Phone Compatibility: Android 11+, iOS 16.4+

Bluetooth 5.4

Fitness tracking: SpO2, steps, heart rate, blood pressure/insulin trends, ECG, VO2 Max, more

Weight: 17.7g

	

The report also mentions support for Gemini, some form of Google Play integration, and that the battery is user-replaceable. 

Also notable here is that Fitbit Edge is apparently compatible with iPhone, something that it shares in common with Fitbit Air, but that the Pixel Watch series lacks. 

A release date for the Fitbit Edge remains unknown at this point, but it’s clear that the tracker is making its debut in the very near future.

title: The iPhone Duo’s Unfolding Animation Is Giving Z Fold 8 Owners FOMO, but Not Me
snippet: Commentary: While there are ways to recreate some of the iPhone Duo’s style on an Android device, it feels a little desperate to me.
fullText:
When I first got my hands on the iPhone Duo, I admittedly dismissed the unfolding animation that would soon become a highlight of online discourse. I was less interested in the smooth transition as content shifted from one screen to another and more focused on details such as the matte inner display and seemingly invisible crease.

But in the weeks since Apple unveiled its first foldable iPhone, which drops Oct. 23, I’ve seen countless examples on social media of people trying to recreate that buzzed-about animation on their Android foldables. While the Play Store offers plenty of launchers for customizing Android phones — including ones that mimic the iPhone’s home screen — this appears to be one iOS design element that users are particularly eager to bring to their devices.

Sometimes, you really can’t predict what people will care about most — or the lengths they’ll go to imitate a feature.

		

			

The primary phone people have used to recreate the iPhone Duo’s cascading transition effect is Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, which debuted in July with a passport-size foldable design ahead of Apple’s release. Unlike iOS, Samsung’s One UI interface, which runs on top of Android on Galaxy devices, doesn’t include a folding animation. Instead, content simply transitions from the Z Fold 8’s cover screen to its inner display once the phone is opened about halfway. I never considered this a deficiency until I saw the flood of positive reactions to the iPhone Duo’s fluid transition effect. 

To bridge that gap, several creators have posted videos explaining how to use third-party apps and developer tools on GitHub to get a similar effect on the Z Fold 8, with caveats like “the smoothness and quality won’t be the same‘” and “install it [at] your own risk.” (That’s encouraging!) The steps don’t seem particularly complicated, and some options appear to have cropped up in the Play Store as well.

I’ve chosen to forgo installing these Duo-copycat apps on my precious Galaxy Z Fold 8 for two reasons. First, I’m not much of a risk-taker. Second, I’m not interested in imitating an aesthetic element of Apple’s software with a derivative version, especially when the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a standout foldable device in its own right. While the value of the Duo’s sleek animation has since grown on me, I’m not quite desperate enough to retrofit it onto a foldable phone that’s just as functional without that flourish.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 might not have a nifty opening animation by default, but I don’t see that as a deficiency.Andrew Lanxon/CNET

Don’t get me wrong: I think Apple’s combination of hardware and software expertise will elevate the iPhone Duo in a way that merits the attention the phone has received, despite being relatively “late” to the foldables game. But I also think it’s more tasteful for consumers to embrace what each phone-maker does best, rather than shoehorning in a competitor’s feature for something as superficial as an animation effect. 

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is one of my favorite phones I’ve tested this year, earning it a CNET Editors’ Choice Award. Its versatile design is optimized for both vertical and horizontal content: I can stream YouTube videos and movies on the 7.6-inch inner display, then rotate it to seamlessly scroll through social posts. The crease is barely noticeable, and the battery easily lasts all day. The 5.5-inch cover screen never feels cramped, while its sharp corners give the phone a highly polished look. And despite lacking a telephoto lens, the Z Fold 8’s dual rear cameras pull their weight, capturing crisp, vibrant photos.

The iPhone Duo shares many attributes with the Z Fold 8, including a palm-size design, 7.6-inch inner display and dual rear cameras. Those similarities prompted Samsung to post a series of salty tweets after Apple debuted its foldable last month, including one that reads, “Let us know when you’re done reheating our leftovers.”

That said, I am curious how app developers might optimize their platforms for the iPhone Duo in ways we haven’t seen with other foldable phones. While the Android operating system spans a wide range of devices and configurations, iOS developers only have to cater to a single foldable, potentially leading to a more tailored and streamlined experience. We got a glimpse of how Netflix is building its app for the Duo, and it’ll be interesting to see how both Apple and other third-party developers take full advantage of the phone’s 1.4:1 aspect ratio in ways that could make its predecessors seem behind the curve in that regard.

“Borrowing” features from each other is what phone-makers do best. Down the road, it’s possible companies such as Samsung will implement foldable capabilities that Apple rolled out first, and vice versa. Heck, Apple’s delayed entry into this space means it had time to analyze what worked well for its competitors before jumping in with its own rendition. It’s just how the industry works. 

So maybe the Galaxy Z Fold 9 — or whatever Samsung decides to call the follow-up to the Z Fold 8 — will have its own nifty opening animation. But until Samsung itself embraces the idea, I’ll stick with using the standout foldable as-is.

title: Google Wallet for Android getting vertically stacked card list [U]
snippet: Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list. more…
fullText:
Following the homepage redesign and fullscreen passes revamp this year, Google Wallet is trialing a vertically stacked card list.

Update 10/6: This revamp is not yet widely rolled out, but we’re slowly seeing it on more devices.

With this stacked redesign, you’ll see one full card preview and the sliver of a second at the top. To expand, you can tap or swipe down to enter the fullscreen view (as seen below). After selecting a card, you can tap-to-pay.

To see card details and transaction history, select the new settings gear icon in the top-right corner. This is more cumbersome than the current design. 

	

	

Original 9/14: The current design shows your saved credit and debit cards as a carousel at the top of the screen. You swipe horizontally to browse, with this approach showing just a sliver of the next and previous cards at the edges. Google lets you reorder the payment methods and set a default card. This interface allows passes to share the homepage.

The new design uses a vertical list, like the Wallet app on iPhone, that really benefits those with multiple saved cards. Google is showing much more of the card design than Apple, which is a nice aspect of the current look.

This approach is definitely friendlier for one-handed use, especially if your most used cards are placed at the bottom.

There are a handful of reports about this rollout over the weekend, with most coming from international users.

title: Apple partners with The King’s Trust on new Creative Labs initiative in the UK
snippet: Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple and The King’s Trust announced today an expansion of their partnership with a new education program that offers workshops to help young people build creative and digital skills. Here are the details.

Apple’s partnership with The King’s Trust dates back to 2019

In a Newsroom post published today, Apple and The King’s Trust announced the “Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs” initiative, which will “offer young people meaningful engagement with Apple experts across industries as they explore a variety of career pathways, equipping them with the technology, resources, skills, confidence, and expertise needed to realize their potential.”

According to Apple, the program’s immersive educational experience began earlier this week with “music industry and creative workshops, aligned to the recent opening of Apple Music Hall.”

Apple says the first cohort will include up to 20 participants aged 18 to 30, with additional sessions and cohorts planned over the next year.

Here’s Alisha Johnson Wilder, Apple’s senior director of Global Community Impact, on what the initiative means for Apple and its partnership with The King’s Trust:

“At Apple, we believe education is a powerful force for equity and opportunity. […] For years, we’ve been proud to work alongside The King’s Trust to spark creativity and open doors for young people across the UK. With the launch of the Apple x King’s Trust Creative Labs, we’re taking that commitment further, connecting the next generation of creators and innovators directly with our experts, technology, and mentorship to help them build vital skills, discover their passions, and thrive in the workforce.”

Jonathan Townsend, The King’s Trust’s UK chief executive, also commented on the initiative, calling it “an exciting new chapter in our partnership that will help even more young people develop the confidence and creative digital skills they need to take their next steps toward employment.”

In the announcement, Apple said it is also working with The King’s Trust on resources to improve AI literacy and help educators incorporate new technologies into their teaching.

title: Why did it take so long for someone to make a magnetic USB-C port? [Video]
snippet: In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything. more…
fullText:
In launching its new Surface Laptop Ultra this week, Microsoft showed off its magnetic USB-C port and I immediately want it on everything.

The Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra is a full-on powerhouse with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chipset, up to 128GB of RAM, and plenty of ports. But it’s one of those ports that is the most unique new features.

“Magnetic Connect” is Microsoft’s name for “the world’s first built-in magnetic USB-C” charging port. The USB-C port itself functions as normal with any standard cable, but the included charger is specially designed to magnetically attach akin to Apple’s MagSafe or any other number of magnetic charging connectors.

I want it.

	

The “how” here is that the charging portion of the cable uses super-strong magnets to align and latch on the charger so the port connects properly, but the charger itself also tapers the edges of the USB-C port so it can more easily slide into place. As such, that end won’t securely connect to your phone or other devices, as it needs that magnet to hold itself in place. 

	

The Verge shows it in action in a video on YouTube:

Microsoft is apparently hoping this idea will catch on and show up on other laptops, and I sure hope that’s the case! As for phones, the size of the magnets implies it probably won’t be feasible in a standard smartphone, but I really hope this idea starts showing up everywhere! Certainly I hope it at least shows up on a laptop that doesn’t cost $2,600 — Surface Laptop Ultra pre-orders are open now.

What do you think?

title: Tesla renames ‘Full Self-Driving’ to ‘Tesla Assisted Driving’ in Europe
snippet: The name change is enough for Germany's transport minister to start advocating for Europe-wide adoption of the driver assistance software.
fullText:
Tesla has changed the name of its advanced driver assistance system in Europe after pushback from Germany’s transportation ministry. It’s now called “Tesla Assisted Driving,” instead of “Full Self-Driving (Supervised).” 

It’s a big capitulation from Tesla, which has been using the “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” name for years despite the system requiring humans to pay attention to the road and take over when necessary. But the name change could help Tesla achieve its goal of wider adoption on the continent, which could unlock a potentially massive new revenue stream for the company. 

Germany’s transport minister, Steffen Bilger, said earlier this month that calling the software “Full Self-Driving” was somewhat misleading because it doesn’t perform the entire task of driving. He spoke with Tesla last month, and the company suggested the name change, according to an official release from the ministry. Bilger said he will now advocate for approval of Tesla Assisted Driving across Europe ahead of an EU-wide vote that could happen later this year. Tesla CEO Elon Musk thanked Bilger on X this week.

Musk has spent years agitating for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), or FSD, to be approved in Europe. “FSD in Europe will save lives of people in the car, as well as vulnerable road users like pedestrians, cyclists, and pets,” he wrote on X in June 2025. “Please let your government know that you want approval.” 

In March of this year, he wrote that the “extreme regulatory burden” of the EU “stifles innovation in Europe,” adding that Europe “will love Tesla self-driving!” 

Just a few weeks later, the Netherlands became the first European country to approve FSD (Supervised). On Wednesday, Reuters reported that Tesla’s campaign for European approval has been “built on faulty company safety research” and “flawed studies.” The outlet also reported that the Dutch vehicle safety regulator, RDW, faced fierce pressure from Tesla and its legion of online supporters.

Tesla’s software has certainly become more capable over the years. What used to be little more than a mix of lane centering and adaptive cruise control is now a driver assistance system that some owners use for nearly 100% of their daily driving. FSD can pull in and out of parking spots and navigate surface streets and highways. Tesla is so confident in the technology that it recently made it possible for FSD to intervene in a human driver’s control of the vehicle if it senses an oncoming collision — even if FSD is not active.

But FSD has been at the center of federal investigations and civil lawsuits over crashes in which it was allegedly in use. Its less capable predecessor, Autopilot, has been associated with dozens of fatalities. Tesla discontinued Autopilot earlier this year after a judge ruled Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing about the system’s capabilities.

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

title: Sketchy rumor again says OLED iPad mini will lack one key feature
snippet: Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support. more…
fullText:
Apple is widely expected to introduce a new OLED iPad mini as soon as later this month. A sketchy new rumor today once again claims the new iPad mini will switch to OLED but still have a 60Hz refresh rate and lack ProMotion support.

This is the second time we’ve heard this rumor, but both times it has come from the same source: the yeux1122 account on Naver. This account has a very mixed track record with Apple rumors. It often seems to regurgitate information from unnamed sources rather than provide its own.

Nonetheless, the latest post from yeux1122 claims “there is mention of 120Hz in some overseas sources” for the new OLED iPad mini, but “domestic production volume has already confirmed” it will use a 60Hz display.

Again, I’m treating this rumor with more than a healthy dose of skepticism, since no other reliable sources have corroborated it.

However, if it does come to fruition, this will be a disappointing limitation for iPad mini buyers. This iPad mini upgrade is expected to bring a number of other notable improvements, including:

An OLED display.

Apple’s A20 Pro chip, up from the current iPad mini’s A17 Pro chip.

A refreshed design with smaller bezels that could be more water-resistant.

The FaceTime camera will be relocated to the horizontal bezel, similar to Apple’s other iPad models.

	

If Apple made all those changes but stopped short of upgrading the display to ProMotion with a 120Hz refresh rate, it’d really sour the launch of the new iPad mini.

The new iPad mini is expected to launch later this month, so we don’t have much longer to wait to know for sure.

title: Google Wallet for Android adds 12th digital state ID
snippet: Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android. more…
fullText:
Following the last launch at the end of August, Google Wallet is rolling out support for Oklahoma state IDs on Android.

Open Google Wallet on your phone and tap the ‘plus’ button next to “View more” at the bottom > IDs & personal info > Driver’s license or state ID. This reveals Oklahoma as the 13th Google Wallet option. It joins Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Maryland, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Ohio, and Puerto Rico.

The card design shows the American Bison (state animal) and the scissor-tailed flycatcher (state bird).

The set-up process requires taking photos of the front and back of your physical card, as well as a short video of your face for verification that gets sent to the SOK. This review can take a few minutes with a notification confirming once it’s available. You’ll also get an email confirmation from the state agency.

	

First, tap on the reader or scan your QR code: Your personal info won’t be shared yet. On your phone, review what info you want to share.

Next, review what info will be shared: Make sure you’re comfortable sharing the info they request

You don’t need to hand your phone to anyone: Your ID will be securely shared using Bluetooth, so make sure it’s on

Lastly, verify it’s you to share your info: For extra security, verify that this ID is yours using your face, fingerprint, password, or PIN

“Details” next to “Show code” lets you enable an “Activity history,” while “Driver’s License information” lists license number, date of expiry, address, and more.

IDs can be read via NFC or by having the QR code scanned. It is accepted at some airports by the TSA. Officially, you still have to carry your ID card as the one on your phone “does not replace the requirement for individuals to carry a physical card.” 

Your device must be running Android 8+ and have a screen lock, with Bluetooth and Nearby devices enabled. A state ID can be deleted from Google Wallet at any time or remotely via myaccount.google.com. As a private pass, it does not get synced to the cloud and is only available on one device.

Tap Personal Info.

Scroll to “Digital ID.”

Tap Manage Digital ID.

Next to the ID or license that you want to remove, tap Delete.

Confirm that you want to delete your ID from your device and Google Account.

title: Leaked Galaxy S27 Ultra color list doesn’t include Purple, for a change
snippet: There’s very little left of the Galaxy S27 Ultra left to surface before launch, but new information might change what to expect in Samsung’s device color options. more…
fullText:
There’s very little left of the Galaxy S27 Ultra left to surface before launch, but new information might change what to expect in Samsung’s device color options.

According to a short and straightforward post on Twitter/X by @UniverseIce, the Galaxy S27 Ultra series will come in four base color variants – Black, Blue, Light Pink, and White. That doesn’t include the Samsung online exclusive colorways, which usually add a couple of hues to the lineup.

Previous leaks claimed Samsung would offer the Galaxy S27 Ultra in five colors, all of the above included except Purple. It’s unclear whether a purple version was excluded this time around, or if Samsung plans to sell the version as an online-exclusive. Those don’t cost more, but they’re only available from the company’s website and not third-party retailers.

It would be a first in four years if Samsung didn’t release a purple Galaxy S Ultra phone. The Galaxy S23 Ultra in 2023 came in Lavender, and since then, every Galaxy S Ultra phone has been available in some similar shade.

	

It’s worth a quick note that Light Pink comes so very close to Lavender on the color wheel, so do with that information what you will.

In combination with the new camera bar, the Galaxy S27 Ultra will take on an entirely new look. Its design is set rather far from the look of nearly every Galaxy S Ultra phone since 2021, thanks to the camera island spanning the entire rear panel.

Whether you like it or not, the Galaxy S27 Ultra will look like an entirely different phone. And now, it will look different in LavenderLight Pink.

Of course, that hinges on whether the leaks we’ve seen prove true. Samsung plans to launch the new devices early next year.

title: Fantastical’s long-awaited Android debut begins today on Googlebook
snippet: Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect. more…
fullText:
Fantastical has long been hailed as one of the greatest calendar apps available today, but if you’re an Android user, there’s a good chance you’ve never used it. Despite a move from Apple exclusivity to cross-platform availability on Windows, Android has long eluded the attention of development team Flexibits. Today, that’s finally changing, as Fantastical is headed to Google’s mobile OS platform — but not precisely in the way you might expect.

Beginning today, Fantastical is now available for Google’s new laptop initiative, Googlebook. Existing Fantastical users who rely on the app on different platforms (like iOS or Windows) can access Fantastical on Googlebook at no additional charge, while new users coming to Fantastical for the very first time can likewise also use the application on any of their other supported devices.

While the underlying OS on Googlebook is Android, Flexibits’ co-founder and CEO Michael Simmons stressed that the application isn’t quite ready yet to debut on phones, tablets, or foldables. Those versions are on the way — bucking what Simmons himself said back in 2024 when he declared the app would never find its way to the Play Store — but they won’t be ready for launch until sometime in 2027. Likewise, today’s announcement does not include bringing the company’s contact management app, Cardhop, to Android; Simmons tells me they have “no announcement” about that app at this time.

Fantastical began life on Mac back in 2011, offering calendar creation tools via a straightforward ordinary language-based interface that isn’t all too dissimilar to today’s LLMs. Though Flexibits unveiled a Windows variant in late 2024, today’s move marks the first step towards compatibility with Google’s mobile OS, and you can thank Googlebooks for building that bridge. Simmons told me development began after Google showed the Fantastical team a demo of its new laptop platform, and he found himself impressed enough to take a chance on finally expanding the app to Android.

	

While most users will have to wait until next year to get their hands on Fantastical, all you early Googlebook adopters out there have the chance to begin using a brand-new calendar app starting today. Individual pricing starts at $57 per year, with family plans starting at $90 annually. A free, less powerful tier is also available.

It’s almost a year since Apple was found to have infringed a Masimo patent for low-power pulse oximeter features used in the Apple Watch.

At the time, the company was ordered to pay $634 million in damages, but a federal judge has now ordered it to pay an additional $184 million in interest …

Apple had been fighting with health tech company Masimo on a couple of fronts. The more serious of them was an International Trade Commission ruling that Apple must remove the blood oxygen feature in two Apple Watch models back in 2023 in order to allow them to be sold in the US. The Cupertino company was forced to redesign the way the feature worked in order to be allowed to bring the devices into the US.

But the company also faced a lawsuit from Masimo, seeking damages for the use of its patented approach to measuring blood oxygen in a power-efficient way. Apple was found to have infringed on this patent and ordered to pay damages amounting to the license fees it should have paid.

Bloomberg Law reports that Apple has now been ordered to pay an additional £184 million in interest on this sum. 

Judge James V. Selna rejected Apple’s argument that awarding interest would constitute a windfall for Masimo, citing US Supreme Court guidance that “interest from the time that the royalty payments would have been received merely serves to make the patent owner whole.”

There was some good news for Apple. Masimo had asked for interest calculated at 7%, but the judge rejected this, saying that the interest rate should instead be equivalent to that paid on Massimo’s own borrowing. However, annual compounding still added a total of $184M to the amount due.
