He also cut 22 percent of Mattel’s workforce, sort of immediately upon getting there. That’s sort of what you bring Ynon Kreiz in to do. You don’t bring him to have lunch at the Polo Lounge and make nice with talent. You bring him in because you need to whip things into shape and cut things, and that’s his deal.

I was talking to a bunch of people the last few days. He strikes me as a guy who doesn’t have terribly high EQ. Other folks say, “No, no, no, no. He’s tough, but he’s actually a teddy bear if you get to know him.” I think most people who get laid off by him won’t consider him a teddy bear, but that’s his job: to go do the unpleasant work of finding $6 billion in synergy.

Because you are a corporate structure lover, you probably have noticed that while Ynon Kreiz is co-CEO of Skydance, David Ellison is not the other co-CEO. David Ellison is the CEO. So at a minimum, we have a one A and one B thing. But also, let’s be clear, David Ellison and his father own the company, so ultimately it’s their deal.

I think quite clearly what David Ellison wants to do is be able to have lunch at the Polo Lounge, the San Vicente Bungalows, or wherever they go, and someone will come up to him and say, “I’m really angry about this layoff or this movie project that you canceled.” And he’ll say, “Oh, that sounds terrible. You should really talk to Ynon about that. My hands are tied.” That’s Ynon Kreiz’s job.

Ellison wants to hang out with Tom Cruise. This whole thing, from start to finish, is like, one guy wants to hang out with Tom Cruise, and he’s gonna manufacture a company that will allow him to do that at scale.

I will give David Ellison more credit than that. David Ellison, when he ran Skydance, his primary achievement was befriending Tom Cruise. And I’m sure he liked hanging out with him, but that’s why Skydance was a company: David Ellison was in the Tom Cruise business. He was in the Mission Impossible business, the Top Gun business.

That is what the job of a producer is: getting people to... You don’t really do anything as a producer. You just sort of package stuff, and he was able to be in the Tom Cruise business, and that’s what got him as far as he’s been able to get. And that is his job. That was his job. Now he’s got a different job.

There’s probably a PhD thesis on the kind of personality that accepts a co-CEO title without another co-CEO.

I’ve thought about that from the get-go because of the chain of events — was it last week? — Roger Lynch, CEO of Condé Nast, who said, “I’m now the CEO of Mattel.” For an hour or so, no one knew where Ynon Kreiz was going, and then the rumor was, “Oh, he’s gonna have a job at Warner’s. I’m like, well, what job could he take?

He’s already been the CEO of a big publicly traded company. These guys don’t usually accept a demotion. And quite clearly what he’s... One, they said, “All right, you’re the co-CEO,” so it’s not a demotion. Two, there are only a handful of these giant media conglomerates. If you can run one, that’s just a big notch to have on your belt.

Number three, they’re gonna pay him $50 million this year. So that will help salve some of those wounds, and I think everyone sort of acknowledged it. Like, he’s effectively the COO of Skydance, if you think about it. You just give him a different title so it sounds better.

There’s some other shuffling under that to do. You’ve got two movie studios. You have James Gunn running DC really well, actually. I think Lanterns is just a bona fide hit for HBO. You’ve got two news divisions, which we should talk about. How are they going to resolve these conflicts? Are they just gonna pick one team or the other?

Yeah. I mean, they’ve already done that with streaming. Cindy Holland, who pioneered Netflix’s move into original programming more than a decade ago, was brought in by David Ellison a year ago to run that streaming service. He’s just bought HBO, which is run by Casey Bloys, very well-regarded, who spent the last year making it clear to everyone that he would not work with or for Cindy Holland.

I don’t think there was personal animus. He’s just like, “I already run HBO. Why would I want to share power with somebody else?” So it seemed pretty clear that David Ellison would pick that horse, and I think he’s gonna make a bunch of those calls. The people who ran the Warner Bros. studio, which a year ago was the toast of the town, were making tons of money and critical acclaim. This year, they produced Digger, Tom Cruise’s biggest bomb ever, and they’re having a rough year. But it was always sort of clear that David Ellison was gonna bring in his people.

David Ellison is not an art film guy — he’s not a guy who’s gonna allow Paul Thomas Anderson to make One Battle After Another again. He’s in the Mission Impossible Tom Cruise-iverse, so that’s not surprising. CNN and CBS, people have been talking about merging those companies almost as long as I’ve been covering the media, so that’s not a new idea.

They have said, I think wisely for now, “Well, we’re not gonna merge those two,” because we just know it’s a fucking shit storm politically if they touch that stuff. And this is pure speculation, but they might also say, “Well, we hired Bari Weiss and gave her CBS News to run, and maybe we told her she’d also get to play with CNN. But it’s been a rough year over at CBS in the Bari Weiss business, and maybe even if we’re gonna give it to Bari Weiss a couple years down the road, let’s not stir that nest right now.”

So Mark Thompson, who’s been running CNN, is gonna continue to run CNN. But again, in the background, no matter what Mark Thompson… He has control of CNN. Ynon Kreiz is still gonna be in there saying, “I know this is your business, but it’s really my business, and you need to cut 10 percent or 20 percent,” or whatever it is, and everyone has to do it.

And so in some ways, yes, it matters who’s running these individual studios and components, but again, the debt is hanging over everything. Everyone is gonna have to work to reduce that debt one way or the other.

The Bari Weiss thesis at CBS, as charitably as I can put it, was that when she showed up, she was like, “No one trusts the news, and it’s because we’re not fair enough, and I’m gonna do more conservative stuff.” And that was part of the regulatory arbitrage with the Trump administration. They were gonna change CBS because Donald Trump did not like the coverage on CBS, and that worked or didn’t work.

But I think we now know that she did not increase trust in CBS News by making it a more conservative-friendly organization. The ratings are down, like precipitously down, such that a lot of people think that she should just be fired and something else should happen. I would —

Yeah, I don’t see that happening.

Well, right, because he’s gotta do regulatory arbitrage on both sides. We have midterms —

And I think he likes Bari Weiss. I think David Ellison is not a political person. I think his father, Larry Ellison, is probably not that political. Tom Dotan in Vanity Fair just did a profile of Larry Ellison and sort of gets at the idea of how he’s bought these big media empires. He also owns a chunk of TikTok. Is there a thing here? And his conclusion is no, it’s not. He really doesn’t have much politics. But the one thing the Ellison family cares a lot about is Israel. Bari Weiss cares a lot about Israel. That is the one ideological through line there. I think they’d be loath to sort of cut her loose.

And also, it’s been a clusterfuck over at CBS, but I don’t know that she’s done a worse job running it than anybody else has recently. It’s just that there’s systemic decline. Now, she may make it even worse. It’s possible. And as a journalist, you may not like what she’s doing. But if you’re running the business, I don’t know that she has made it that much worse. I think the Ellisons probably don’t like the headaches and headlines generated by it, but I also don’t think they care that much.

I mean, I go on TikTok, and I see any clip from any 60 Minutes or CBS News account, and all of the comments are, “You ruined this. I blame Bari Weiss. I can’t trust you.”

That is a decline in trust from where they were before, when no one knew who was running CBS News. I would actually —.

I think you should not know who the heads of network news are.

Yeah. I think it’s bad that the kids on TikTok are like, “I hate this one person that has nothing to do with the video clip I’m seeing now.”

I bring that up because of the TikTok of it all. The idea that TikTok was a national security threat, that the United States Congress voted unanimously to ban it, that Biden voted to ban it, but then he knew it was political suicide, so he kicked the imposition of the ban to the Trump administration. 

All of that, as you peel apart the reporting, what did members of Congress see in their closed-door meetings? It comes down, as far as any of the reporting I’ve ever seen, to how they thought it was spreading pro-Palestinian propaganda, anti-Israel propaganda. Now the Ellisons own it. 

As you said, they care very deeply about the issue of Israel, and I can’t say that their ownership of TikTok has meaningfully moved the needle on how people feel about the war in Gaza in any way, shape, or form. Did they try? 

Perhaps people were disappointed with Israel’s conduct prior to the invention of TikTok. Perhaps there are other reasons they may not be concerned. And, you know, the reason Congress voted for this. It’s maybe the only thing Congress has passed in years is this rule saying China can’t own TikTok, which they then immediately forgot about during the first year of the Trump administration.

I do think the China of it all was meaningful for some people, but they clearly also just didn’t care. It’s kinda wild to see Congress pass a bill that becomes a law and then not try to enforce it at all.

They knew it was suicide. I don’t know if you remember this, but there was a day when it was the House committee, and AOC was on this committee, and they went into a SCIF to view some intelligence about TikTok. They all came out and voted unanimously to ban this thing, and no one for months could figure out what they saw in there.

And it was like, “Did you see a picture of Chinese intelligence services turning the knobs in the algorithm to poison the minds of American youth?” And they’re like, “No, no, no.” 

“They showed us some videos.”

Yeah, it was like, “What, what are you looking at in there?” And then we just sold it to someone who may or may not have some political leanings, but they have some control that is equivalent to the Chinese control, which was so scary that we had to ban this platform.

I’m bringing this all up because that is the thing that is reducing trust in the news media. It is not the news media itself, right? The news media makes its mistakes in whatever ways it makes its mistakes. But it’s a bunch of influencers on social platforms who start every video by saying, “Here’s what they’re not telling you,” which is actually the mechanism of reducing trust.

And then they read you The New York Times. As somebody who now makes these videos —

“No one’s covering this! Let me read you a New York Times story about it.”

The other thing that has reduced trust in the media is that Republicans, for 40 years, have been saying the media is biased. And if you say something for 40 years and you’re one of the two parties running the country, I think that message sort of seeps in, before TikTok, before social media.

But if I had to pick the two things that are the biggest threats to the businesses that David Ellison now owns, I would pick AI, and I would pick social media, and those are the other big investments of the Ellison family. Is this all just an elaborate hedge, or does he have a plan to use TikTok to amplify his content? To market these movies?

I don’t think they have a plan. One of the through lines when David Ellison was buying Paramount was that David Ellison’s a successful producer. You add his dad, who runs Oracle; he’s got a lot of tech know-how. And also, David Ellison is not just a movie producer; he’s a technologist. This was the thing they stood up and said at a press conference. And he said, “Yes, yes, I was mentored by Steve Jobs.” He wasn’t mentored by Steve Jobs.

But anyway, the whole premise was we’re gonna techify this and cloud and Oracle. And maybe they could save $10, $20, maybe $100 million on sort of back-office-y things by swapping in an Oracle contract for something else. Although, I think in the normal world, you’d say just because your dad owns this company, we don’t get to bring it in as a technology company for this publicly traded company. Whatever. But there’s never been any indication that they’ve got any other plan other than shaving some costs.

I don’t think David Ellison is ideologically inclined. Maybe he will see something outrageous on TikTok that he doesn’t like and say, “Hey, Dad, could you bring that down?” I don’t even know if his dad has the capacity to bring something down. You know, TikTok is a black box. We don’t actually know how the algorithm works, who actually controls it, and who can steer it.

The potential for TikTok content to end up on whatever this new Paramount HBO streaming service is high.

Mm-hmm.

I know the other big media companies have long looked at the user-generated content platforms and been envious of their cost structure. YouTube barely pays any money for its content, and it’s destroying this industry.

YouTube pays the most. YouTube pays 55 percent. Everyone else pays zero percent.

Right. But for an average creator on YouTube, you’re getting nothing, effectively.

I’m just saying it is a great business model, and the Reels and TikTok business models are much better than the YouTube one because they pay zero percent for content.

There’s something there. Like, Disney has made some noise about putting creator videos in Disney+. They’ve all looked at it. They’ve all talked about it. This one seems easy, right? It’s HBO Max plus your favorite commentary about whatever HBO Max show you’re watching, sourced directly from TikTok, right here. We’re all gonna integrate it. 

Maybe this is way harder than I’m making it sound.

I think they all believe that… They all move in herds, right? All these companies always do. We’re all doing vertical video now. And you’re like, well, vertical video, yes, people like the format. What they really like is unlimited free content. Which, again, TikTok doesn’t pay anything for.

So you, Paramount, or you, Peacock, or you, Disney, you are not in the business of getting free content from people. You are still paying for stuff, and also you care about your brand still, so you don’t wanna just have a platform where anyone can watch anything. And I think that is kind of the fundamental question for all these media companies.

You’re not platforms. The dominant media companies are platforms. Can you turn yourself into a platform? Should you turn yourself into a platform? Should you just say, “Nope, what we make is super high-quality, specific stuff that people value as a brand, and maybe that’s just gonna be our place, and we’re not gonna compete with the YouTubes of the world”?

Netflix seems to be going in that direction. They’re gonna be more platform-y. I do think you’ll probably see not just Paramount, but every company try to say, “Oh, we’re a platform, too.” I don’t think it will be successful, though

Do you foresee a tighter connection between Skydance and TikTok? These are all companies operated by a family. They’re not close right now. They could get closer.

I don’t know that TikTok cares, right? TikTok, which is still really run by ByteDance, I don’t know that they care about making Larry Ellison that much happier. I don’t think that’s the direction of travel here.

I’m only curious because I’m watching Meta just relentlessly promote Muse, its AI agent, across all of its platforms. OpenAI launches Dots, and where do they go to buy ads? They go buy ads on Meta platforms. And like, this is a massive structural advantage for Meta, right? They are not buying their own ad space.

And if I ran a movie studio and I had to put out 30 movies per year and pay to market them to try to get these kids to go to a theater, I’d be like, “Boy, I could really use that TikTok juice.”

Do you know who’s winning the microdrama wars in the US? I don’t know if you’ve paid attention to microdramas yet, but they are what they sound like.

Meta. Meta is not in the microdrama business. Meta is in the “Oh, you wanna advertise microdramas? Come talk to us.”

So they are getting all of the microdrama money right now. It’s a great place to be if you’re, if you’re Meta. And by the way, the microdrama companies are uploading their content to Meta as ads, so Meta both gets paid for the advertising and then has free engaging content that it can show its users. It’s a great place to be.

If only Meta cared about its actual businesses instead of trying to win in AI agents. The amount that they would succeed would be out of control. That’s another episode of the show. 

Let me end with the conspiracy theory that I brought up at the beginning. There was a bidding process. David Zaslav’s initial plan was to split Discovery into two, to sell the cable networks to whoever was dumb enough to buy them. Netflix really wanted Warner, and they bid. They were actually the announced winners until David Ellison did his regulatory arbitrage.

They won the deal in December of last year. They gave up on it in February of this year. So they won for a couple of months.

David is very good at just kicking the door back open. He made it happen.

As Logan Roy said, “Congratulations on saying the biggest number.”

No one has succeeded in buying Warner. You could argue that Netflix did nothing but make the price so high that it was unsustainable, that they had to create massive amounts of leverage on this deal, pay an unsustainable amount of debt. And at the end of this all, Ted Sarandos is gonna be standing there waiting to buy, yet again, the distressed assets of Warner Bros. at a fire-sale price.

Do you think that’s likely?

I think Netflix, and other people as well, will definitely be in the business of, “Oh, Ynon Kreiz fired you? Ynon Kreiz told you you couldn’t make your movie or television show? Come talk to us.” Which, by the way, a lot of other companies were doing to Netflix back in 2022 when Netflix went through its retrenchment.

So I think that is likely but also standard, right? You just have this turmoil. You have a standard thing in any media company of, “Oh, this project this other guy brought in, we’re not doing that anymore. That was a failure. We’re doing new stuff. And oh, by the way, if the last guy’s project turns out to be successful, we’ll take credit for that. But we’re gonna bring in new stuff.”

I don’t think Ted Sarandos was playing 3D/4D chess here. I think they thought this was a good idea. But I think the much more obvious answer is Wall Street hated the idea. Wall Street kept telling Netflix, “We hate this. We hate this. Please don’t spend $80 billion on this. And also, by the way, you’re gonna have a tough time getting this through regulation.” And I think Ted Sarandos eventually said, “Okay, you’re right.”

I’ve seen him speak publicly about this and in other venues. He seems quite upset about the fact that he didn’t get this deal. I think there are also feelings involved here. But I don’t think this was all a master plan on their part.

I think they went for it. They didn’t get it. They’re bummed out. They’re gonna move on.

I think an angry, aggressive Netflix might actually be the best thing that could happen to Hollywood right now, because they were headed towards their own vertical video slop fest, and maybe now they’re not going to do that.

I think that’s the question for — I mean, it’s a question for everybody. But for Netflix, it’s: you guys have been super successful for a couple of decades by doing one thing. Well, initially you were doing DVD by mail, then you went to streaming, and that’s all you did. And you didn’t ever sell movies. You didn’t do a la carte stuff. You didn’t do advertising. You didn’t do sports.

Now you do advertising. Now you do sports. Now you’re doing games. Now you’re doing podcasts. Maybe you’re gonna integrate with other kinds of TV stuff. And so this laser focus that Netflix had, which proved very successful, they are moving away from. They may have to move away from it. They may have sort of reached the limit of that growth.

But it gets trickier and trickier the more things you add to that stack to make sure you’re doing a good job. And I think that is the real challenge for them.

We’ve been at it for about 45 minutes. I still don’t know how David Ellison is gonna make one more dollar than he made last year. Have you come to any conclusions?

We’re recording this Tuesday morning. Tuesday night, like at 7:30? I don’t know why they’re doing it at 7:30 or 8:30. They’re gonna have a press conference, the first Skydance press conference. So if we re-record this on Wednesday, maybe all this will be answered, but maybe it won’t be answered.

Well, Ynon will be there. He’ll be there wielding his scythe.

It’s gonna be interesting because he is not gonna be a high-profile person, but I think a lot of people are gonna learn his name anyway. And this is a thing that Hollywood does, right? You find a person to blame for your troubles.

Sometimes it’s a company like Netflix, sometimes it’s an evil Jason Kilar. Remember when he was running WarnerMedia for a minute or two? And everyone said, “You’re wrecking the business. Thank God we have David Zaslav, who’s an authentic media guy to come in and save us.”

And then, you know, six months later, David Zaslav’s name is an epithet. Presumably there’ll be a new epithet associated with this company.

Yeah. Well, this deal is gonna wind its way through. We’re gonna check in on it a lot. We’re gonna have you back, Peter. Thank you so much for being on Decoder.

See you, Nilay. Thanks.

excerpt:
Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at Business Insider and host of the Channels podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.

Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.

title: Apple TV just unveiled the new season of last year’s hit comedy
snippet: One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return. more…
fullText:
One of Apple TV’s hit comedy series from last year, Stick, is coming back for season 2 soon. Here’s the new trailer for Stick’s highly anticipated return.

Stick season 2 is coming November 4, here’s the trailer

Ted Lasso just wrapped up its fourth season, but Apple TV has another heartfelt sports comedy ready to take its place.

Stick returns for season 2 on Wednesday, November 4, with two episodes available initially then weekly releases through December 30.

Watch Stick on Apple TV

For the unfamiliar, Stick stars Owen Wilson as an ex-pro golfer—Pryce Cahill—whose career ended prematurely. But after helping train a 17-year-old golf phenom in season 1, the new season sees Cahill get back to the game himself.

And he’ll do it with the help of a new coach played by Rhea Seehorn (“Pluribus”).

Here’s Apple’s official season summary, followed by the new trailer:

In season two, Santi takes the next step in his pursuit of professional golf, only to discover how quickly the game changes when talent becomes expectation. As Santi chases his dream, Pryce finds himself wondering what might still be possible for him. Urged on by his former rival Clark Ross (Timothy Olyphant), Pryce does something nobody expects: he bets on himself, launching an improbable comeback in hopes of becoming the oldest golfer ever to win a major. But the road back proves far harder than he imagined. And the closer Pryce gets to the golfer he once was, the more he is forced to confront why he never fulfilled the promise everyone once saw in him. With brilliant new coach Amanda (Rhea Seehorn) and trusted caddie Mitts (Marc Maron) in his corner, Pryce sets out to prove — to the golf world and, more importantly, to himself — that maybe he really was as good as everyone always said he was.

In my experience, you don’t have to care about golf at all to enjoy Stick.

The show feels similar in spirit to other Apple comedies like Ted Lasso and Shrinking. In my view it especially hit its stride near the end of the season, so I’m excited to see it return.

If you’re looking for more Apple series to check out, Small Prophets just premiered and is being hailed as a “masterpiece” and in contention for the streamer’s best show this year.

Are you a fan of Stick? Or do you plan to watch it ahead of season 2? Let us know in the comments.

title: I Asked Meta Muse to Fix an Issue With My Phone Provider. It Got Blocked at Every Turn
snippet: This tech to-do has been on my list for too long. Can an agent do it for me?
fullText:
Something weird has been happening with my phone for years. I thought I’d fixed the issue, but it always comes back. Years ago, I bought a SIM-only plan through Visible, Verizon’s cheap sibling. $25 a month gets me unlimited calls, texts and a decent amount of data… and a lot of spam calls and messages looking for someone called Andrew. 

Given Visible is all-digital with no number to call, it’s a pain to wrestle with a customer service chatbot to fix it. I’ve tried before, and it said the number is in my name, but I’m not convinced. I still receive multiple messages per month from people trying to reach Andrew. 

These messages almost always have something to do with a home trades project. Weird, I know.

			

More from CNET

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

It’s one of those life admin tasks that just never gets done because I can easily ignore these messages – making it the perfect job for a personal AI agent like Meta Muse. I want to make sure my name is formally listed as the number owner, as I don’t want people thinking I’m this elusive Andrew. 

I tried using Meta Muse as my personal shopper, which was fun, but I ran into an issue at checkout. Let’s see how it can handle an annoying task like this, without a number to call. One AI agent versus another.

Setting up Meta Muse with the task

I opened the Muse app and started a new conversation, instead of picking up on my previous chat with the AI agent. Keeping tasks and chats separate prevents context overload and helps Muse stay focused on the specific objective at hand. Just hit the new side chat button. 

Here’s how I instructed it: “I am a Visible customer on the $25 per month plan. I often get calls and texts looking for someone called Andrew. I think he was the previous owner of my number. It’s not a coincidence, because every time someone reaches out, they always ask for Andrew. I’ve contacted Visible before, and it said I own the number, but can you check I’m formally listed as the number owner? Check government websites, etc.” 

I also uploaded an example of a text I got. 

This was Muse’s response:

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I told Muse to talk to the Visible chatbot, search my number online and find anywhere that references Andrew. Within seconds, it found a link where my number showed up on a data broker page.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

But Muse couldn’t get through, as Visible blocks bot visits. Muse suggested changing my number (no) and making some changes on my phone to minimize unknown senders and silence unknown callers. This wasn’t super helpful either, as I often receive work calls from numbers I haven’t saved. 

I told Muse I didn’t want to change my number. It advised me against claiming the number, as that can encourage spam calls directed at me instead of Andrew. 

It said the Andrew data will go stale at some point. 

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

I had to take over the browser for Muse to chat with Visible. That was taking forever, so Muse did a workaround via the guest option. This took a good 10 minutes, which I spent cleaning the kitchen. But it had no luck.

“Quick honest update,” Muse told me, “I got into Visible’s guest chat, but their send button wouldn’t submit my message, and then their help pages temporarily blocked me.”

It advised me to paste the following chat into my Visible app: “My number is recycled — I get monthly spam calls and texts for ‘Andrew,’ the previous owner. I don’t want to change my number. What are my options? Do you offer spam/scam protection, and how do I turn it on? Can I report the number as recycled?”

Of course, such advice could have been delivered to me by a regular AI chatbot like ChatGPT or Gemini. The advantage of using an AI agent like Muse is that it’s supposed to do all of that for me.

But with a lot of these websites blocking AI agents, it makes autonomous task completion a challenge. I attempted to take over the browser again, but got a 403 forbidden error.

Meta/Screenshot by CNET

Muse told me the 403 error is a dead end and that my taking over the browser didn’t change the network address, which was annoying. Muse said it’s the bot protection that’s the problem, not Muse. It drafted a message to send to Visible chat manually, via a live agent.

Screenshot by Amanda Smith/CNET

While I chatted with Visible, Muse gave me a link that showed Andrew and my number. What’s interesting is that the last reported date was when I owned the number. 

When I ran a quick manual search on my phone number, the top two websites referenced Andrew. I asked Muse how to update these, and it gave me good advice, like requesting a suppression or removal of records from WhitePages and FastBackgroundCheck, but no instant resolution. 

Muse said this would clean the public record, but the messages are coming from old marketing lists, so it said I should keep reporting those as junk. Brokers re-scrape, so it should resolve in time. 

I tried it via WhitePages, but quickly hit a roadblock. It wouldn’t let me click Next.

I couldn’t follow the second instruction as I don’t have Andrew’s email address. It advised me to use my email (no thanks) or to call the number.

In another browser, I got escalated to Visible’s “advanced” support. Its instruction was to keep the browser open for 4 to 24 hours.

At this point, I gave up. 

The verdict on Meta Muse for this task

I wouldn’t say this was Muse’s fault specifically. It seems most websites have mechanisms in place to block any bots. Most AI agents would struggle to complete this autonomously. For me, in this situation, Muse still feels like a regular chatbot, giving guidance for me to follow. 

While I better understand the issue — spammers using outdated data — it still didn’t fix the problem. I’m hoping Visible pulls through with a solution and, if so, this was still time well spent. Without testing Muse to see if it could do it for me, I wouldn’t have prioritized this task. 

So, that’s a win, I guess.

title: Googlebook gets Luminar photo editing app with ‘Continue On’ support
snippet: One of the biggest questions around Googlebook is what app support will look like and, as the platform officially arrives for customers this week, Luminar is debuting a rebuilt photo editing app for Googlebook. more…
fullText:
One of the biggest questions around Googlebook is what app support will look like and, as the platform officially arrives for customers this week, Luminar is debuting a rebuilt photo editing app for Googlebook.

Luminar is a photo editing app that’s available across desktop platforms like Mac and Windows, but it’s also on Android, iOS, iPad, and ChromeOS. Now, it’s also making the jump to Googlebook.

The Luminar app has been rebuilt with support for Googlebok OS and meets “Tier 1” quality standards for the platform including keyboard shortcuts, resizable windows, drag-and-drop, and more. 

That’s on top of Luminar’s existing Android support for photo editing which includes the ability to adjust qualities of your photo, handle RAW edits, and use AI for features such as swapping out a background, masking, and more. You can even start edits on your phone and finish on your Googlebook as Luminar supports “Continue On.”

	

Luminar explains in a press release:

Luminar for Googlebook is fully adapted for large screens, meeting Google’s Tier 1 quality standards and introducing capabilities such as drag-and-drop, keyboard shortcuts, and resizable windows that weren’t previously available on phones and tablets. After several rounds of testing, Luminar has built a range of capabilities specifically for Googlebook OS:  

Built for the laptop: resizable windows, full mouse and keyboard support, shortcuts, hover states, multitasking, drag and drop, and file handling

New for launch: Generative Erase, HDR Merge, and batch editing – features usually associated with professional editing

One app, one subscription: use Luminar on an Android phone and on a Googlebook with the same account. [If available at launch:] With Continue On, you can start an edit on your phone and finish it on the laptop

Googlebook owners can download Lunimar via the Play Store. A temporary offer gives 12 months of access to Luminar for free, with a later one-time purchase unlocking the app’s premium features permanently.

title: Apple Mail added four convenient new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it packs key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to Apple Wallet, Maps, Notes, Messages, and more—and it packs key upgrades for the Mail app too. Here’s everything new for Apple Mail in iOS 27.

Upgraded search

If you have much history using Apple Mail, you’ll know that its search feature hasn’t always been the best. But in iOS 27, search has gotten a big upgrade.

From Apple’s website:

More relevant search in Mail. A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.

I can’t count the number of times search has previously failed to find messages that I knew existed. So far in my testing, iOS 27 seems to have fixed that.

New suggestions that include third-party apps

Suggestions at the top of messages have been in Apple Mail for years. But in iOS 27, they get a new, more flexible design and expand to support third-party apps.

When Mail detects that you might want to take action on the contents of an email, a suggestion might appear at the top of the message. These include: directions in Maps, creating events in Calendar, tracking a shipment with Apple Wallet, and more.

In iOS 27, third-party apps can offer suggestions too. And when multiple apps are available with suggested actions, there’s a drop-down menu to show you all available options.

Smart Reply improvements

Smart Reply is a keyboard feature that automatically surfaces reply options you can utilize with a single tap.

In iOS 27, the next generation of Apple Intelligence comes with improvements to Smart Reply.

Apple says that Smart Reply “can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.” Essentially, rather than offering fairly generic reply options, now Smart Reply suggestions will actually sound a lot more like you.

Siri AI capabilities

Apple has added ‘Ask Siri’ buttons throughout Apple Mail, just like the rest of its system apps. And Siri AI brings a bunch of new powers for Mail users.

One example I’ve seen several times on social media already is that you can ask Siri to delete all messages from a specific sender that’s spamming you.

Bug fixes

Beyond new features, Apple also says that iOS 27 makes the Mail app run better than ever thanks to bug fixes and performance improvements. Here are some specific examples given:

Faster message loading in Mail

More reliable search indexing in Mail

Improved list formatting in Mail

Improved unread badge accuracy in Mail

title: Googlebooks with Intel chipsets might have trouble with ‘complex’ Android apps
snippet: According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps. more…
fullText:
According to a statement from Google, Intel-based Googlebooks will apparently still struggle with some Android apps.

When Android apps made their debut on ChromeOS, one of the big downsides was that ARM-based machines ran those apps better than those using Intel chips. It was never a surprise given that Android apps are generally designed for devices running on an ARM architecture vs the x86 used on Intel chips.

Yet, the problem remains on Googlebook.

Despite the whole platform being Android-based this time around, Google confirmed in a statement to Android Authority that Intel-based Googlebook machines will still run into the occasional hiccup with “complex” Android apps and games, though the company emphasizes that “the vast majority” will work just fine.

	

The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box.

Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio.

Update 10/6: In an email to 9to5Google, Google further clarifies that “96.6% of the top 10k+ most-used applications” in Google Play work “flawlessly” on Intel-powered Googlebooks. 

The company stresses that 32-bit x86 emulation is not to blame as Googlebooks use a “highly advanced binary translation layer that dynamically compiles modern 64-bit Arm (arm64-v8a) code directly into native 64-bit Intel (x86_64) instructions” and that apps not compatible with Googlebook are “primarily due to app incompatibility with large screens for all platforms (eg require gyroscope).”

	

Still, this is noteworthy as the first wave of Googlebook hardware includes mostly Intel-based machines. Laptops from Lenovo, Asus, and Acer all run on Panther Lake-generation Intel chips, while Dell and HP machines both use the Snapdragon X Elite (the 2024 chip, not the newer version).

Another chip used for Googlebook from MediaTek is also in the works, though no machines are using it just yet.

The first batch of Googlebook laptops are all available as of today.

fullText:

title: These Prime Day headphones deals are actually worth looking at
snippet: Everything is getting more expensive these days, so it’s almost necessary to wait until a scheduled sale like Prime Day or Black Friday to purchase big-ticket items. I’ve been looking for a new pair of headphones recently, and came across a few Prime Day sales that I think are worth considering. more…
fullText:
Everything is getting more expensive these days, so it’s almost necessary to wait until a scheduled sale like Prime Day or Black Friday to purchase big-ticket items.

I’ve been looking for a new pair of headphones recently, and came across a few Prime Day sales that I think are worth considering.

The Nothing Headphone (1) is down to $189, its lowest price ever and a very good deal if you’re looking for great-sounding over-ear headphones. The Nothing Ear (3) earbuds are also down to $99, far below their previous low of $129.

Most of Sony’s high-end headphones are on sale, including the WH-1000XM5s at $198, which matches their lowest price ever. The newer WH-1000XM6s are also down to their lowest price ever at $378, $20 lower than during Prime Day in June. And the WF-1000XM6 earbuds are at $258, also an all-time low. You can also get the same deals from Sony directly, if you’re into that.

	

Bose’s last-gen QuietComfort Headphones are down to an easy-to-digest $169, while the better-sounding (and newer) QC Ultra headphones (2nd Gen) have matched their lowest price ever at $369.

If you insist on staying in the Google ecosystem, the Pixel Buds Pro 2 are $179, which is not the $169 we saw it during Black Friday last year, but it’s close.

Finally, the AirPods Pro 3 are down to $179, which is a great deal on the most popular earbuds on earth. And the AirPods Max 2 are still too expensive at $429, but at least they’re under $500.

Did I miss anything obvious? Let me know and I’ll add it to the list.

You’ll need a Prime membership to get these deals, too.

title: How to Disable Some Apple Intelligence Features on Your iPhone or Mac and Reclaim Valuable Space
snippet: The new AI features could be taking up a lot of storage on your device.
fullText:
Apple launched iOS 27 and MacOS 27 in September, and those updates introduced a revamped Siri AI powered by Apple Intelligence to Apple devices. While the new Siri was better at most tasks in my testing, it can still take up a significant amount of on-device storage space. On my iPhone, for example, it takes up about 6.4GB of data, while it takes up about 17.9GB of space on my MacBook Neo.

If you aren’t using the new AI features, you can disable some of them, and depending on what system you’re on, you can reclaim some of that valuable storage space. That way you can stave off for a little while the dreaded pop-up that tells you your storage is full – I need that extra storage for photos of my wife, son and dog.

		

			

Here’s how to see how much storage Apple Intelligence is taking up on your devices and how to disable – or at least limit – it on different operating systems. And don’t forget, Apple Intelligence is only available on certain devices.

How much space is Apple Intelligence taking up on your device?

How much space Apple Intelligence is taking up on your device is easy to check. If you’re on iPhone, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage > iOS. From here, look for the Apple Intelligence tab to see how much space it takes up on your iPhone.

On a MacBook, click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > General > Storage, and click the i next to MacOS. A new pop-up will open to show you how much space Apple Intelligence uses on your MacBook.

Disabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone that’s running iOS 27 or later is straightforward. Go to Settings > Siri > Turn Off Siri and follow the on-screen prompts. You can then go back and check your storage, and Apple Intelligence should be gone from that menu.

Disabling Siri AI can free up a few gigabytes on iOS 27.CNET

If you’re running iOS 26, you can disable Apple Intelligence by going to Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and tapping the toggle next to Apple Intelligence. This should free up some space on your iPhone.

You might also have to disable other Apple Intelligence features across your iPhone. To do this, go to Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy Restrictions and tap the toggle next to Content & Privacy Restrictions. Then, tap Intelligence & Siri. From here, you’ll need to tap into Image Creation, Writing Tools and Intelligence Extensions and tap Don’t Allow in each one.

This should free up a few gigabytes of space on your iPhone.

You can free up a few gigabytes of space in iOS 26 by disabling Apple Intelligence features.CNET

How to disable Apple Intelligence on your Mac

Disabling Apple Intelligence and freeing up storage space on your device can be weird, depending on which operating system you’re using. For instance, if you’re on MacOS 26, it’s easy to disable the feature and free up space. If you’re on MacOS 27, it’s a little more complicated. 

We’ll start off with the easy one. To disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26, first click the Apple logo in the top left corner of your screen. Then go to System Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri and click to toggle next to Apple Intelligence. That should free up a few gigabytes of data on your device.

Disabling Apple Intelligence on MacOS 26 frees up a little bit of storage.CNET

There are a couple of potential ways to disable Apple Intelligence on MacOS 27. The easiest way I found to free up a few gigabytes of space is to click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then go to System Settings > Siri and change your language to something like English (Irish). Siri AI isn’t available in every region yet, so changing your Siri language to a language from one of those regions could trick your device. Granted, it freed up only about 4 GB for me.

I changed my Siri language, and it freed up a few gigabytes of space.CNET

CNET’s sister site PCMag has a more in-depth way of turning off Apple Intelligence and freeing up some space. However, I couldn’t get this method to work. I’m not sure why I couldn’t get this method to work, other than that my device is running MacOS 27.0.1 and not MacOS 27. Maybe this will work for you, though.

According to PCMag, you have to go to System Settings > Screen Time > Content & Privacy. Then, toggle Content & Privacy off. Click Siri and change it to Siri Classic. Then go through the list of Capabilities and turn each feature off.

You’re not finished yet. Then, go to System Settings > Siri and select Don’t Allow Siri or Siri Classic.

Finally, you’ll need to go into individual Apple Intelligence settings and disable those features. Some easy ones include going to System Settings > Notifications > Summarize Notifications and turning the toggle off, or going to System Settings > Messages > Settings and turning off Message Summaries.

You could do all that work, or you could just switch your Siri language as I did. The choice is yours.

For more iOS news, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and iOS 27.0.1.

snippet: I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. fullText:
I have been a huge Sonos fan and customer for years, dating back to the original Sonos One. So, about two years ago, when I heard that Sonos was entering the over-ear headphone market, I knew I had to give it a try. The Sonos Ace looked great, was very comfortable, and brought some cool Sonos ecosystem features. But for a premium pair of headphones, there were still a few areas that left me wanting more, like strong bass, better ANC, and a better app experience. But now, the new Sonos Ace Ultra feels like they went down that list and addressed nearly every complaint that most customers had, including me. I have been using them as my main headphones for almost a month now, for travel, video editing, workouts, walks, and everyday listening. So I have a good grasp on them now, and here is what you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on video review for the Sonos Ace Ultra below:

Sonos Ace Ultra

At first glance, the Sonos Ace Ultra does not look much different from the original Sonos Ace. They decided to keep the same clean, understated design with a few differently placed chrome accents and some additional colors. But the biggest differences are inside these headphones. 

What’s new versus the original Sonos Ace

Here are some of the biggest changes from the original Sonos Ace to the Ace Ultra:

Redesigned 40mm drivers

10-microphone array, up from eight mics on the original

Improved adaptive ANC, stating up to 2X more effective and being able to adjust to things like glasses, hair, and changes in the seal around your ears

Longer battery life with up to 35 hours with ANC turned on

Bluetooth 6.0 versus 5.4 on the older generation

Expanded EQ controls with three and an advanced eight-band EQ options

Headphones linking with the Sonos Ecosystem

User-replaceable batteries

Updated ear and headband cushion materials  

More rotation of the ear cups so they can sit flat when around your neck

Two new colors: Agave and Sand

The main things that I noticed in these changes are the redesigned acoustics, better bass response, and stronger ANC. With the original Sonos Ace, I would sometimes get this hissing noise when I was in ANC mode. This would rarely happen, but I did notice it. So far, the new Sonos Ace Ultra has alleviated that issue. You also still get some of the great specs from the previous model like:

Spatial audio and Dolby Atmos

Dynamic head tracking

Lossless audio on supported devices

USB-C and 3.5mm wired audio support

Bluetooth multipoint

Fast charging with up to three hours of playback from a three-minute charge

TV Audio Swap with compatible Sonos soundbars

They still have the same super high-quality design, combining plastics and metals to give you a premium, lightweight feel. The Sonos Ace Ultra also keeps the magnetically replaceable ear cups, and one of the best things that I have noticed is the new EQ settings that really let me hone in on how I like to listen to my music. But how were they as an everyday pair of headphones?

My experience

Again, it’s easy to put specs on paper, but the biggest reason I’ve enjoyed the Ace Ultras is that they actually sound noticeably better. My biggest complaint about the original Sonos Ace was the lack of bass depth. The bass was not bad, but for a pair of $450 headphones, I felt like they were lacking a bit. I listen to a lot of R&B, hip-hop, and pop music, so bass is important to me. I wanted more low-end impact and to feel the bass. The Ace Ultra finally delivers the experience that I wanted. 

There is substantially more punch and depth at the low end. But one thing to note here is that Sonos hasn’t achieved that by simply turning up the bass slider. Any headphone brand can crank up the bass, but the difficult part is maintaining separation so that the bass doesn’t overwhelm the vocals, instruments, and higher-end frequencies. That is where the Ace Ultra has really impressed me. The bass hits harder, but the vocals are still clear, crisp, and easy to listen to. And it’s not just for music; all media sounds better, like podcasts, movies, and all the YouTube videos I watch. They have sounded fantastic in all media listening situations. 

The improved ANC is something else I noticed immediately. The new 10 mic array allows even more sound to be dynamically pushed away from the headphones. Even when there is no media playing, it’s insane how quiet the headphones are in so many different environments. It’s almost too good! The biggest improvement to ANC is the unpredictable noises. It’s one thing to block out a consistent noise like an airplane engine, but another to block out passing cars, construction, sirens, or sudden loud sounds while walking outside.

Two final things I want to bring up are comfort and the Sonos ecosystem. These headphones are the most comfortable headphones I have worn. Even on a long 8-10-hour airplane ride, I wore them 95% of the time, and I felt no aches, pain, or heat at all. Lastly, I have a lot of Sonos speakers around my house, and they introduced a new feature that lets you move music from a speaker to your headphones with the press of a button. It’s a very cool feature, but I personally haven’t used it much.

My only complaint is that they need a new zipper or mechanism for the headphone case because that sticker gets stuck way too often!

Pricing and availability 

The Sonos Ace Ultra is available today on Sonos’s site and Amazon for $449, keeping the same launch price as the original Sonos Ace. They come in four colors: Black, White, Agave, and Sand. I also noticed that the original Sonos Ace is available on Amazon for $239 while supplies last. At $240, now that could be a good choice as well.

At $450, the Sonos Ace Ultra is firmly in the premium noise-canceling headphone category alongside options from Apple, Bose, and Sony.

Final take

The original Sonos Ace felt like a good first-generation product. The Sonos Ace Ultra feels like a complete and finished product. As we saw, they did not reinvent the look or design, but they improved in all the areas that mattered and even added a few new cool features. The sound is noticeably better, the ANC is strong and smarter, battery life lasts longer, the app experience is smoother, and that Agave color is amazing.

If you already own the OG Sonos Ace, I actually think there is enough here to justify the upgrade, depending on what you value. If you are in the market for a premium set of headphones, I think the Sonos Ace Ultra needs to be on your shortlist. At $449, they are certainly not cheap, but if you want one of the best premium headphones and are a Sonos fan, then you will love these.

title: Redesigned MacBook Pro will reportedly include these three changes
snippet: Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching soon, its first new design since 2021. Here are three design changes reportedly coming. more…
fullText:
Apple has a fully redesigned MacBook Pro launching soon, its first new design since 2021. Here are three design changes reportedly coming.

#1: No notch

One of the defining traits of the current MacBook Pro design is its display cutout: the notch.

The MacBook Pro introduced the notch to the Mac line in 2021, and the redesigned model that’s about to launch will reportedly remove it. Instead, the new MacBook Pro will have a small camera cutout and Dynamic Island built in. Per Mark Gurman:

The Dynamic Island on the Mac will be built around a hole-punch-sized cutout for the computer’s camera. It’s smaller than the pill-shaped notch in current iPhones.

It sounds like the notch replacement could be similar to iPhone Duo’s hole-punch camera on its outer display.

#2: Thinner and lighter

The current MacBook Pro is a hefty powerhouse, but Apple reportedly has a thinner, lighter design coming for the new MacBook Pro. Per Bloomberg earlier this week:

The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

It’s unknown whether slimming the MacBook Pro will result in any ports being removed. Apple’s current MacBook Pro design brought back many ports that had been removed in the prior iteration. It would be surprising for the company to strip ports yet again.

#3: Slightly larger displays

An Omdia report this summer said the redesigned MacBook Pro will come in two screen sizes:

14.3 inches

16.3 inches

	

If accurate, this is a very slight increase over the current 14.2- and 16.2-inch sizes. It’s possible Apple will reduce the bezels a bit to achieve a larger usable display area.

It’s also possible that the overall form factor will get slightly larger to help provide extra space for components despite the thinner body. But there are no specific rumors around these details yet.

fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

A jury found an Ohio political blogger guilty of telecommunications harassment after he sent an explicit image of Shrek to a Republican state senator. On Friday, a judge ordered DJ Byrnes, owner of political commentary blog The Rooster, to pay a $200 fine, according to a report from the Columbus Dispatch.

Byrnes texted Ohio Sen. Jerry Cirino in May after he dropped out of the state’s Senate presidential race. As reported by the Columbus Dispatch, Byrnes sent a nude image of Shrek alongside the message: “Good to see you finally made your humiliation public, Young Mussolini! THE PATRIOTS CAUCUS sends its regards!!!!!!!!!!”

Cirino filed a police report against Byrnes, “describing his messages as pornographic and harassing,” according to the Columbus Dispatch. Four state police officers arrested Byrnes at the Ohio statehouse in June, the Columbus Dispatch reports. Byrnes was reportedly held in jail overnight even though he posted bail.

”I can’t wait for the jury to see the image that he sent to me,” Cirino said ahead of the trial, according to the Columbus Dispatch. Byrnes pleaded not guilty to telecommunications harassment, claiming that the text was protected free speech.

“This wasn’t a free speech issue; this was a harassment statute that I believed he was in violation of,” Cirino said following the ruling, as reported by News 5 Cleveland. “Obviously, he’s free to write on his blog whatever he wants. I just don’t want to be accosted in the Statehouse in the future.”

title: These are the best times to save money on your next flight, according to Google Flights
snippet: Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the busy holiday travel season, Google is detailing the best time to book your next flight to get the best possible price.

With surging fuel prices have also come much higher plane ticket costs and, with that, everyone’s looking for a deal. In a blog post this week, Google Flights details the best times to book your next flight.

For domestic US flights, the best time is apparently 39 days prior to departure, but the lowest price can fall anywhere between 57 days prior and 22 days prior to the actual flight date. International flights should be booked much further out, with 89 days being the magic number there.

Thanksgiving and Christmas flights bend the rules a bit. Thanksgiving flights are actually cheapest 34 days prior to departure, but Christmas flights need to be booked much earlier at around 56 days.

	

Here’s the full breakdown from Google:

Domestic flights: 39 days before departure (low price range is 22–57 days)

International flights: 89 days before departure, but the average price drop during the low range (50–133 days out) is insignificant

Thanksgiving: Lowest prices hit 34 days before departure (low price range is 21–57 days)

Christmas: 56 days before departure (low price range is 33–67 days)

Spring break: 50 days before departure (low price range is 29–64 days) for trips in March or April

Summer vacation: 21 days before departure (low price range is 20–47 days) for trips in July or August

Trips to Europe: 49 days or more before departure

Trips to Mexico or the Caribbean: 43 days before departure (low price range is 24–69 days)

The post goes on to detail trending destinations for the 2026 travel season, with Hawaii being the top Thanksgiving destination and international trips to Greece and Canada trending around Christmas and New Year’s Eve.

title: Google Pixel at 10: Successes, failures, and fun along the way [Video]
snippet: A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though. more…
fullText:
A decade of Pixel, it’s only in the last few years that we have seen Google settle into a rhythm with smartphones. It hasn’t been smooth sailing, though.

Look back at the line-up, and it’s still hard to believe we’ve had a decade of Pixel. If you asked me back in 2016 whether Google’s in-house hardware experiment would stick around long enough to reach fully custom 3nm silicon, I’m not sure I’d have believed you.

To say that Google was late to the market is an understatement. By 2016, Apple and Samsung were already well into the swing of things. To be fair, that still is the case a decade later, but now with an even tighter iron grip over the space. I was personally distraught when the Nexus lineup was canceled to the point that I actually went with the Galaxy S8 rather than wait to see what Google had in store next.

	

Google’s answer to the ‘big two’ was Pixel. A phone not “officially” made by partners, but still sort of relying on OEMs while the production pipeline or groundwork was laid.

Pixel and Pixel XL (2016)

The original Google Pixel was built in a close manufacturing partnership with HTC, featuring a wedge-shaped profile that famously tapered down to eliminate any camera bump. 

Let’s be real, the hardware wasn’t tearing up trees, and it looked more than a little similar to the iPhone 7/8 series. It was a conservative design, but pretty darn self-assured.

The main thing that helped differentiate the device was its built-in Google Assistant integration and HDR+ image processing pipeline for photos. Rightly or wrongly, this simple formula has more or less defined the Pixel for the past decade of Google’s mobile computing efforts.

Smart, simple software and artificial intelligence have been at the forefront from the very beginning and will remain so over the next 10 years.

Pixel 2 series (2017)

With the second generation, Google finally figured out design. The LG-made Pixel 2 XL gave us the iconic “Panda” colorway with its stark black-and-white glass back and the bright orange accent power button. You’ve told us time and time again that it’s a personal favorite for Pixel fans. It also debuted the Pixel Visual Core, Google’s first attempt at custom co-processing to let apps like Instagram use HDR+.

Add single-lens Portrait Mode that put dual-camera rivals to shame, squeeze-to-activate Active Edge, ambient Now Playing track identification, and the persistent At a Glance widget, and the Pixel 2 series genuinely felt like magic in your hand.

The first major problems started to appear, though. The blue shift on the 2 XL meant that viewing from an angle is not recommended. Screen burn-in was also something people suffered.

Pixel 3 series (2018)

The Pixel 3 era was peak camera software dominance mixed with a few just flat-out bizarre hardware choices. 

That Pixel 3 XL “bathtub” notch was an absolute eyesore and was thoroughly roasted by the tech community and reviewers alike. I think in some ways, once you fired up the camera, all was forgiven. I’ve taken some incredible photos with the Pixel 3. Pictures that I still look at very fondly 8 years later.

This was the first Pixel to come with Night Sight, which arrived via a software update and single-handedly changed low-light smartphone photography forever. It wasn’t the first, but it was one of the best implementations.

You could shoot in near pitch-black conditions and walk away with a clean, detailed photo without ever touching the flash. Pair that with yet more AI-powered functions such as Call Screen, which handles telemarketers and spam in real time, and the software was doing all the heavy lifting.

In trademark fashion, the Pixel 3 had issues with RAM management and poor battery life. It was a mixed bag, but it was followed up by something truly interesting because the Pixel 3a is one of the best midrangers ever. It set the stage for a change of pace…but that wasn’t for a couple of years.

Pixel 4 series (2019)

Let’s be honest, Google swung for the fences with the Pixel 4, but it didn’t quite land. 

It is almost the least Pixel-y of the entire lineup because it stands apart from all that have since followed. The black sheep in many ways. It ditched the trusty rear fingerprint scanner, they threw Project Soli into a chunky top bezel for wave-to-snooze Motion Sense gestures and 3D Face Unlock.

We also got a silky smooth 90Hz display and a telephoto lens rather than the industry-preferred and marginally more flexible ultrawide. It felt like a zig to everyone else’s zag.

Alas, it was a big risk and one that ended up compromising the most. The small Pixel 4 had a tiny 2,800 mAh battery that struggled to get through an afternoon, let alone a full day. High launch prices and Soli radar frequency restrictions in key markets meant commercial success was hard to come by, and the negatives really held back the lineup. It actually triggered a reshuffle in Google’s hardware team.

Pixel 4a, 4a 5G and Pixel 5 (2020)

Faced with global disruptions in 2020 due to the emergence of COVID-19 and maybe due to some, at the time, unknown future plans, Google completely pivoted with the Pixel lineup. The Pixel 4 was a big swing, but the follow-up series went in a very different direction.

The mid-range Pixel 4a launched at just $349/£349 and became an immediate hit because it kept that flagship-grade camera performance in an understated, no-nonsense plastic body. This was an appetizer for what was to come.

Then came the flagship Pixel 5, but this wasn’t the premium phone that many expected. It skipped top-tier Qualcomm silicon entirely for the upper-mid-range Snapdragon 765G. It was the same chip used by many cheaper phones and even the more affordable Pixel 4a 5G, which was basically a bigger, bolder version of the 4a.

The 5 was coated in a bio-resin finish over a recycled aluminum frame, it brought back the rear fingerprint scanner, swapped the telephoto for an ultrawide lens, and gave us uniform bezels with reliable battery life. It lacked raw processing grunt, but it earned a cult following for simply being a reliable, compact everyday phone.

On one hand, it was good to see Google right some issues with the previous generation. On the other hand, it was confusing as it sort of signaled that maybe Pixels were not high-end phones. It was a reset.

Pixel 6 series (2021)

After a fairly unassuming and, arguably, boring preamble, 2021 was without a doubt the biggest turning point in Pixel history. 

Google overhauled the design, introducing the now iconic camera bar running across the back, creating a silhouette you could spot from a mile away. We were given a proper two-tier lineup with a Pro phone that packed in a triple camera system, a larger 120Hz display, and a cheaper but still competent base model. 

Most importantly, though, was the debut of original Tensor (now G1) silicon. Moving away from standard Qualcomm chips meant Google could tailor hardware directly for on-device ML—powering features like Magic Eraser, Live Translate, and Material You dynamic color themes.

As well-received as it was at launch, the Pixel 6 had some serious growing pains with a slow optical fingerprint reader, terrible modem performance, and overheating issues galore, but despite what were fairly major issues, the foundation was set.

Pixel 7 series (2022)

The Pixel 7 and 7 Pro took the foundational groundwork of the Pixel 6 and smoothed out the rough edges. Visually, the camera bar evolved into a seamless piece of 100% recycled aluminum that flowed directly out of the side rails, swapping out the all-glass visor for a sleeker metal shell with pill-and-cutout camera cutouts.

Under the hood sat Tensor G2, which paired with an upgraded Samsung Exynos 5300 modem. This finally resolved the signal drops and battery drain that plagued the previous generation. While raw computational gains were modest, Tensor G2 unlocked key software capabilities: Photo Unblur in Google Photos (which could restore old, blurry archival photos taken on any camera), Macro Focus via the ultrawide lens, and the return of a fast 2D Face Unlock system.

Mid-2023 also saw the Pixel lineup expand its footprint. The Pixel 7a raised the bar for mid-range phones by bringing a 90Hz refresh rate and wireless charging to the A-series for the first time. Meanwhile, Google made its long-awaited entry into new form factors with the original Pixel Fold, showcasing a short, wide “passport” design that prioritized a usable outer display over tall, narrow screens. It was a bit of a “fail” in the sense that it didn’t move the needle and was quickly overshadowed by others due to launching with the previous-generation processor and, admittedly, strange aspect ratios.

Pixel 8 series (2023)

In my mind, the Pixel 8 and 8 Pro were the moment the lineup transitioned from an enthusiast recommendation with caveats to a phone you could comfortably recommend to everyday consumers. Never perfect, but quietly the last Pixel that felt truly like a Pixel. These are bubbly, friendly phones in all the ways that matter.

A few more AI functions made their debut: Best Take, Audio Magic Eraser, Video Boost, and, as a headline addition, 7 years of full updates for the first time. Basically, making these the industry standard for smartphone support. Google leapfrogged Samsung and even Apple for software support windows.

No, no reinvention of the wheel. Tensor still didn’t hit the heights many wanted, which is to say it was fine.

Pixel 9 series (2024)

The Pixel 9 was a rapid design departure in a number of ways. Firstly, it ditched the friendly, playful looks that had been a trademark of the series. Instead, it took a very boxy route that instantly felt familiar to anyone who may have tried an iPhone.

It was a really polished upgrade and sort of put to bed some of the tricky hardware issues that plagued many of the older Pixel models. Google also began leaning into yet more AI-powered functionality, with Gemini now being a key component.

Google unified the launch across all phones, coming on day one, but also switched from the standard October release cadence to a late-summer August release. Pitching the Pixel ahead of the iPhone has been a huge change. Allowing the company to lay out plans and getting even more hype around a launch lineup.

Pixel 10 series (2025)

Although on the surface, almost the exact same, the Pixel 10 was the first 3nm chip for the lineup, and it was the first to be fabricated by TSMC. It signaled the end of the Samsung Foundry partnership that was the start of the Tensor era.

Any lingering thermal issues were gone, Gemini was integrated even further and into even more places, like the camera, and the first steps of multimodel intelligence were added with Magic Cue. I’d stop short of saying the Pixel 10 delivers on some of the promises made way back on October 4, 2016, but it came as close as it ever had until that point.

Finally, we had a flagship-level device with Qi2 magnets at the back too. It took until 2025 for one of the biggest Android brands to adopt Magsafe or, in this case, Pixelsnap. With that one move, the Pixel 10 opened up a whole world of accessories to be attached without the need for a case. It’s so elementary, it’s a wonder we haven’t seen more try to do it.

Pixel 11 series (2026) and beyond

A decade later, we’re here with the Pixel 11. The peak of the Made by Google series thus far. There are still pain points, namely a design that hasn’t evolved too drastically, performance from the Tensor processor still feels decidedly mid-range at times, and a heavy emphasis on AI functionality to make up for this raw performance gap.

A sometimes lazy observation of the original Pixel was that it was the “iPhone of Android,” but that seems to have been taken to heart, and a decade after launch, we have the most “iPhone-y” Pixel to date. Maybe that is a symptom of where smartphones have stalled, but it’s a really interesting evolution. The advantage is that you know what to expect. Gemini is becoming more and more prominent and yet a more integral component in Pixel phones, and that isn’t likely to cease any time soon.

What’s easy to see is that Pixel has been a bigger success than the Nexus lineup. Getting hold of the full end-to-end user experience has helped drastically. I don’t think anyone can argue that the best Nexus phone is easily surpassed by the best Pixel phone.

It would be remiss of anyone talking about Google products without some fears over whether we’ll get another decade of Pixel, but with so many internal changes at the company and bigger marketing budgets thrown at actually marketing the devices, it seems that, at least for now, the Pixel is here to stay. 

The past decade has proved that Google was never really trying to build the highest-spec hardware on the market. Instead, Pixel has always been an engine designed to deliver Google’s software vision. From early HDR+ algorithms on single camera lens setups and now to custom TSMC Tensor silicon wired for Gemini integration, it’s hard to argue that Google’s Pixel has succeeded in changing how we evaluate a smartphone: not by how fast its CPU clocks, but by how helpful it is throughout the day.

Maybe sales will eventually catch up, but the main thing is to keep making solid devices, and playing the long game might start to be the best decision Google could have made after entering the market late.

There have been plenty of bumps in the road along the way, but here’s the next decade of Pixel. I’m sure it’ll be a wild ride.

title: New Xbox Division XP Will Adapt More Video Games for Movies and TV
snippet: Xbox already had success with A Minecraft Movie and Fallout.
fullText:
The Xbox reset continues. Despite a rough year of revenue losses, layoffs and major restructuring, the Microsoft gaming division announced Thursday that it’s going big into the entertainment industry and elsewhere.

After the resounding success of A Minecraft Movie and the Fallout TV series — both of which are longtime video game titles — Xbox is creating a division called XP to expand its video game brands into movies, TV, merchandise and even live events, the company said.

Xbox has hundreds of games in its catalog, with only Minecraft, Fallout and Halo adapted for film and TV. But there are a few other adaptations in the works — movies for Call of Duty and Gears of War, and a Netflix animated series for Diablo.  

			

More from CNET

“Our ambition at Xbox is to be the number one entertainment company in the world,” Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball said in the announcement.

XP, which refers to “experience points” in the gaming world, will consist of four departments. Xbox Pictures will create more film and TV adaptations; Xbox Products will develop licensing and merchandise; Xbox Places will host live events and broadcast events in theme parks and other locations; and Xbox Partnerships will collaborate with creators and brands to make new experiences.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma named Kayleen Walters as president of XP. Walters was executive producer of A Minecraft Movie, which led all movies in US ticket sales and grossed $424 million in the US last year. She is now a producer for the sequel, A Minecraft Movie Squared, scheduled for release in theaters on July 23, 2027.

Before joining Xbox’s Mojang Studios in February 2025, Walters spent 13 years at Lucasfilm running successful global marketing campaigns for the Star Wars franchise.

Sharma also announced Maria Angelidou-Smith, a former VP at Meta and chief product officer at Reddit, will become CEO of Mojang and Minecraft.

It’s been an eventful tenure for Sharma since becoming Xbox CEO in February. Revenue dropped $1.7 billion, or about 7%, from July 2025 through June 2026. On July 6, Sharma announced a reset — “the most significant restructure in Xbox history” — laying off 3,200 people by mid-2027 and moving four studios out of Xbox and under new management.

Expansion is smart, analyst says

With its gaming business struggling, Xbox is making a smart move, says streaming media analyst, author and speaker Dan Rayburn. 

“They have to expand outside of the core gaming audience,” Rayburn told CNET. “They’re realizing, with how much content is being licensed these days and all the different platforms out there, let’s create more content off our brand that others might want to license for their streaming services.”

Moving beyond the confines of the console definitely worked for A Minecraft Movie and Fallout, and their success on screens boosted Xbox’s gaming business. There was a 75% increase in weekly active users of Minecraft after the movie’s release in spring 2025, and there was a fivefold increase in hours played on the various Fallout game titles during the TV series’ first season on Prime Video.

But whereas Minecraft and Fallout found enthusiastic audiences in the entertainment world, that won’t be true for all of Xbox’s games, Rayburn said.

“They’re going to know that certain brands aren’t going to resonate with certain individuals outside of gaming, so you have to pick and choose the right content,” Rayburn told CNET. “That’s why hiring someone from the film business (Walters) is the key point here. They took a film executive as opposed to a gaming executive. You can’t have a gaming executive running that.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Alex Valdes

title: Move Over ‘Carrie’: Mike Flanagan Teases ‘The Exorcist: Martyrs’ at NYCC 2026
snippet: The prolific horror filmmaker unveiled the trailer for The Exorcist: Martyrs, which he said is “the scariest movie” he’s ever made.
fullText:
Mike Flanagan is a busy man. Just this week, his TV series remake of Stephen King‘s horror classic, Carrie, premiered on Prime Video. Clayface, the body-horror movie inspired by the DC Comics character, for which he cowrote the script, hits theaters on Oct. 23.

Now, he’s onto promoting his next completed project, The Exorcist: Martyrs, a film he called “the scariest movie I’ve ever made,” while at Friday’s Blumhouse panel at New York Comic Con.

If you’ve been keeping track, Flanagan’s name has been attached to the iconic horror franchise, which began in 1973 and is based on the William Peter Blatty novel of the same name. Since Linda Blair terrified audiences as the demon-possessed young girl, Regan MacNeil, the movie series expanded. There have been sequels, a prequel and even a short-lived TV show.

			

More from CNET

In 2023, David Gordon Green attempted to reboot the franchise with The Exorcist: The Believer. Now, it’s Flanagan’s turn.

The Exorcist: Martyrs gives a new spin on the Exorcist canon and injects a Minderhunter-style serial killer narrative element into the mix. If you watched the TV series I mentioned above, you’ll notice a similar procedural vibe in the brand-new trailer that dropped during the panel. And if you’re an Exorcist III stan, I’m sure you’ll be happy with the just released clip, as it’s got that similar brooding feeling here.

The Exorcist: Martyrs stars Scarlett Johansson as an NYPD detective tracking a serial killer named Father Sunday (John Leguizamo), who uses Catholic iconography in his kills. Chiwetel Ejiofor, fresh out of The Backrooms, also stars in the film, opposite Laurence Fishburne, Sasha Calle and Jacobi Jupe.

If you’ve been yearning for the Mike Flanagan era of Oculus and The Haunting of Hill House, The Exorcist: Martyrs feels like the filmmaker is back in his terrifying groove. While I’m still waiting for his adaptation of Stephen King’s The Dark Tower to see the light of day, this will have to do.

The Exorcist: Martyrs premieres in theaters on Friday, March 12, 2027.
