title: Automattic interim CFO resigns just weeks after boardroom shakeup
snippet: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's leadership turmoil.
fullText:
Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”

Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit. 

He was meant to replace the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

A source at Automattic told TechCrunch that Klaperman was upset the board was considering external candidates for the CFO role. Though he was announced internally as interim CFO, the board never legally approved his title, the source said. In addition, there was a disagreement with Mullenweg over a work project related to employee performance reviews, which led to Mullenweg’s demotion of Klaperman back to his former position at VIP. Klaperman resigned shortly thereafter.  

Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure. The company is still performing an external search for a qualified CFO candidate, we understand. 

After publication, the company issued a statement via X post, which implies that Klaperman was offended by the board’s search for external CFO candidates.

It read, “At Automattic, we consider it best practice to evaluate external candidates for critical roles alongside internal people stepping up. We are always talking to and recruiting the best talent. Sometimes people are offended or surprised by this and they resign, sometimes it has led to amazing mentoring or advising situations. We won’t comment on any specific person, but as a company we’re always trying to optimize and redefine ourselves to serve our customers better and promote the ideals we aspire to around Open Source, freedom, liberty, autonomy, and hackers.” 

At Automattic, we consider it best practice to evaluate external candidates for critical roles alongside internal people stepping up. We are always talking to and recruiting the best talent. Sometimes people are offended or surprised by this and they resign, sometimes it has led…

— Automattic (@automattic) October 9, 2026

When the company originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO internally on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.

Updated after publication with more information about Klaperman’s departure.

title: Xona’s commercial GPS alternative is about to go live
snippet: Xona's precision timing and navigation service will enter beta testing after SpaceX launches six satellites designed by the company.
fullText:
The first precision commercial alternative to GPS is preparing to go live when six satellites designed by the startup Xona Space Systems launch into orbit this month.

A service that competes with free signals provided by governments around the world may seem foolhardy, but Xona is hoping to add navigation and timing to the list of de facto government space monopolies disrupted by venture-backed startups.

Xona was founded in 2019 by a team of five engineers who originally met at Stanford University’s aerospace engineering graduate program. One, Tyler Reid, went on to earn a PhD, writing his thesis on the possibilities of using satellites in low-earth orbit to improve navigation.

GPS and analog satellite networks built by Europe, China, and Russia provide huge value, but are also easy to jam and aren’t precise enough to be used alone for applications like farming robots or self-driving cars. Over “pizza and beer chats,” the friends mulled whether fixing those problems could be a business.

“My knee jerk was like, this is dumb,” Xona CEO Brian Manning told TechCrunch during a recent visit to the company’s headquarters. “Why would anybody replace GPS? It’s free, right? And I started digging into it. People think of GPS as a free service, but the market isn’t the service. The market’s the hardware, and you have billions of devices being sold every year; those things aren’t being given away for free. There’s an immense market that is desperately looking for better performance.”

That didn’t mean the road to delivering such a service was simple. Improving GPS with a stronger signal that offers more precise timing and location data remained a technical challenge. The company needed to develop a unique architecture that would allow its satellites to keep time without expensive atomic clocks onboard, taking advantage of the spacecraft’s proximity to Earth and close communication with ground-based sources of truth.

The other technical challenge the company solved was making sure its signals could be received by existing GPS receivers with a relatively simple software modification. That gives Xona immediate access to the market and smoothes the way through the regulations for broadcasting navigation signals.

Later this month, a SpaceX rocket is scheduled to launch six satellites for Xona. Four are similar to a prototype the company launched last year that proved its technology; those satellites are built around a satellite platform from Aerospace Labs. The other two satellites were built entirely by Xona at its Burlingame, California, headquarters, and are intended to be the foundation of the company’s 258-satellite operational constellation, called Pulsar.

Xona’s Pulsar satelliteImage Credits:Xona Space Systems under a Xona Space Systems license.

Pulsar will offer centimeter-level precision for geolocation, instead of the meter-level precision provided by GPS, and its signal is strong enough to be detected inside buildings and in urban environments. Manning also believes its signal is powerful enough to deter would-be jammers and spoofers, too.

Xona can begin beta-testing Pulsar with real customers once its satellites are in orbit and passing overhead the mid-latitudes about eight times a day. 

Ian Gough, the CEO of TimeBeat, a company that specializes in electronic timing, says the initial pilot will allow his engineers to check and correct the timing provided by its devices around the world. By 2028, Xona hopes to offer full coverage in the U.S., Europe, Japan, and South Korea.

Xona has raised just over $300 million from venture investors since its founding, including $20 million from the U.S. Space Force. While the company is focused on offering a commercial service, the U.S. government is clearly interested in the technology, as jamming and spoofing of satellite navigation services become increasingly common in conflicts.

While there are literally billions of potential users for a new precision timing signal, Xona is also looking ahead to a world of growing autonomy. Reid, whose thesis inspired the company and who now serves as its CTO, worked on self-driving cars at Ford and saw that a service like Pulsar would be needed to realize the potential of autonomous vehicles of all stripes.

Xona’s headquarters boasts an incredible view of planes landing at San Francisco International Airport. Watching the jets come in, Manning points out that among “all the forms of mass transportation, the gold standard for safety is civil aviation. We see Xona and what we’re building being able to play a big part in that … to provide the service to a car, so you can feel as safe taking your hands off the wheel as you are laying back in an airliner.”

fullText:
The first two episodes of “Small Prophets” are now available to stream on Apple TV, following a wave of glowing reviews for the British comedy series. Watch the trailer below.

’Small Prophets’ now streaming on Apple TV

Earlier today, my colleague Ryan covered the raving reviews for “Small Prophets,” a British comedy series Apple TV acquired for international distribution earlier this year.

The move marked a first for Apple TV, as the streamer had never previously acquired an existing English-language series that had already aired elsewhere.

“Small Prophets” premiered on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two in the U.K. earlier this year, before Apple picked it up for international distribution in August.

It is now available to Apple TV subscribers globally, except in the U.K., where it will arrive on the service in 2027.

“Small Prophets” was created, written, and directed by Mackenzie Crook (Detectorists), who also stars alongside Pearce Quigley (The Way Back), Lauren Patel (The Effects of Lying), Sir Michael Palin (Monty Python), Sophie Willan (Ludwig), Jon Pointing (Big Boys), and Paul Kaye (Game of Thrones), among others.

Following the two-episode premiere, the show will run every Wednesday through November 4.

Here’s Apple TV’s synopsis of “Small Prophets”:

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Michael gets help from his young coworker Kacey (Lauren Patel), an unlikely friendship that blossoms partly (but not wholly) through their mutual dislike of store manager Gordon (Mackenzie Crook). title: Google seems to finally understand why it bought Fitbit
snippet: Good morning! Today, I’m searching for Prime Day deals, watching Chris Rock masterfully dodge questions about The Slap, questioning Sam Altman about whether we have to accept “some bad things” to justify AI’s exponential growth, and brushing up on my chess game after many years of neglect. fullText:
Good morning! Today, I’m searching for Prime Day deals, watching Chris Rock masterfully dodge questions about The Slap, questioning Sam Altman about whether we have to accept “some bad things” to justify AI’s exponential growth, and brushing up on my chess game after many years of neglect.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

When Google bought Fitbit back in 2019, it wasn’t clear that the brand had a future. 

As many companies are wont to do, Google had good reason to ingest the accessory maker’s IP and set fire to the rest — but that didn’t happen. After a few fallow years, Fitbit became the software powering the Pixel Watch’s health capabilities, and is now shifting once again to working as a standalone hardware brand within Google.

	

After the monumental success of the Fitbit Air in May, the company is poised to release a Charge follow-up called the Edge. The Charge series hasn’t seen a refresh since 2023, and it appears that Google is updating its design and adding a number of app-like features that should bridge the proverbial gap between tracker and smartwatch.

Of course, Google may not have known Fitbit’s true trajectory back in 2019, but it’s arrived at a place that makes sense: Fitbit’s software is now tightly integrated into all of Google’s health-related endeavors, so the brand is pivoting back to hardware where it made its mark originally.

So the question is whether the Edge, or something like it, is the right move. The Air’s success came from its accessible price ($100) and the growing trend of screenless trackers. I wear a Fitbit Air alongside either a smartwatch or a regular one, and that’s its biggest appeal. And people are going to great lengths to hide the diminutive tracker in places most wearables can’t go. 

The Edge, on the other hand, is a traditional fitness tracker with a few tricks up its sleeve. Judging from the leaks, it will offer notifications, Google Maps, music controls, along with Find My Device support. And of course health tracking that, with a Google Health Premium account, includes an AI-powered fitness coach that’s proven its mettle over the past few months.

I doubt the Edge will have the same cultural impact as the Air, but I also see its existence as proof that Google understands why it bought Fitbit in the first place. Now that it’s plumbed the company for all of its wares, Fitbit rises once again where it all started: with cheap hardware that does just enough well to keep users happy.

✉️ Inbox

Samsung reportedly confirms November launch for first Android XR glasses. You’d be forgiven for forgetting that Samsung’s first pair of Android XR smart glasses is slated to ship in 2026. Because I’d forgotten too.

Huawei’s Mate 90 Pro Max says ‘why not’ and just lets you add an entire camera. This is possibly the most insane phone that I’ve seen this year, and that’s saying something.

Samsung officially raises Galaxy S26 prices by $100, but it hasn’t changed everywhere. Phones are getting more expensive, but raising the price by $100 three months before its successor is not a good look.

Samsung just raised the price on several more Galaxy phones in the US

HP’s MacBook Neo competitor is $699 with an OLED display and plenty of catches. This is a really nice laptop, but you absolutely won’t be paying $699 for it when all’s said and done.

Vivo X Fold 6 skips the wide form factor, but will launch globally with strong cameras

Samsung’s open-ear Galaxy Buds On go official with late October release. I’m not a fan of this style of headphone, but at least these ones will be checks price only $200.

Google Messages rolls out new long-press menu with partial copying [Updated]. Our long non-copying nightmare is over.

Nvidia Shield TV Pro is now $299 – a $100 price hike seven years after the Android TV box launched. Nvidia almost singlehandedly caused the RAM crisis, so I think the company should be giving these away free, not increasing the price by 50%.

Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599. Oof, this one hurts.

Nothing will let you test new products early with its ‘Community Review’ program. This is how OnePlus got such a loyal following, and Carl Pei is doing it again with Nothing.

YouTube says Shorts recommendations won’t surface unoriginal content. I don’t really understand why this hasn’t always been the case.

Gemini app gains new ‘Map’ tool, replacing ‘/’ with ‘@’. /@/@/@/@

Google already rolling out Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 for Pixel. Big update, tiny changelog.

Here’s everything new in Android 17 QPR3 Beta 1 [Gallery]

Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think. It won’t be a popular decision, but it makes sense as Google prepares to widely release Gemini 4 Argon to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Pixel 12 series leak allegedly reveals model numbers, display specs, no wide Fold. Nothing interesting here except for the fact that Google doesn’t seem to be interested in following the wide foldable trend.

Fantastical’s long-awaited Android debut begins today on Googlebook. Flexibits is an Apple-first company, so it’s pretty interesting that it’s bringing Fantastical to Googlebook. I love this app so I’m pretty stoked that it’s going to come to Android proper next year, too.

Google Maps now lets you turn your car into a McLaren F1. Vroom, vroom.

🤝 Cc: Myriam Joire

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Myriam Joire (aka. @tnkgrl), a tech & car journalist and host of the Mobile Tech Podcast.

Who are you?

Myriam Joire (aka. @tnkgrl)

What do you do for work?

I’m a tech & car journalist, podcaster, product & media strategy consultant, speaker, and ex-game developer. I host the Mobile Tech Podcast.

What do you do for fun?

Listen to music, take photos, drive.

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

It’s complicated. I still very much love tech, but I strongly dislike the tech industry, tech bros, Silicon Valley’s greed, and the enshittification of tech.

What are three apps you can’t live without?

Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Photos. Sorry I’m boring (I’m not an app person).

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro, Google Pixel Watch 5, Oppo Find X9 Ultra, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8, Dell XPS 13.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

I mostly use Gemini, mostly for work, to brainstorm headlines for SEO, to create short review summaries, to summarize long documents, and to transcribe my podcast. I use AI photo editing tools (from Google/Samsung/Oppo/Xiaomi/Honor/Apple) for minor edits. I also use Auphonic to clean up audio for my podcast when traditional processing falls short.

What’s a recent book you loved, and why?

Tomboy Survival Guide by Ivan Coyote (because I’m a tomboy).

What’s a recent album you loved, and why?

Echoes — Ancient and Modern by Trevor Horn (because it features covers of artists I love, performed by artists I love, with Trevor Horn’s exquisite production work).

What’s a recent TV show you loved, and why?

Star City on Apple TV+ (because I enjoyed For All Mankind and The Man in the High Castle and generally like alternative universe stories).

What’s a recent movie you loved, and why?

Sinners (because of the vampires, non-white protagonists, and impeccable cinematography).

What’s a recent game you loved, and why?

I don’t play games beyond classics like Tetris (shhh, don’t tell anyone!) What kind of ex-game dev am I?

What’s something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

I walk to the coffee shop every morning after I wake up, get my Americano with cream in my own cup, and then sit (preferably outside) and enjoy drinking it while watching people.

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

I’ve been an Ember Mug user for years, despite being told by practically everyone that it’s a waste of money. But I can’t put a price on drinking perfect-temperature coffee on a busy Saturday morning.

The Ember Mug 3 has an upgrade I appreciate more than any other: you can put it in the dishwasher. The 14-ounce mug also lets you set the temperature directly on the mug, and Ember claims over three hours of battery life with the included sliding lid. It’s $150, so it remains an expensive answer to cooling coffee.

If you don’t need the additional battery life and waterproofing over the previous generation, the Ember Mug 2 is down to $100 right now for Prime Big Deal Days.

If you’ve never sat down for a Noclip documentary, you need to set aside a weekend or two to catch up. The studio has covered everything from classics like Half-Life and Dishonored to modern gems like Disco Elysium and Hades.

Now they’re back with a six-part series on Hades II, the first of which is available now. Supergiant Games feels like an anomaly in the gaming industry, a small, tight-knit studio based in San Francisco that makes ambitious, weird games that always seem to sell well. It’s a good news story in an industry that lacks a lot of it right now.

🤑 Action items

It’s Fall Prime Day (also known as Prime Big Deal Days), and I’ve been looking for headphone discounts.

The Nothing Headphone (1) is down to $189, its lowest price ever and a very good deal if you’re looking for great-sounding over-ear headphones. The Nothing (3) earbuds are also down to $99, far below their previous low of $129.

Most of Sony’s high-end headphones are on sale, including the WH-1000XM5s at $198, which matches their lowest price ever. The newer WH-1000XM6s are also down to their lowest price ever at $378, $20 lower than during Prime Day in June. And the WF-1000XM6 earbuds are at $258, also an all-time low. You can also get the same deals from Sony directly, if you’re into that.

Finally, the AirPods Pro 3 are down to $179, which is a great deal on the most popular earbuds on earth.

Inbox is taking a week off, so I’ll talk to you on October 15th. Thanks for reading, and have a great day.

-Daniel

title: These US states just said ‘no’ to Apple Wallet driver’s licenses
snippet: Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps expanding to more US states, but two states recently indicated they won’t launch support anytime soon—if at all.

Florida and Rhode Island won’t be getting Apple Wallet driver’s licenses anytime soon, per key leaders

The number of US states offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses keeps growing, and we even have a good idea of three states launching support soon.

Plenty of states likely intend to support digital driver’s licenses at some point, and haven’t gotten around to it. But there are two who recently indicated they have no plans to launch support.

Those two states are:

Florida

Rhode Island

Last week, Florida rolled out a brand new driver’s license and ID card. Many states take such occasions to launch digital versions too, but the state made zero announcements around digital ID.

That’s no coincidence, as Governor Ron DeSantis actively opposes the idea of digital driver’s licenses. He posted the following on X last November:

The convenience of a digital drivers license is outweighed by the potential for government to abuse it.  

Not gonna happen in FL.  

No digital ID. https://t.co/YD7J6PtBgR

— Ron DeSantis (@RonDeSantis) November 28, 2025

Florida previously did offer a digital ID but abruptly ended support in 2024. Perhaps the next governor will take a different stance.

In Rhode Island, Walter “Bud” Craddock was on a podcast last week discussing mobile driver’s licenses (“MDL”). Craddock is currently Chair of the American Association of Motor Vehicle Administrators (AAMVA) International Board of Directors.

	

Here’s what he said:

“I want to see more universal adoption or need for an MDL. I had one of my senators approach and try to talk me into doing it. I had to give him the old Heisman move and push him back…the main user right now is TSA. Up until recently, there was no airport in New England area that could accept an MDL. So why would I spend the money in the development of it? And also, I’m looking to do a solution that is across all platforms. Instead of just doing one for Apple or the Google Wallets, I don’t want to replicate and duplicate efforts.”

Like DeSantis, Craddock’s position of leadership is slated to end in the next few months. So depending on his successor’s stance, perhaps Rhode Island could get Apple Wallet driver’s licenses sometime in 2027.

Here’s the full list of US states currently offering Apple Wallet driver’s licenses, and three expected to launch next.

fullText:
I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.

The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.

The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.

People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights

Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.

Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”

1/6

How Telo was born

Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.

Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”

— Telo cofounder Forrest North

Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.

“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.

1/5Forrest North, left, and Jason Marks were initially going to build an electric motorcycle — until a number of investors expressed interest in a different concept: a tiny electric truck. 

Battery, range, and layout

For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.

Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.

For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range

I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.

The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.

How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks

Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.

Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.

“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.

“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”

The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety

AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.

Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.

“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”

Pricing, delivery, and other features

The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.

North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”

Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.

Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.

Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.

Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”

While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

Abigail Bassett
excerpt:
I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.

The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

title: Review: Rhinoshield’s iPhone 18 Pro bumper case is minimalist but surprisingly protective
snippet: iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case. more…
fullText:
iPhone bumper cases have been a fan-favorite since the iPhone 4 bumpers, but options these days are few and far between. Rhinoshield offers a decent option for those wanting a minimal case.

Apple finally got back into the bumper business with the iPhone Air last year. I was hoping Apple would expand their bumper case to the iPhone 18 Pro (like they did with the clear case and iPhone 11), but unfortunately they did not. In my search for another option, I came across Rhinoshield’s Minimalist Impact Bumper case. 

Key Details

The Impact Bumper Case has a fit similar to most other bumpers, where the lip on the screen is fairly minor, while the lip on the back is a little larger. A unique feature of this case, and one that I quite like, is that it has special supports that keep the camera plateau and lenses off of wherever your phone is resting, which I particularly appreciate considering the aluminum 17 Pro and 18 Pro. This results in a far more protective case than your typical bumper would be. It also eliminates the annoying wobble when using your phone on a flat surface.

The case’s fit, however, is not quite what I was hoping for. It’s somewhat loose, and you can easily bend the edges outward, and I do wonder if over time they may end up getting stretched out. I don’t think the phone flying out of the case when dropped will be an issue though (and I have unintentionally tested that). That said, the material of the entire case is a hard plastic rather than rubber, so hopefully it will be fine in the long run. Rhinoshield says that it is made entirely of just one material, and is therefore 100% recyclable.

The case comes in three colors, which are matched to the iPhone 18 Pro colors: white, blue, and black (sorry Burgundy fans). The blue, which is what I have, is close to Glacier but not perfect. 

Downsides

There are some downsides, however. My primary gripe with the case is that the buttons can be hard to press. For some reason they went with a nearly flush design, and the way that the buttons are designed makes them mushy. 

The material choice as a whole may be a downside. To me, it feels cheaper than the likes of Apple’s iPhone Air bumper, but some may end up preferring it. I certainly prefer it to the materials of a typical TPU/rubber clear case. The material and loose design also seem to attract pocket dust.

If you use Apple’s Wrist Strap or Crossbody Strap, be aware that this case does not have the required loop connection points. 

Conclusion

The Rhinoshield bumper is definitely not perfect, and I still hope that Apple will extend their bumpers to other iPhones. In the end though, I have decided to keep the case, for one primary reason: it lets me have a near-caseless experience without worry of the fragile aluminum getting chipped or dented. As far as I can tell, the bumper case is usually only available from their own website, so the price of about $30 matches the price of Apple’s ($39) after shipping. You can get the Rhinoshield Minimalist Impact Bumper case here. (Occasionally, an Amazon listing will pop up, so you can give that a try as well.)

title: Googlebooks don’t have the same web app or Linux app support as Chromebooks
snippet: Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either. more…
fullText:
Googlebooks don’t have the same level of web app support as Chromebooks, as only “compliant” apps can be installed, and that’s not the only regression from ChromeOS, as Linux apps don’t work in the same way either.

Googlebooks rely on Android apps and web apps for virtually all core functionality, with the Play Store actively directing users to which app is the most ideal on the platform. 

As it turns out, though, support for Progressive Web Apps on Googlebook isn’t quite at the same level as Chromebook. While most PWAs we’ve tried so far are easily installed, we ran into an issue installing the Slack PWA. Google, in a statement today, confirmed this is because Slack is not a “compliant” PWA, with Chromebooks instead relying on “manual installation.” It’s unclear what differs regarding Slack’s PWA — it functions just fine on other platforms such as Windows and ChromeOS — but it can’t be installed on Googlebook or Android devices.

Google says:

	

Installing PWAs is fully supported on Googlebooks. But, the Slack web app isn’t a compliant PWA. Chrome on ChromeOS allows manual installation even though it’s not a PWA. This capability will also be coming to Chrome on Googlebooks soon.

This mirrors another regression in app support compared to Chromebooks.

Googlebooks also, at least for now, lack the same level of Linux app support.

Chromebooks started adding support for installing Linux apps way back in 2018 and, after a few years in development, it became a secret super power of Google’s platform. Linux app support on Chromebook allowed users to bridge the app gap with the ability to install full desktop apps via Linux ports and, while it wasn’t the easiest process, it got the job done.

Googlebooks are in a very different state.

There’s little to no documentation around Linux apps on Googlebook right now, with Google’s only page on the matter describing how you can use the Terminal app to access a Debian command line interface. Google says:

You can use the Terminal app to access a powerful Debian Linux command-line environment directly on your Googlebook. You can install and run developer tools, code environments, and access other Linux applications. It expands your device’s capabilities for advanced tasks and software development.

But installing apps via this portal doesn’t put them within easy reach of the end user. It’s a far cry from Chromebook’s support, which placed most apps within the app drawer once they were installed. 

	

Google says that it’s possible to run apps, but that GUI apps “aren’t the main focus” of the Linux environment on Googlebook:

Just wanted to confirm that yes, there will be a Terminal app available on Googlebook out of the box, and yes it lets you run a Debian Linux environment on your device.

Also yes, you CAN run Linux GUI apps in this environment, but note that for this initial release of Googlebook, GUI apps aren’t the main focus. We’ll have more to share soon on the Terminal app!

One Linux user far more experienced than myself who dug into how Googlebook supports Linux apps, detailing that they show up in a single Terminal display window without their own Android windows or taskbar items. Another user saw the same behavior and noted reliability issues with GIMP, a popular photo editing app for Linux.

As mentioned, there’s no documentation yet on how to get Linux GUI apps running on Googlebook, so this is not functionality for the “average Joe” — not to say Linux apps on Chromebook were either, but it’s certainly odd to see that this has regressed in functionality rather than expanded.

title: Pixel 11 series still not on Android 17 QPR1 with October update
snippet: With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1. more…
fullText:
With yesterday’s October 2026 update, the Pixel 11 series is not yet running Android 17 QPR1.

The Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold launched in August with the base Android 17 release. In September, the Pixel 11 series received two early updates that presumably addressed issues that emerged since launch. 

	

Later in the month, Google rolled out QPR1 to all other devices. Visual changes in the quarterly release include system blur for the volume slider and power menu, while there’s an updated system media player that gets narrower when other apps are available. The Mobile Data Quick Settings Tile gets a time-saving “Don’t ask me again” toggle, while there’s now a Keyboard QS Tile.

Meanwhile, the Pixel 11 series did not get the initial Android 17 QPR2 Beta 6 release and had to wait a few days for Beta 6.1, which introduced HiLight support for message notifications. It did get the 17 QPR3 Beta without issue a few days later. 

	

This week’s October release does contain fixes for the Pixel 11:

Fix for issue causing the virtual keyboard to occasionally not appear when interacting with search input fields*[1]

Fix for issue occasionally causing captured photos or recorded videos to save in the incorrect orientation*[3]

It’s unlikely that we’ll get a second October release, with all eyes on November. With QPR2 just a month away at that point, Google might wait for December to align all the devices.

title: Call Screening has made a big difference to my iPhone experience
snippet: iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier. Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls … more…
fullText:
iOS 27 has brought a lot of new features to the iPhone, but one of the things that has made the biggest difference to my experience of the device as a phone actually dates back a year earlier.

Apple introduced Call Screening to the Phone app in iOS 26, but I only started using it a few months ago – and the feature has protected me from a growing number of spam and spam calls …

I’ve tried to be reasonably protective of my phone number, only providing it when it is not only demanded by an organization, but where I accept that it will be useful for them to have it. In many cases where a web form insists on it, I’ve used a fictitious number.

The UK’s telecoms regulator actually provides a range of 1,000 mobile numbers that have never been allocated so I can be sure my fake number won’t lead to someone else being spammed.

However, I’ve owned my mobile number for literally decades now, so it’s unavoidable that it has made its way onto some marketing lists, and there are also companies that use robocallers to dial random numbers. I haven’t been bothered by many of these historically, but for some reason there was a significant uptick earlier this year.

When Apple introduced the call screening feature last year, I was concerned about missing genuine calls, so didn’t immediately enable it. However, I did so earlier this year, selecting the Ask Reason for Calling option, and I have to say I highly recommend it.

	

The main spam/scam calls I received were from companies pretending to be my mobile carrier. I think some are likely third-party resellers hoping to trick me into switching network, while others are either trying to obtain payment details or carry out more general data harvesting. I’ve never let any of these calls get far enough to find out, but it reached the point where I was getting at least one of these calls every week. I’d also been getting a growing number of job scam calls.

Since switching on the feature, not a single one of these has got through to me. I think in the vast majority of cases, they immediately hang up when they get the automated response, while a few of them have bothered to give me their claimed reason for the call, and it’s been immediately obvious that I should reject it.

I also haven’t seen any indication of anyone genuine failing to reach me. I’ve had a number of genuine calls get filtered by the screening feature, but all of these have explained who they are and the reason for the call, and I’ve then been able to answer it.

If you don’t currently have Call Screening enabled, I highly recommend it. Open the Settings app, scroll down to the App section, select Phone, and then scroll down to Screen Unknown Callers.

title: Apple may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU in a tax compromise
snippet: Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan. The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House … more…
fullText:
Apple and other tech giants may have to pay an annual lump sum to the EU under a modified version of a digital services tax plan.

The EU hopes a revised version of earlier proposals will enable it to raise tax revenues without incurring the wrath of the White House …

There has long been debate within EU countries about taxes on digital services, with Apple examples including iCloud, Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Creator Studio, and more.

Some point to the significant revenues earned from selling subscription services to EU citizens without necessarily paying any tax in Europe on these receipts. Others are concerned that a digital tax could disproportionately hit European companies, while yet others are concerned about threatened retaliation by the White House for additional taxes on US companies.

The Financial Times reports that the European Commission has now come up with a compromise it hopes will keep everybody happy – other than the companies like Apple, Google and Meta who would be paying the new taxes, of course.

Brussels was considering changes to an existing proposal that would require all companies operating in the EU with revenue of more than €100mn a year to pay an annual lump-sum tax contribution, the officials said […] 

Adjusting the thresholds and contributions under the Core proposal to cover only very large corporates would both increase the amount raised from tech groups and defuse criticism in Europe that Core would hit many medium-sized European companies, officials argued.

The revised version of the plan would not single out companies selling digital services, but would apply to all large corporations. Since it was the former proposal that led the White House to threaten retaliatory tariffs, the EU hopes that the new version won’t provoke a new trade war with the US.

	

The amount that would be levied on each company has not yet been decided. The plan is to seek agreement on the principle across the 27 EU countries before setting a rate for the tax.

9to5Mac’s Take

This whole mess was supposed to have been resolved by a global agreement, brokered by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). This would have ensured that all companies worldwide pay at least some taxes in each of the countries in which they operate, and the plan had Apple’s support.

However, Donald Trump withdrew the US from this agreement, leading to calls for an EU-specific version. The idea that Trump won’t object to the revised plan seems to me rather optimistic.

title: Everything We Expect From Apple’s Surprise Smart Home Event Next Week
snippet: Here’s what will reportedly be announced at Apple’s Welcome Home event, and what we think is unlikely.
fullText:
We now have confirmation of Apple’s massive ‘Welcome Home” smart home event happening on Tuesday. Invitations went out on Thursday with a distinctive rainbow-colored Apple logo. So many things are expected to be announced, centering on Apple and Siri entering the home tech space in all-new ways. The tech giant’s smart home devices will face serious competition from Amazon, Google and other players.

Over the past few weeks, I’ve been collecting the reports, insider claims and possible leaks to see just what Apple could be announcing. It all points to a major shake-up for home security, smart home devices and how Siri AI can be used. CNET will be there in person to see what Apple has cooked up, but in the meantime, here are the latest rumors.

A representative from Apple didn’t respond to a request for comment.

			

More from CNET

A Siri smart display at last

An Apple smart display could allow Siri to get much more creative.Bloomberg/Contributor/Getty

For more than a year, Apple has been rumored to be readying a Siri-focused smart display hub for the home, sometimes referred to as a HomePad, though we don’t know for sure that’ll be the name. This display would focus heavily on Siri AI and compete with products like Amazon’s Echo Show and the Google Nest Hub line by acting as a HomeKit hub.

Smart displays can add a lot of functionality to smart speakers, if you don’t mind using voice assistants. Rumors suggest the display could swivel and/or be attached to a wall, be at least several inches wide and allow Siri to recognize different people in a conversation. In terms of size, we’ve heard rumors putting it around 6 inches, with the screen attached to a HomePod-like speaker and powered by regular AC power rather than USB-C.

Smart touchscreens are great for getting visual information, watching videos or viewing to-do lists, so a display like this is likely to have a bit of Apple TV and Safari in it, too. While the Apple TV 4K, iPad and current HomePod models can already act as HomeKit hubs, I expect Apple to offer a real UI and UX experience designed for smart displays, making it a stronger argument for having in your home alongside other devices.

Is it likely? I think it’s quite likely, based on how many insider reports have mentioned this smart display, but I don’t think we have a good idea how it will look yet. 

Updates to the HomePod line

Is a new HomePod Mini on the way?Chris Monroe/CNET

Along with a smart display, rumors are flying that Apple will give its HomePod smart speaker line the first major update in years. It’s the ideal time to update the HomePod line, too, although it’s possible some of these reports have confused plans for a smart display with a new smart speaker, both of which could fall under the HomePod label.

If a new HomePod speaker is on the horizon, reports indicate that it would be a new type of HomePod Mini. That’s not surprising — the original HomePod has often been critiqued for being over $300, which is why Apple focused on the less expensive Mini model afterward. One welcome leak I’ve seen is that there will be new colors for the HomePod Mini 2, including green and pink, and a faster S-series chip.

Is it likely? Yes, I’d say this is about as likely as a Siri smart display, if Apple wants to continue developing the HomePod line. 

A new Apple TV

Apple TV is due for an upgrade, too.Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The same reports that say a smart display and new HomePod are on the way also mention Apple is planning to release a new Apple TV model. This model is rumored to have upgraded specs, with a faster N1 processor, 8GB RAM, Wi-Fi 7 and an upgraded Siri remote.

It’s a product line that’s sort of connected to the smart home, especially if Apple is launching a smart display. The company hasn’t released a new set-top box since 2022, so it’s about time for another. This could also give the Apple TV new hardware for extra Siri AI tricks. There’s also been some speculation that this will be compatible with the new HomePods, allowing you to set up multiple units in a surround sound-style home cinema. 

Is it likely? I think it’s less likely than a speaker or display. It’s not quite as much of a smart home gadget, and it seems to have gotten swept into the wide net of rumors, but without as many reports.

Little Apple security cams — with no recording

Recent rumors says Apple is ready to enter the home security world with its own products. Although we don’t know much, reports from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman say these will be tiny cameras that, interestingly, won’t record any video. No recording means Apple won’t have to worry about cloud storage and may be able to avoid charging extra subscriptions for them.

The cameras are rumored to have some kind of presence-sensing or human-recognizing technology as well as AI video descriptions, suggesting Apple Home will be running analysis on the video even if it won’t record permanently. The phrase “facial recognition” was also mentioned, but this doesn’t seem nearly as likely to me. This may be related to a rumor about Apple’s Ring-like doorbell camera, which may come with Face ID for unlocking a door, but this would likely be separate from the non-recording indoor security cameras.

Is it likely? I’m betting on some kind of home security announcement, and I expect Apple would like to have its own camera line, but I don’t know if this exact product will be released. However, the extra details do lend this rumor legitimacy.

An LG collab for a new thermostat

Apple may be partnering with LG for some smart home devices, and there are even reportedly leaked product concept photos circulating on the internet. One of the biggest potential releases is an Apple-friendly thermostat. The photos show a round, Nest-like thermostat dial, and rumors say it will include far-sight presence sensing, a humidity sensor and several temperature calibration options.

2. LG Smart Thermostat

•  Settings for Far Sight Display, Humidity Display, Brightness, Language.

•  Calibrated Temperature/Temperature Offset options. pic.twitter.com/Q8AAaxy4ey

— pdfu (@itspdfu) October 7, 2026

Alongside the thermostat, the Apple/LG combo is expected to release a sensor that can measure the temperature at specific locations and feed that information back to the thermostat hub. That would be no surprise, because models from Nest, Ecobee and others have similar satellite sensors, although Apple’s may have adhesive strips to attach its version to the wall.

Apple partnered with LG years ago to support Apple-friendly security cameras, but those lines were rarely updated and quickly became obsolete. Maybe Apple is ready to try again with a different approach.

Is it likely? If Apple really is partnering with LG for a new wave of home devices, I think a thermostat is likely. But this is starting to be a lot of products to announce at a single October event that won’t be publicly streamed. 

Further LG collabs for smart lock and maybe more 

The other big rumor centering around an LG collaboration is an Apple smart lock. While many smart locks work with Apple and Apple Home Keys, the tech giant hasn’t been involved in the development of a smart lock before. 

It could have automatic unlocking, tapping your phone to unlock and a variety of keypad management options. That’s not surprising, but the rumored product images show a round, twist-to-unlock, light-up outdoor keypad, and I haven’t seen anything like that before.

If Apple does release a smart lock, Ring will have beaten it to the punch with its own announcement of its first-ever lock, which will include Alexa compatibility and a unique thumbturn that can generate a charge when the battery dies.

EXCLUSIVE 👀

First look at LG’s upcoming smart home lineup:

LG Video Doorbell Wired

LG Floodlight Cam

LG Outdoor Cam Plug-In

LG Indoor Cam Plug-In pic.twitter.com/vblGECQLM1

— そすのふか (@ringo_tech) October 7, 2026

Other rumors and purported product images suggest the LG partnership could also yield a video doorbell, floodlight camera, outdoor camera and indoor camera. These seem to be LG-branded devices, however, and I can’t imagine Apple releasing products that look like this. 

Is it likely? Now this is a lot of new gadgets to announce at once. I think a smart lock is about as likely as a smart thermostat; those are both strong fields for Apple to enter. For the rest of the cameras, I’m doubtful. The indoor camera could be connected to the rumors of Apple’s no-video model. If the LG partnership line is this large, I wouldn’t be surprised if Apple is saving it for a separate announcement later on.

What role will Apple Intelligence play in all this?

Apple Intelligence will fuel many Siri AI capabilities in the Apple Home app. That’s especially true of AI video descriptions, which Apple is bringing to supported security cameras (there are very few right now, but some of Aqara’s camera hubs are compatible). I’m testing these uses of Apple Intelligence now, but if Apple releases any of its own security cameras, you can bet they’ll use AI features in the same way.

Will there be any iPad news at this event?

There are rumors that Apple will announce an iPad Mini sometime this month, but it probably doesn’t have much to do with this event. This is a strictly smart home-focused release.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: You can unlock a Googlebook’s bootloader, Magisk support in the works
snippet: Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works. more…
fullText:
Googlebook is an Android-based platform and, with that, comes the potential to do a bit more with it. Google has confirmed you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook, and now Magisk root support is already in the works.

On a support page, Google details how you can unlock the bootloader on a Googlebook. Google says that a “developer or advanced user can unlock their device’s bootloader to install a custom version of the operating system or test an app,” but stresses that “most users don’t need to unlock their Googlebook’s bootloader.”

Like on a Pixel or other Android phone that easily supports bootloader unlock, you’ll need to enable OEM unlocking via the Settings menu and Developer options, then press and hold Esc + F2 and press the power button, releasing all keys when the screen lights up. From there, bootloader unlock is located under “advanced options.”

And, with that, root support is also coming.

	

Magisk developer John Wu confirmed on Twitter/X that support for Magisk is in the works for Googlebook. In a separate post, Wu called Googlebook “the ideal platform for Android modding” since modern Android smartphones suffer from broken apps including banking apps when they are rooted. Wu says that there are some tweaks needed to bring Magisk and, in turn, all of the benefits that come with a rooted device to Googlebook, but it’s coming.

title: Google rolling out ‘massive’ Pixel Buds Pro 2 and 2a update [U]
snippet: Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update. more…
fullText:
Following last month’s addition of Gemini control, Google is rolling out a sizable Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a firmware update.

Update 10/7: Google has reached out to clarify that these updates are only for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a. The original Pixel Buds Pro, which has since been removed from the announcement, are not getting these new features.

The only feature exclusive to the Pixel Buds Pro 2 is Dynamic Active Noise Cancellation. Google will “automatically adjust audio or noise cancellation based on your ear seal.” This compensates for “subtle shifts” when the buds move in your ear.

The remaining features are available for the Pixel Buds Pro 2 (2024) and 2a (2025). When these features were previewed in August, Google did not mention that the original Pro model would be getting this update.

	

With last month’s Pixel Buds companion app update, you can turn on Active Noise Cancellation, adjust EQ, and enable touch controls with Gemini voice commands.

	

During phone calls, Tap to Mute lets you mute and unmute the microphone by tapping the buds. This gesture requires a paired Pixel phone.

Pixel Buds can now auto-pause media playback when you fall asleep, which is determined by Pixel Watch sleep sensing. This will also disable touch gestures and silence notifications.

The final update is Enhanced Live Translate that allows you to “leave your phone in your pocket and start translating instantly with a simple touch on your earbuds.”

Whether you’re conversing with someone or using listening mode to stay aware of your surroundings in a foreign language, Pixel Buds work seamlessly with the Google Translate app to make on-the-go translation easier than ever.

Make sure you’re running the latest version of the Pixel Buds app, and be on the lookout for software release_6.144. Open the companion client and scroll down for More settings > Firmware update to check.

title: iOS 27.2 gives Apple Books new design updates as iPhone Duo nears
snippet: Apple Books is my favorite app for reading, and it’s getting several welcome design updates in iOS 27.2. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Apple Books is my favorite app for reading, and it’s getting several welcome design updates in iOS 27.2. Here’s what’s new.

Here’s what’s changed in Apple Books with iOS 27.2 beta 3

New Apple Books menu (left) and old (right)

Likely in anticipation of iPhone Duo proving a great device for reading, Apple has several design updates coming soon for its Books app.

iOS 27.2 beta 3 introduces the changes, all of which involve the reading experience itself.

When reading a book, iOS 27.2 brings the following design updates:

Progress bars are now available to track your reading location

Menu in the bottom-right has a new three-dot icon and it’s redesigned into a standard Liquid Glass menu for consistency with other apps

Bookmark has been removed from that menu and now lives in the upper-right as a standalone button

‘X’ button has moved to the upper-left corner

title: Apple’s MacBook Pro overhaul is coming soon, here’s what to expect
snippet: Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. more…
fullText:
Apple just released a MacBook Pro update in March, but there’s more coming soon. Apple is expected to debut one of its biggest MacBook Pro updates ever as soon as later this year. Here’s everything we know so far … including details on a surprising recent twist. 

9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Sony is running a massive sale on its best BRAVIA TVs, ranging from its entry-level to flagship options — shop now to save! 

New MacBook Pro features

OLED display

The new MacBook Pro will switch from mini-LED to OLED display technology. This will mark the first time Apple has used OLED in a Mac, having previously used it on the iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch. This has been reported by sources including Ming-Chi Kuo and Bloomberg.

The MacBook Pro’s rumored OLED display would offer true blacks, higher contrast, and potentially more vibrant colors compared to today’s mini-LED screens. That’s because OLED can turn individual pixels completely off, while mini-LED still relies on a backlight system.

Touchscreen

OLED isn’t the only big display change coming with the refreshed MacBook Pro, though. It will also be Apple’s first-ever touchscreen Mac.

As reported by Bloomberg, Apple is optimizing macOS to take advantage of the MacBook Pro’s touchscreen. For example, when you touch a button or a control, macOS will dynamically adjust to show you relevant touch controls. If you tap on the menu bar, controls will automatically enlarge to make it easier to navigate with your finger.

It will also support common touch interface interaction methods, like pinching and zooming, and faster scrolling.

So, it’s a lot more than Apple simply adding a touchscreen to a Mac. It’s a rethink of macOS to make touch navigation feel fluid and natural.

Dynamic Island

Currently, the MacBook Pro features a notch cutout that houses the FaceTime camera. With this year’s MacBook Pro, however, Apple will reportedly ditch the notch in favor of a hole-punch cutout for the camera.

Additionally, Apple is planning to bring the Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. This will likely work like the iPhone, where the Dynamic Island masks the cutout for the FaceTime camera and displays software interface elements such as Live Activities and notifications.

Thinner and lighter design

With the 2021 MacBook Pro, Apple reversed course and made it thicker than its predecessor. It also added back ports, including MagSafe, HDMI, and an SD card slot. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro’s industrial design famously had only four USB-C ports.

This year, however, Apple is reportedly planning to make the MacBook Pro thinner once again. We don’t have any specifics on this just yet, and it’s unclear whether Apple will remove any ports to accommodate this change.

One key difference nowadays is Apple Silicon. The 2016-2020 MacBook Pro models used Intel chips that were less efficient than Apple’s own M-series chips. Apple Silicon should mean Apple can make the MacBook Pro thinner without compromising on those things.

The new MacBook Pro will also be “significantly” lighter than its predecessor, according to Mark Gurman: 

But there is one other major difference, I’m told: The new MacBook Pros are lighter — significantly lighter. Apple has reengineered the machine’s interior, miniaturizing parts and rearranging components to make the computer much easier to carry.

M5

It was widely expected that the new MacBook Pro models would be powered by the M6 Pro and M6 Max chips. 

In a new twist, however, it sounds like this update will actually use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chips as the current MacBook Pro models. 

The decision comes as Apple is reportedly skipping higher-end chips in the forthcoming M6 generation. Instead, the M6 will be available only in its base configuration, with no M6 Pro, M6 Max, or M6 Ultra variants. 

Apple is shifting its focus to the M7 generation, including the M7 Pro and M7 Max chips. These will reportedly focus on significant improvements to AI performance. 

MacBook Ultra?

Finally, it wouldn’t be an Apple rumor cycle without speculation about naming.

Mark Gurman has speculated that Apple might brand these laptops as MacBook Ultra. This name would “more clearly signal their position at the top of the lineup,” he reasoned.

The latest development that the new MacBook models will use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips adds a new wrinkle to the marketing decisions Apple will have to make. 

New MacBook Pro release date

Apple is expected to debut the new MacBook Pro lineup in October or November. It may seem weird that Apple would update the MacBook Pro twice this year, but it’s not unprecedented.

Wrap up

title: Apple, Prosser, and Ramacciotti trade blame over delays in trade secret lawsuit
snippet: In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a joint status report made public earlier today, Apple said it is still waiting on additional documents from Jon Prosser and wants to depose Michael Ramacciotti again, while both defendants pushed back on the company’s handling of the case. Here are the details.

According to a joint status report to Judge James Donato, Apple, leaker Jon Prosser, and Michael Ramacciotti are increasingly at odds over who is responsible for delays in the trade secret lawsuit Apple filed against both defendants in July 2025.

A bit of context

As a refresher, soon after announcing iOS 26, Apple filed a trade secret misappropriation lawsuit against Prosser and Ramacciotti over Prosser’s videos, where he leaked aspects of the system, including what turned out to be the Liquid Glass visual revamp.

Apple said Ramacciotti improperly accessed the development iPhone of an employee, who was later fired over the incident, and held a FaceTime call with Prosser to show him unreleased iOS features running on the device.

Since then, the case has had its own share of drama, with the clerk’s entry of default after Prosser failed to respond to Apple’s complaint by the deadline (although Prosser has disputed the characterization that he had ignored the case).

Then, eight months later, the court agreed to set that default aside and give him another chance to formally contest the allegations.

Court documents show that Ramacciotti, on the other hand, responded to Apple’s complaint and has largely cooperated with the company’s discovery requests.

Since Prosser retained representation and formally entered the case, however, things have taken a turn, with all three sides increasingly disagreeing over who is responsible for the alleged trade secret disclosure and for the delays that have followed.

The new joint status report

Back to the new status report, Apple says it wants Ramacciotti to update his interrogatory responses and sit for another deposition to address what it describes as “inconsistencies between his and Mr. Prosser’s testimony.”

Ramacciotti, however, says he will sit for another deposition once Apple provides “a roadmap to resolution of its claims against him, including what more, if anything, Apple needs from him.”

When it comes to Prosser, Apple says it “continues to await his production of certain additional documents that it requested over three months ago. These include revenue reports and data analytics for his YouTube channels and relevant communications with third parties that he identified during his deposition.”

Prosser, in turn, argues that “[i]t appears that the Trade Secrets at issue are no longer trade secrets and are in the public domain.” In other words, his argument appears to be that since Apple released the iOS update with Liquid Glass, the information at the center of the lawsuit is now publicly available and therefore no longer qualifies as secret.

As part of the joint status update, Ramacciotti asks the court to hold a status conference this month, at which Apple would be required to explain what additional information it still needs from him. He also wants Apple to then have 30 days to either dismiss its claims against him or commit to taking the case to trial.

Apple, meanwhile, wants discovery to continue, including a second deposition of Ramacciotti and the outstanding documents from Prosser. Prosser argues that he has already complied with the discovery obligations he agreed to and pushes back on Apple’s continuing requests for additional material.

If Judge Donato does not grant Ramacciotti’s request for a status conference, the parties propose filing another joint status report on December 2.
